{{ssp|section-pauses}}
==Rules for inserting pauses==
{{ind|general-imported|pauses|rules for}} Summarized in one place, here are the rules for inserting pauses between Lojban words:
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|between words}}  {{ind|general-imported|pause|proscribed within words}} Any two words may have a pause between them; it is always illegal to pause in the middle of a word, because that breaks up the word into two words.
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|and consonant-final words}}  {{ind|general-imported|consonant-final words|necessity for pause after}} Every word ending in a consonant must be followed by a pause. Necessarily, all such words are cmene.
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|and vowel-initial words}}  {{ind|general-imported|vowel-initial words|necessity for pause before}} Every word beginning with a vowel must be preceded by a pause. Such words are either cmavo, fu'ivla, or cmene; all gismu and lujvo begin with consonants.
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|and cmene}}  {{ind|general-imported|cmene|rules for pause before}} Every cmene must be preceded by a pause, unless the immediately preceding word is one of the cmavo {{vla|la}}, {{vla|lai}}, {{vla|la'i}}, or {{vla|doi}} (which is why those strings are forbidden in cmene). However, the situation triggering this rule rarely occurs.
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|and final-syllable stress}}  {{ind|general-imported|final syllable stress|rules for pause after}}  {{ind|general-imported|stress|final syllable|rules for pause after}} If the last syllable of a word bears the stress, and a brivla follows, the two must be separated by a pause, to prevent confusion with the primary stress of the brivla. In this case, the first word must be either a cmavo or a cmene with unusual stress (which already ends with a pause, of course).
* {{ind|general-imported|pause|and Cy-form cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|cmavo|rules for pause after Cy-form}}  {{ind|general-imported|Cy-form cmavo|rules for pause after}} A cmavo of the form “Cy” must be followed by a pause unless another “Cy”-form cmavo follows.
* {{ind|general-imported|non-Lojban text|rules for pause with}}  {{ind|general-imported|pause|and non-Lojban text}} When non-Lojban text is embedded in Lojban, it must be preceded and followed by pauses. (How to embed non-Lojban text is explained in 
{{ls|section-more-quotations}}.)



{{ssp|section-lujvo-considerations}}
==Considerations for making lujvo==
Given a tanru which expresses an idea to be used frequently, it can be turned into a lujvo by following the lujvo-making algorithm which is given in {{ls|section-lujvo-making}}.

In building a lujvo, the first step is to replace each gismu with a rafsi that uniquely represents that gismu. These rafsi are then attached together by fixed rules that allow the resulting compound to be recognized as a single word and to be analyzed in only one way.

There are three other complications; only one is serious.

{{ind|general-imported|rafsi|multiple for each gismu}} The first is that there is usually more than one rafsi that can be used for each gismu. The one to be used is simply whichever one sounds or looks best to the speaker or writer. There are usually many valid combinations of possible rafsi. They all are equally valid, and all of them mean exactly the same thing. (The scoring algorithm given in {{ls|section-lujvo-scoring}} is used to choose the standard form of the lujvo &ndash; the version which would be entered into a dictionary.)

{{ind|general-imported|linguistic drift in Lojban|possible source of}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|consideration in choosing meaning for}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|unambiguity of}} The second complication is the serious one. Remember that a tanru is ambiguous &ndash; it has several possible meanings. A lujvo, or at least one that would be put into the dictionary, has just a single meaning. Like a gismu, a lujvo is a predicate which encompasses one area of the semantic universe, with one set of places. Hopefully the meaning chosen is the most useful of the possible semantic spaces. A possible source of linguistic drift in Lojban is that as Lojbanic society evolves, the concept that seems the most useful one may change.

{{ind|general-imported|za'e|use to avoid lujvo misunderstandings}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|meaning drift of}} You must also be aware of the possibility of some prior meaning of a new lujvo, especially if you are writing for posterity. If a lujvo is invented which involves the same tanru as one that is in the dictionary, and is assigned a different meaning (or even just a different place structure), linguistic drift results. This isn't necessarily bad. Every natural language does it. But in communication, when you use a meaning different from the dictionary definition, someone else may use the dictionary and therefore misunderstand you. You can use the cmavo 
{{vla|za'e}} (explained in 
{{ls|section-bahe}}) before a newly coined lujvo to indicate that it may have a non-dictionary meaning.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|ultimate guideline for choice of meaning/place-structure}} The essential nature of human communication is that if the listener understands, then all is well. Let this be the ultimate guideline for choosing meanings and place structures for invented lujvo.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|dropping elements of}}  {{ind|general-imported|Zipf's Law}} The third complication is also simple, but tends to scare new Lojbanists with its implications. It is based on Zipf's Law, which says that the length of words is inversely proportional to their usage. The shortest words are those which are used more; the longest ones are used less. Conversely, commonly used concepts will be tend to be abbreviated. In English, we have abbreviations and acronyms and jargon, all of which represent complex ideas that are used often by small groups of people, so they shortened them to convey more information more rapidly.

Therefore, given a complicated tanru with grouping markers, abstraction markers, and other cmavo in it to make it syntactically unambiguous, the psychological basis of Zipf's Law may compel the lujvo-maker to drop some of the cmavo to make a shorter (technically incorrect) tanru, and then use that tanru to make the lujvo.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|based on multiple tanru}} This doesn't lead to ambiguity, as it might seem to. A given lujvo still has exactly one meaning and place structure. It is just that more than one tanru is competing for the same lujvo. But more than one meaning for the tanru was already competing for the “right” to define the meaning of the lujvo. Someone has to use judgment in deciding which one meaning is to be chosen over the others.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|shorter for more general concepts}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|considerations for retaining elements of}} If the lujvo made by a shorter form of tanru is in use, or is likely to be useful for another meaning, the decider then retains one or more of the cmavo, preferably ones that set this meaning apart from the shorter form meaning that is used or anticipated. As a rule, therefore, the shorter lujvo will be used for a more general concept, possibly even instead of a more frequent word. If both words are needed, the simpler one should be shorter. It is easier to add a cmavo to clarify the meaning of the more complex term than it is to find a good alternate tanru for the simpler term.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|and plausibility}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|and the listener}} And of course, we have to consider the listener. On hearing an unknown word, the listener will decompose it and get a tanru that makes no sense or the wrong sense for the context. If the listener realizes that the grouping operators may have been dropped out, he or she may try alternate groupings, or try inserting an abstraction operator if that seems plausible. (The grouping of tanru is explained in {{lch|chapter-selbri}}; abstraction is explained in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}.) Plausibility is the key to learning new ideas and to evaluating unfamiliar lujvo.

{{ssp|section-lujvo-making}}
==The lujvo-making algorithm==
{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|algorithm for}} The following is the current algorithm for generating Lojban lujvo given a known tanru and a complete list of gismu and their assigned rafsi. The algorithm was designed by Bob LeChevalier and Dr. James Cooke Brown for computer program implementation. It was modified in 1989 with the assistance of Nora LeChevalier, who detected a flaw in the original “tosmabru test”.

Given a tanru that is to be made into a lujvo:
*Choose a 3-letter or 4-letter rafsi for each of the gismu and cmavo in the tanru except the last.
*Choose a 3-letter (CVV-form or CCV-form) or 5-letter rafsi for the final gismu in the tanru.
*Join the resulting string of rafsi, initially without hyphens.
* {{ind|general-imported|hyphens in lujvo|proscribed where not required}} Add hyphen letters where necessary. It is illegal to add a hyphen at a place that is not required by this algorithm. Right-to-left tests are recommended, for reasons discussed below.
*If there are more than two words in the tanru, put an 
r-hyphen (or an 
n-hyphen) after the first rafsi if it is CVV-form. If there are exactly two words, then put an 
r-hyphen (or an 
n-hyphen) between the two rafsi if the first rafsi is CVV-form, unless the second rafsi is CCV-form (for example, 
:{{jbo|saicli}} requires no hyphen). Use an 
r-hyphen unless the letter after the hyphen is {{lerfu|r}}, in which case use an 
n-hyphen. Never use an 
n-hyphen unless it is required.
*Put a 
y-hyphen between the consonants of any impermissible consonant pair. This will always appear between rafsi.
* {{ind|general-imported|tosmabru test}} Put a 
y-hyphen after any 4-letter rafsi form.
*Test all forms with one or more initial CVC-form rafsi &ndash; with the pattern “CVC ... CVC + X” &ndash; for “tosmabru failure”. X must either be a CVCCV long rafsi that happens to have a permissible initial pair as the consonant cluster, or is something which has caused a 
y-hyphen to be installed between the previous CVC and itself by one of the above rules.

The test is as follows:
*Examine all the C/C consonant pairs up to the first y-hyphen, or up to the end of the word in case there are no y-hyphens.
These consonant pairs are called "joints”.
*If all of those joints are permissible initials, then the trial word will break up into a cmavo and a shorter brivla. If not, the word will not break up, and no further hyphens are needed.
*Install a y-hyphen at the first such joint.


{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|selection of best form of}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|scoring of}} Note that the “tosmabru test” implies that the algorithm will be more efficient if rafsi junctures are tested for required hyphens from right to left, instead of from left to right; when the test is required, it cannot be completed until hyphenation to the right has been determined.

{{ssp|section-lujvo-scoring}}
==The lujvo scoring algorithm==
This algorithm was devised by Bob and Nora LeChevalier in 1989. It is not the only possible algorithm, but it usually gives a choice that people find preferable. The algorithm may be changed in the future. The lowest-scoring variant will usually be the dictionary form of the lujvo. (In previous versions, it was the highest-scoring variant.)
*Count the total number of letters, including hyphens and apostrophes; call it 
L.
*Count the number of apostrophes; call it 
A.
*Count the number of {{lerfu|y-}}, {{lerfu|r-}}, and 
n-hyphens; call it 

H.
*For each rafsi, find the value in the following table. Sum this value over all rafsi; call it 
R: 
<tab class=wikitable header=true>CVC/CV (final)	({{raf|-sarji}})	1
CVC/C	({{raf|-sarj-}})	2
CCVCV (final)	({{raf|-zbasu}})	3
CCVC	({{raf|-zbas-}})	4
CVC	({{raf|-nun-}})	5
CVV with an apostrophe	({{raf|-ta'u-}})	6
CCV	({{raf|-zba-}})	7
CVV with no apostrophe	({{raf|-sai-}})	8
</tab>
*Count the number of vowels, not including {{lerfu|y}}; call it 
V.


{{ind|general-imported|lujvo form|hierarchy of priorities for selection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|hierarchy of priorities for selecting lujvo form}} The score is then:
{{math|(1000 * L) - (500 * A) + (100 * H) - (10 * R) - V}}
{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|scored examples of}} In case of ties, there is no preference. This should be rare. Note that the algorithm essentially encodes a hierarchy of priorities: short words are preferred (counting apostrophes as half a letter), then words with fewer hyphens, words with more pleasing rafsi (this judgment is subjective), and finally words with more vowels are chosen. Each decision principle is applied in turn if the ones before it have failed to choose; it is possible that a lower-ranked principle might dominate a higher-ranked one if it is ten times better than the alternative.

{{ssp|section-lujvo-making-examples}}
==lujvo-making examples==

{{ind|general|doghouse|example}}
This section contains examples of making and scoring lujvo. First, we will start with the tanru 
:{{jbo|gerku zdani}} ( “dog house”) and construct a lujvo meaning “doghouse”, that is, a house where a dog lives. We will use a brute-force application of the algorithm in {{ls|section-lujvo-scoring}}, using every possible rafsi.

The rafsi for {{vla|gerku}} are:

*'''{{raf|-ger-}}, '''
*'''{{raf|-ge'u-}}, '''
*'''{{raf|-gerk-}}, '''
*'''{{raf|-gerku}}'''

The rafsi for {{vla|zdani}} are:

*'''{{raf|-zda-}}, '''
*'''{{raf|-zdan-}}, '''
*'''{{raf|-zdani}}.'''

Step 1 of the algorithm directs us to use 
{{raf|-ger-}}, 
{{raf|-ge'u-}} and 
{{raf|-gerk-}} as possible rafsi for {{vla|gerku}}; Step 2 directs us to use 
{{raf|-zda-}} and 
{{raf|-zdani}} as possible rafsi for {{vla|zdani}}. The six possible forms of the lujvo are then:

*'''{{raf|ger}}{{raf|-zda}}'''
*'''{{raf|ger}}{{raf|-zdani}}'''
*'''{{raf|ge'u}}{{raf|-zda}}'''
*'''{{raf|ge'u}}{{raf|-zdani}}'''
*'''{{raf|gerk}}{{raf|-zda}}'''
*'''{{raf|gerk}}{{raf|-zdani}}'''

We must then insert appropriate hyphens in each case. The first two forms need no hyphenation: 
{{vla|ge}} cannot fall off the front, because the following word would begin with 
'''rz''', which is not a permissible initial consonant pair. So the lujvo forms are {{vla|gerzda}} and {{vla|gerzdani}}.

The third form, 
{{raf|ge'u}}{{raf|-zda}}, needs no hyphen, because even though the first rafsi is CVV, the second one is CCV, so there is a consonant cluster in the first five letters. So {{vla|ge'uzda}} is this form of the lujvo.

The fourth form, 
:{{false|ge'u-zdani}}, however, requires an 
r-hyphen; otherwise, the 
{{raf|ge'u-}} part would fall off as a cmavo. So this form of the lujvo is {{vla|ge'urzdani}}.

The last two forms require 
y-hyphens, as all 4-letter rafsi do, and so are 
{{vla|gerkyzda}} and {{vla|gerkyzdani}} respectively.

{{ind|general|boat class|example}}
The scoring algorithm is heavily weighted in favor of short lujvo, so we might expect that {{vla|gerzda}} would win. Its L score is 6, its A score is 0, its H score is 0, its R score is 12, and its V score is 3, for a final score of 5878. The other forms have scores of 7917, 6367, 9506, 8008, and 10047 respectively. Consequently, this lujvo would probably appear in the dictionary in the form {{vla|gerzda}}.

For the next example, we will use the tanru 
:{{jbo|bloti klesi}} ( “boat class”) presumably referring to the category (rowboat, motorboat, cruise liner) into which a boat falls. We will omit the long rafsi from the process, since lujvo containing long rafsi are almost never preferred by the scoring algorithm when there are short rafsi available.

The rafsi for {{vla|bloti}} are 
{{raf|-lot-}}, 
{{raf|-blo-}}, and 
{{raf|-lo'i-}}; for {{vla|klesi}} they are 
{{raf|-kle-}} and 
{{raf|-lei-}}. Both these gismu are among the handful which have both CVV-form and CCV-form rafsi, so there is an unusual number of possibilities available for a two-part tanru:

*{{vla|lotkle}}
*{{vla|blokle}}
*{{vla|lo'ikle}}

*{{vla|lotlei}}
*{{vla|blolei}}
*{{vla|lo'irlei}}

Only {{vla|lo'irlei}} requires hyphenation (to avoid confusion with the cmavo sequence {{jbo|lo'i lei}}). All six forms are valid versions of the lujvo, as are the six further forms using long rafsi; however, the scoring algorithm produces the following results:

	{{vla|lotkle}}	5878
	{{vla|blokle}}	5858
	{{vla|lo'ikle}}	6367
	{{vla|lotlei}}	5867
	{{vla|blolei}}	5847
	{{vla|lo'irlei}}	7456

{{ind|general|Logical Language Group|example}}
So the form {{vla|blolei}} is preferred, but only by a tiny margin over {{vla|blokle}}; "lotlei" and "lotkle" are only slightly worse; {{vla|lo'ikle}} suffers because of its apostrophe, and {{vla|lo'irlei}} because of having both apostrophe and hyphen.

Our third example will result in forming both a lujvo and a name from the tanru 
:{{jbo|logji bangu girzu}}, or “logical-language group” in English. ( “The Logical Language Group” is the name of the publisher of this book and the organization for the promotion of Lojban.)

{{raf|-bang-}}; and 
{{raf|-gri-}} and 
{{raf|-girzu}}, and (for name purposes only) 
{{raf|-gir-}} and 
{{raf|-girz-}}. The resulting 12 lujvo possibilities are:

{{ind|general|sexual teacher|male|example}}  

{{ind|general|male sexual teacher|example}}
The only fully reduced lujvo forms are 
{{vla|lojbangri}} and {{vla|lojbaugri}}, of which the latter has a slightly lower score: 8827 versus 8796, respectively. However, for the name of the organization, we chose to make sure the name of the language was embedded in it, and to use the clearer long-form rafsi for {{vla|girzu}}, producing 
{{cmevla|lojbangirz.}}

Finally, here is a four-part lujvo with a cmavo in it, based on the tanru 
:{{jbo|nakni ke cinse ctuca}} or “male (sexual teacher)”. The 
{{vla|ke}} cmavo ensures the interpretation “teacher of sexuality who is male”, rather than “teacher of male sexuality”. Here are the possible forms of the lujvo, both before and after hyphenation:

:{{jbo|cinse ctuca}} (which would be {{vla|cinctu}}) since the sex of the teacher is rarely important. If there was a reason to specify “male”, then the simpler tanru 
:{{jbo|nakni cinctu}} ( “male sexual-teacher”) would be appropriate. This tanru is actually shorter than the four-part lujvo, since the {{vla|ke}} required for grouping need not be expressed.

{{ssp|section-gismu-making}}
==The gismu creation algorithm==
{{ind|general-imported|source languages|use in creating gismu}} The gismu were created through the following process:
* {{ind|general-imported|gismu|creation|scoring rules}} At least one word was found in each of the six source languages (Chinese, English, Hindi, Spanish, Russian, Arabic) corresponding to the proposed gismu. This word was rendered into Lojban phonetics rather liberally: consonant clusters consisting of a stop and the corresponding fricative were simplified to just the fricative (
'''tc''' became {{lerfu|c}}, 
'''dj''' became {{lerfu|j}}) and non-Lojban vowels were mapped onto Lojban ones. Furthermore, morphological endings were dropped. The same mapping rules were applied to all six languages for the sake of consistency.
*All possible gismu forms were matched against the six source-language forms. The matches were scored as follows: 
*If three or more letters were the same in the proposed gismu and the source-language word, and appeared in the same order, the score was equal to the number of letters that were the same. Intervening letters, if any, did not matter.
*If exactly two letters were the same in the proposed gismu and the source-language word, and either the two letters were consecutive in both words, or were separated by a single letter in both words, the score was 2. Letters in reversed order got no score.
* {{ind|general-imported|gismu|creation|considerations for selection after scoring}} Otherwise, the score was 0.
* {{ind|general-imported|gismu|creation|proscribed gismu pairs}}  {{ind|general-imported|gismu|too-similar}} The scores were divided by the length of the source-language word in its Lojbanized form, and then multiplied by a weighting value specific to each language, reflecting the proportional number of first-language and second-language speakers of the language. (Second-language speakers were reckoned at half their actual numbers.) The weights were chosen to sum to 1.00. The sum of the weighted scores was the total score for the proposed gismu form.
*Any gismu forms that conflicted with existing gismu were removed. Obviously, being identical with an existing gismu constitutes a conflict. In addition, a proposed gismu that was identical to an existing gismu except for the final vowel was considered a conflict, since two such gismu would have identical 4-letter rafsi.
{{ind|general-imported|gismu|creation|and transcription blunders}} More subtly: If the proposed gismu was identical to an existing gismu except for a single consonant, and the consonant was "too similar” based on the following table, then the proposed gismu was rejected.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>proposed gismu	existing gismu{{lerfu|b}}	{{lerfu|p}}, {{lerfu|v}}{{lerfu|c}}	{{lerfu|j}}, {{lerfu|s}}{{lerfu|d}}	{{lerfu|t}}{{lerfu|f}}	{{lerfu|p}}, {{lerfu|v}}{{lerfu|g}}	{{lerfu|k}}, {{lerfu|x}}{{lerfu|j}}	{{lerfu|c}}, {{lerfu|z}}{{lerfu|k}}	{{lerfu|g}}, {{lerfu|x}}{{lerfu|l}}	{{lerfu|r}}{{lerfu|m}}	{{lerfu|n}}{{lerfu|n}}	{{lerfu|m}}{{lerfu|p}}	{{lerfu|b}}, {{lerfu|f}}{{lerfu|r}}	{{lerfu|l}}{{lerfu|s}}	{{lerfu|c}}, {{lerfu|z}}{{lerfu|t}}	{{lerfu|d}}{{lerfu|v}}	{{lerfu|b}}, {{lerfu|f}}{{lerfu|x}}	{{lerfu|g}}, {{lerfu|k}}{{lerfu|z}}	{{lerfu|j}}, {{lerfu|s}}
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|gismu|source-language weights for}} See {{ls|section-gismu}} for an example.
*The gismu form with the highest score usually became the actual gismu. Sometimes a lower-scoring form was used to provide a better rafsi. A few gismu were changed in error as a result of transcription blunders (for example, the gismu {{vla|gismu}} should have been {{vla|gicmu}}, but it's too late to fix it now).

The language weights used to make most of the gismu were as follows:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>Chinese	0.36
English	0.21
Hindi	0.16
Spanish	0.11
Russian	0.09
Arabic	0.07
</tab>
reflecting 1985 number-of-speakers data. A few gismu were made much later using updated weights:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>Chinese	0.347
Hindi	0.196
English	0.160
Spanish	0.123
Russian	0.089
Arabic	0.085
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|gismu|coined}}  {{ind|general-imported|gismu|exceptions to gismu creation by algorithm}} (English and Hindi switched places due to demographic changes.)


{{ind|general-imported|gismu|Lojban-specific}} Note that the stressed vowel of the gismu was considered sufficiently distinctive that two or more gismu may differ only in this vowel; as an extreme example, 
{{vla|bradi}}, {{vla|bredi}}, {{vla|bridi}}, and {{vla|brodi}} (but fortunately not {{vla|brudi}}) are all existing gismu.

{{ssp|section-cultural-gismu}}
==Cultural and other non-algorithmic gismu==
The following gismu were not made by the gismu creation algorithm. They are, in effect, coined words similar to fu'ivla. They are exceptions to the otherwise mandatory gismu creation algorithm where there was sufficient justification for such exceptions. Except for the small metric prefixes and the assignable predicates beginning with 
{{raf|brod-}}, they all end in the letter {{lerfu|o}}, which is otherwise a rare letter in Lojban gismu.

{{ind|general-imported|gismu|scientific-mathematical}} The following gismu represent concepts that are sufficiently unique to Lojban that they were either coined from combining forms of other gismu, or else made up out of whole cloth. These gismu are thus conceptually similar to lujvo even though they are only five letters long; however, unlike lujvo, they have rafsi assigned to them for use in building more complex lujvo. Assigning gismu to these concepts helps to keep the resulting lujvo reasonably short.

;{{vla|broda}}
:1st assignable predicate

;{{vla|brode}}
:2nd assignable predicate

;{{vla|brodi}}
:3rd assignable predicate

;{{vla|brodo}}
:4th assignable predicate

;{{vla|brodu}}
:5th assignable predicate

;{{vla|cmavo}}
:structure word (from {{jbo|cmalu valsi}})

;{{vla|lojbo}}
:Lojbanic (from {{jbo|logji bangu}})

;{{vla|lujvo}}
:compound word (from {{jbo|pluja valsi}})

;{{vla|mekso}}
:Mathematical EXpression

It is important to understand that even though {{vla|cmavo}}, {{vla|lojbo}}, and {{vla|lujvo}} were made up from parts of other gismu, they are now full-fledged gismu used in exactly the same way as all other gismu, both in grammar and in word formation.

The following three groups of gismu represent concepts drawn from the international language of science and mathematics. They are used for concepts that are represented in most languages by a root which is recognized internationally.

Small metric prefixes (values less than 1):

</tab>
Large metric prefixes (values greater than 1):
<tab class=wikitable header=true>{{vla|dekto}}	10	deka{{vla|xecto}}	100	hecto{{vla|kilto}}	1000	kilo{{vla|megdo}}	{{math|10<sup>6</sup>}}	mega{{vla|gigdo}}	{{math|10<sup>9</sup>}}	giga{{vla|terto}}	{{math|10<sup>12</sup>}}	tera{{vla|petso}}	{{math|10<sup>15</sup>}}	peta{{vla|xexso}}	{{math|10<sup>18</sup>}}	exa{{vla|zetro}}	{{math|10<sup>21</sup>}}	zetta{{vla|gotro}}	{{math|10<sup>24</sup>}}	yotta
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|gismu|for Lojban source languages}}  {{ind|general-imported|gismu|for languages}} The gismu {{vla|sinso}} and {{vla|tanjo}} were only made non-algorithmically because they were identical (having been borrowed from a common source) in all the dictionaries that had translations. The other terms in this group are units in the international metric system; some metric units, however, were made by the ordinary process (usually because they are different in Chinese).

Finally, there are the cultural gismu, which are also borrowed, but by modifying a word from one particular language, instead of using the multi-lingual gismu creation algorithm. Cultural gismu are used for words that have local importance to a particular culture; other cultures or languages may have no word for the concept at all, or may borrow the word from its home culture, just as Lojban does. In such a case, the gismu algorithm, which uses weighted averages, doesn't accurately represent the frequency of usage of the individual concept. Cultural gismu are not even required to be based on the six major languages.

The six Lojban source languages:

;{{vla|jungo}}
:Chinese (from "Zhong <sup>1</sup> guo <sup>2</sup>")

;{{vla|glico}}
:English

{{ssp|section-rafsi-fuhivla}}
==rafsi fu'ivla: a proposal==
The list of cultures represented by gismu, given in {{ls|section-cultural-gismu}}, is unavoidably controversial. Much time has been spent debating whether this or that culture “deserves a gismu” or “must languish in fu'ivla space”. To help defuse this argument, a last-minute proposal was made when this book was already substantially complete. I have added it here with experimental status: it is not yet a standard part of Lojban, since all its implications have not been tested in open debate, and it affects a part of the language (lujvo-making) that has long been stable, but is known to be fragile in the face of small changes. (Many attempts were made to add general mechanisms for making lujvo that contained fu'ivla, but all failed on obvious or obscure counterexamples; finally the general {{vla|zei}} mechanism was devised instead.)

The first part of the proposal is uncontroversial and involves no change to the language mechanisms. All valid Type 4 fu'ivla of the form CCVVCV would be reserved for cultural brivla analogous to those described in {{ls|section-cultural-gismu}}. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-PMb2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PMb2}}
{{ind|general|Chilean desert|example}}
{{judri|c4e16d1}}
:{{false|tci'ile}}
:''Chilean''

is of the appropriate form, and passes all tests required of a Stage 4 fu'ivla. No two fu'ivla of this form would be allowed to coexist if they differed only in the final vowel; this rule was applied to gismu, but does not apply to other fu'ivla or to lujvo.

The second, and fully experimental, part of the proposal is to allow rafsi to be formed from these cultural fu'ivla by removing the final vowel and treating the result as a 4-letter rafsi (although it would contain five letters, not four). These rafsi could then be used on a par with all other rafsi in forming lujvo. The tanru

{{dsp|example-random-id-hcR6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hcR6}}
{{judri|c4e16d2}}
:{{false|tci'ile ke canre tutra}}
:<code>Chilean type-of 
:{{comment|sand territory}}</code>
:''Chilean desert''

could be represented by the lujvo

{{dsp|example-random-id-0rzn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0rzn}}
{{judri|c4e16d3}}
:{{false|tci'ilykemcantutra}}

which is an illegal word in standard Lojban, but a valid lujvo under this proposal. There would be no short rafsi or 5-letter rafsi assigned to any fu'ivla, so no fu'ivla could appear as the last element of a lujvo.

The cultural fu'ivla introduced under this proposal are called 
:{{jbo|rafsi fu'ivla}}, since they are distinguished from other Type 4 fu'ivla by the property of having rafsi. If this proposal is workable and introduces no problems into Lojban morphology, it might become standard for all Type 4 fu'ivla, including those made for plants, animals, foodstuffs, and other things.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{csp|chapter-selbri}}
=“Pretty Little Girls' School”: The Structure Of Lojban selbri=
{{image|chapter-selbri-picture|The picture for chapter 5|CLL-chapter-selbri.gif}}
{{ssp|section-content-words-brivla}}
==Lojban content words: brivla==
{{ind|general-imported|bridi|relation to selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|relation to bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi|definition}} At the center, logically and often physically, of every Lojban bridi is one or more words which constitute the selbri. A bridi expresses a relationship between things: the selbri specifies which relationship is referred to. The difference between:

{{dsp|example-do-mamta-mi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-do-mamta-mi}}
{{judri|c5e1d1}}
:'''do mamta mi'''
:<code>You are-a-mother-of me</code>
:''You are my mother''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-B0aR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-B0aR}}
{{judri|c5e1d2}}
:'''do patfu mi'''
:<code>You are-a-father-of me.</code>
:''You are my father.''

lies in the different selbri.

{{ind|general-imported|brivla|types}}  {{ind|general-imported|brivla as selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|brivla as}} The simplest kind of selbri is a single Lojban content word: a brivla. There are three different varieties of brivla: those which are built into the language (the gismu), those which are derived from combinations of the gismu (the lujvo), and those which are taken (usually in a modified form) from other languages (the fu'ivla). In addition, there are a few cmavo that can act like brivla; these are mentioned in {{ls|section-cmavo-selbri}}, and discussed in full in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}.

For the purposes of this chapter, however, all brivla are alike. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-483c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-483c}}
{{judri|c5e1d3}}
:'''ta bloti'''
:<code>That is-a-boat.</code>
:''That is a boat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-mdxB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mdxB}}
{{judri|c5e1d4}}
:'''ta brablo'''
:<code>That is-a-large-boat.</code>
:''That is a ship.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-UMjE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UMjE}}
{{ind|example|schooner|example}}
{{judri|c5e1d5}}
:'''ta blotrskunri'''
:<code>That is-a-(boat)-schooner.</code>
:''That is a schooner.''

illustrate the three types of brivla (gismu, lujvo, and fu'ivla respectively), but in each case the selbri is composed of a single word whose meaning can be learned independent of its origins.

The remainder of this chapter will mostly use gismu as example brivla, because they are short. However, it is important to keep in mind that wherever a gismu appears, it could be replaced by any other kind of brivla.

{{ssp|section-simple-tanru}}
==Simple tanru==

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|simple}} Beyond the single brivla, a selbri may consist of two brivla placed together. When a selbri is built in this way from more than one brivla, it is called a tanru, a word with no single English equivalent. The nearest analogue to tanru in English are combinations of two nouns such as “lemon tree”. There is no way to tell just by looking at the phrase “lemon tree” exactly what it refers to, even if you know the meanings of “lemon” and “tree” by themselves. As English-speakers, we must simply know that it refers to “a tree which bears lemons as fruits”. A person who didn't know English very well might think of it as analogous to “brown tree” and wonder, “What kind of tree is lemon-colored?”

{{ind|general-imported|adjective-noun combination|with tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|adverb-verb combination|with tanru}} In Lojban, tanru are also used for the same purposes as English adjective-noun combinations like “big boy” and adverb-verb combinations like “quickly run”. This is a consequence of Lojban not having any such categories as “noun”, “verb”, “adjective”, or “adverb”. English words belonging to any of these categories are translated by simple brivla in Lojban. Here are some examples of tanru:

{{dsp|example-lemon-tree}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-lemon-tree}}
{{ind|example|lemon tree|example}}
{{judri|c5e2d1}}
:'''tu pelnimre tricu'''
:<code>That-yonder is-a-(lemon tree).</code>
:''That is a lemon tree.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHNA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHNA}}
{{judri|c5e2d2}}
:'''la djan. barda nanla'''
:<code>That-named John is-a-big boy.</code>
:''John is a big boy.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-eD63}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eD63}}
{{ind|example|quick runner|example}}
{{judri|c5e2d3}}
:'''mi sutra bajra'''
:<code>I quick run</code>
:''I quickly run./I run quickly.''

Note that {{vla|pelnimre}} is a lujvo for “lemon”; it is derived from the gismu {{vla|pelxu}}, yellow, and {{vla|nimre}}, citrus. Note also that {{vla|sutra}} can mean “fast/quick” or “quickly” depending on its use:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cjhN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cjhN}}
{{judri|c5e2d4}}
:'''mi sutra'''
:<code>I am-fast/quick</code>

shows {{vla|sutra}} used to translate an adjective, whereas in {{lex|example-random-id-eD63}} it is translating an adverb. (Another correct translation of {{lex|example-random-id-eD63}}, however, would be “I am a quick runner”.)

{{ind|general-imported|tertau|definition of}}  {{ind|general-imported|seltau|definition of}} There are special Lojban terms for the two components of a tanru, derived from the place structure of the word {{vla|tanru}}. The first component is called the {{vla|seltau}}, and the second component is called the {{vla|tertau}}.

{{ind|general-imported|tertau|effect on meaning of tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|primary meaning of}} The most important rule for use in interpreting tanru is that the tertau carries the primary meaning. A 
:{{jbo|pelnimre tricu}} is primarily a tree, and only secondarily is it connected with lemons in some way. For this reason, an alternative translation of {{lex|example-lemon-tree}} would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hP9j}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hP9j}}
{{judri|c5e2d5}}
That is a lemon type of tree.

This “type of” relationship between the components of a tanru is fundamental to the tanru concept.

{{ind|general-imported|modifier|seltau as}}  {{ind|general-imported|seltau|effect on meaning of tanru}} We may also say that the seltau modifies the meaning of the tertau:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4fvn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4fvn}}
{{judri|c5e2d6}}
That is a tree which is lemon-ish (in the way appropriate to trees)

would be another possible translation of {{lex|example-lemon-tree}}. In the same way, a more explicit translation of {{lex|example-random-id-qHNA}} might be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-asRA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-asRA}}
{{judri|c5e2d7}}
John is a boy who is big in the way that boys are big.

This “way that boys are big” would be quite different from the way in which elephants are big; big-for-a-boy is small-for-an-elephant.

{{ind|general-imported|ambiguity of tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|ambiguity of}} All tanru are ambiguous semantically. Possible translations of:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aIfM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-aIfM}}
{{ind|example|goer table|example}}
{{judri|c5e2d8}}
:'''ta klama jubme'''
:<code>That is-a-goer type-of-table.</code>

include:
*  That is a table which goes (a wheeled table, perhaps).
*That is a table owned by one who goes.
*That is a table used by those who go (a sports doctor's table?).
*That is a table when it goes (otherwise it is a chair?).

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|as ambiguous}} In each case the object referred to is a “goer type of table”, but the ambiguous “type of” relationship can mean one of many things. A speaker who uses tanru (and pragmatically all speakers must) takes the risk of being misunderstood. Using tanru is convenient because they are short and expressive; the circumlocution required to squeeze out all ambiguity can require too much effort.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|meaning of}} No general theory covering the meaning of all possible tanru exists; probably no such theory can exist. However, some regularities obviously do exist:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Lczh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Lczh}}
{{judri|c5e2d9}}
:'''do barda prenu'''
:<code>You are-a-large person.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ldb1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ldb1}}
{{judri|c5e2d10}}
:'''do cmalu prenu'''
:<code>You are-a-small person.</code>

are parallel tanru, in the sense that the relationship between {{vla|barda}} and {{vla|prenu}} is the same as that between {{vla|cmalu}} and {{vla|prenu}}. {{ls|section-asymmetric-tanru}} and {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}} contain a partial listing of some types of tanru, with examples.

{{ssp|section-three-part-tanru}}
==Three-part tanru grouping with {{vla|bo}}==

The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|bo}}
:{{s|BO}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|three-part}} Consider the English sentence:

<!-- FIXME: The indexterm "girls' school" applies to all three of the following examples; should it go in all three or just the first? -->

{{dsp|example-random-id-gCLr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gCLr}}
{{ind|example|girls' school|little|example}}
{{judri|c5e3d1}}
That's a little girls' school.

What does it mean? Two possible readings are:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5UBW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5UBW}}
{{ind|example|girls' school|little|example}}
{{judri|c5e3d2}}
That's a little school for girls.

{{dsp|example-random-id-5UBJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5UBJ}}
{{ind|example|girls' school|little|example}}
{{judri|c5e3d3}}
That's a school for little girls.

{{ind|general-imported|speech rhythm|for grouping in English}} This ambiguity is quite different from the simple tanru ambiguity described in {{ls|section-simple-tanru}}. We understand that “girls' school” means “a school where girls are the students”, and not “a school where girls are the teachers” or “a school which is a girl” (!). Likewise, we understand that “little girl” means “girl who is small”. This is an ambiguity of grouping. Is “girls' school” to be taken as a unit, with “little” specifying the type of girls' school? Or is “little girl” to be taken as a unit, specifying the type of school? In English speech, different tones of voice, or 
exaggerated speech rhythm showing the grouping, are used to make the distinction; English writing usually leaves it unrepresented.

Lojban makes no use of tones of voice for any purpose; explicit words are used to do the work. The cmavo {{vla|bo}} (which belongs to selma'o BO) may be placed between the two brivla which are most closely associated. Therefore, a Lojban translation of {{lex|example-random-id-5UBW}} would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nwuU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nwuU}}
{{judri|c5e3d4}}
:'''ta cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small girl [] school.</code>{{lex|example-random-id-5UBJ}} might be translated:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jquh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jquh}}
{{judri|c5e3d5}}
:'''ta cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small [] girl school.</code>

The {{vla|bo}} is represented in the literal translation by a hyphen because in written English a hyphen is sometimes used for the same purpose: “a big dog-catcher” would be quite different from a “big-dog catcher” (presumably someone who catches only big dogs).

{{ind|general-imported|tanru nested within tanru}} Analysis of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} and {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}} reveals a tanru nested within a tanru. In {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, the main tanru has a seltau of {{vla|cmalu}} and a tertau of 
:{{jbo|nixli bo ckule}}; the tertau is itself a tanru with {{vla|nixli}} as the seltau and {{vla|ckule}} as the tertau. In {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}, on the other hand, the seltau is 
:{{jbo|cmalu bo nixli}} (itself a tanru), whereas the tertau is {{vla|ckule}}. 
This structure of tanru nested within tanru forms the basis for all the more complex types of selbri that will be explained below.

What about {{lex|example-random-id-9FPm}}? What does it mean?

{{dsp|example-random-id-9FPm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9FPm}}
{{judri|c5e3d6}}
:'''ta cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small girl school.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|default left-grouping of}}  {{ind|general-imported|left-grouping rule|definition of}} The rules of Lojban do not leave this sentence ambiguous, as the rules of English do with {{lex|example-random-id-gCLr}}. The choice made by the language designers is to say that {{lex|example-random-id-9FPm}} means the same as {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}. This is true no matter what three brivla are used: the leftmost two are always grouped together. This rule is called the “left-grouping rule”. Left-grouping in seemingly ambiguous structures is quite common &ndash; though not universal &ndash; in other contexts in Lojban.

Another way to express the English meaning of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} and {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}, using parentheses to mark grouping, is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ERBx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ERBx}}
{{judri|c5e3d7}}
:'''ta cmalu [] nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-small type-of (girl type-of school).</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-ERBQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ERBQ}}
{{judri|c5e3d8}}
:'''ta cmalu bo nixli [] ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(small type-of girl) type-of school.</code>

Because “type-of” is implicit in the Lojban tanru form, it has no Lojban equivalent.

Note: It is perfectly legal, though pointless, to insert {{vla|bo}} into a simple tanru:

{{dsp|example-random-id-q6br}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-q6br}}
{{judri|c5e3d9}}
:'''ta klama bo jubme'''
:<code>That is-a-goer [] table.</code>

is a legal Lojban bridi that means exactly the same thing as {{lex|example-random-id-aIfM}}, and is ambiguous in exactly the same ways. The cmavo {{vla|bo}} serves only to resolve grouping ambiguity: it says nothing about the more basic ambiguity present in all tanru.

{{ssp|section-complex-grouping}}
==Complex tanru grouping==

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|complex}} If one element of a tanru can be another tanru, why not both elements?

{{dsp|example-random-id-m5SD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-m5SD}}
{{judri|c5e4d1}}
:'''do mutce bo barda gerku bo kavbu'''
:<code>You are-a-(very type-of large) (dog type-of capturer).</code>
:''You are a very large dog-catcher.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-m5SD}}, the selbri is a tanru with seltau 
:{{jbo|mutce bo barda}} and tertau 
:{{jbo|gerku bo kavbu}}. It is worth emphasizing once again that this tanru has the same fundamental ambiguity as all other Lojban tanru: the sense in which the “dog type-of capturer” is said to be “very type-of large” is not precisely specified. Presumably it is his body which is large, but theoretically it could be one of his other properties.

{{ind|general-imported|pretty|English ambiguity of}} We will now justify the title of this chapter by exploring the ramifications of the phrase “pretty little girls' school”, an expansion of the tanru used in 
{{ls|section-three-part-tanru}} to four brivla. (Although this example has been used in the Loglan Project almost since the beginning &ndash; it first appeared in Quine's book {{cite|book|Word and Object}} (1960) &ndash; it is actually a mediocre example because of the ambiguity of English “pretty”; it can mean “beautiful”, the sense intended here, or it can mean “very”. Lojban {{vla|melbi}} is not subject to this ambiguity: it means only “beautiful”.)

Here are four ways to group this phrase:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjmr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjmr}}
{{judri|c5e4d2}}
:'''ta melbi cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-((pretty type-of little) type-of girl) type-of school.</code>
:''That is a school for girls who are beautifully small.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjNi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjNi}}
{{judri|c5e4d3}}
:'''ta melbi cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of little) (girl type-of school).</code>
:''That is a girls' school which is beautifully small.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjog}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjog}}
{{judri|c5e4d4}}
:'''ta melbi cmalu bo nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of (little type-of girl)) type-of school.</code>
:''That is a school for small girls who are beautiful.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjop}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjop}}
{{judri|c5e4d5}}
:'''ta melbi cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of (little type-of (girl type-of school)).</code>
:''That is a small school for girls which is beautiful.''

{{ind|general-imported|bo|for right-grouping in tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|with bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|right-grouping in tanru|with bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|right-grouping rule|definition of}} {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}} uses a construction which has not been seen before: 
:{{jbo|cmalu bo nixli bo ckule}}, with two consecutive uses of {{vla|bo}} between brivla. The rule for multiple {{vla|bo}} constructions is the opposite of the rule when no {{vla|bo}} is present at all: the last two are grouped together. Not surprisingly, this is called the “right-grouping rule”, and it is associated with every use of 
{{vla|bo}} in the language. Therefore,

{{dsp|example-random-id-snKn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-snKn}}
{{judri|c5e4d6}}
:'''ta cmalu bo nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-little type-of (girl type-of school).</code>

means the same as {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, not {{lex|example-random-id-jquh}}. This rule may seem peculiar at first, but one of its consequences is that {{vla|bo}} is never necessary between the first two elements of any of the complex tanru presented so far: all of {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}} could have {{vla|bo}} inserted between {{vla|melbi}} and {{vla|cmalu}} with no change in meaning.

{{ssp|section-ke-grouping}}
==Complex tanru with {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}}==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ke}}
:{{s|KE}}
:''description''

:{{c|ke'e}}
:{{s|KEhE}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|with ke}}  {{ind|general-imported|grouping parentheses}} There is, in fact, a fifth grouping of “pretty little girls' school” that cannot be expressed with the resources explained so far. To handle it, we must introduce the grouping parentheses cmavo, 
{{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} (belonging to selma'o KE and KEhE respectively). Any portion of a selbri sandwiched between these two cmavo is taken to be a single tanru component, independently of what is adjacent to it. Thus, {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}} can be rewritten in any of the following ways:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjqu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjqu}}
{{judri|c5e5d1}}
:'''ta ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( pretty little ) girl school.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJQz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJQz}}
{{judri|c5e5d2}}
:'''ta ke ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( ( pretty little ) girl ) school.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjSA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjSA}}
{{judri|c5e5d3}}
:'''ta ke ke ke melbi cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule ke'e'''
:<code>That is-a-( ( ( pretty little ) girl ) school ).</code>

Even more versions could be created simply by placing any number of {{vla|ke}} cmavo at the beginning of the selbri, and a like number of {{vla|ke'e}} cmavo at its end. Obviously, all of these are a waste of breath once the left-grouping rule has been grasped. However, the following is equivalent to {{lex|example-random-id-qjog}} and may be easier to understand:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zV26}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zV26}}
{{judri|c5e5d4}}
:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-( pretty type-of ( little type-of girl ) ) type-of school.</code>

Likewise, a {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} version of {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}} would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AUdM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AUdM}}
{{judri|c5e5d5}}
:'''ta melbi cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-(pretty type-of little) ( girl type-of school ).</code>

The final {{vla|ke'e}} is given in square brackets here to indicate that it can be elided. It is always possible to elide 
{{vla|ke'e}} at the end of the selbri, making {{lex|example-random-id-AUdM}} as terse as {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}}.

Now how about that fifth grouping? It is

{{dsp|example-random-id-tz0L}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tz0L}}
{{judri|c5e5d6}}
:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( ( little type-of girl ) type-of school ).</code>
:''That is a beautiful school for small girls.''
{{lex|example-random-id-tz0L}} is distinctly different in meaning from any of Examples 4.2 through 4.5. Note that within the {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} parentheses, the left-grouping rule is applied to 
:{{jbo|cmalu nixli ckule}}.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|with ke and bo}} 
It is perfectly all right to mix {{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} in a single selbri. For instance, {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}}, which in pure {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} form is

{{dsp|example-random-id-uBS4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uBS4}}
{{judri|c5e5d7}}
:'''ta melbi ke cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e] [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( little type-of ( girl type-of school ) ).</code>

can equivalently be expressed as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ei5U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ei5U}}
{{judri|c5e5d8}}
:'''ta melbi ke cmalu nixli bo ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-pretty type-of ( little type-of ( girl type-of school ) ).</code>

and in many other different forms as well.

{{ssp|section-logical-connection}}
==Logical connection within tanru==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|je}}
:{{s|JA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ja}}
:{{s|JA}}
:''description''

:{{c|joi}}
:{{s|JOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|gu'e}}
:{{s|GUhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|gi}}
:{{s|GI}}
:''description''

Consider the English phrase “big red dog”. How shall this be rendered as a Lojban tanru? The naive attempt:

{{dsp|example-random-id-riAq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-riAq}}
{{ind|example|big red dog|example}}
{{judri|c5e6d1}}
:'''barda xunre gerku'''
:<code>(big type-of red) type-of dog</code>

will not do, as it means a dog whose redness is big, in whatever way redness might be described as “big”. Nor is

{{dsp|example-random-id-6MqF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6MqF}}
{{judri|c5e6d2}}
:'''barda xunre bo gerku'''
:<code>big type-of (red type-of dog)</code>

{{ind|general-imported|adjective ordering}} much better. After all, the straightforward understanding of the English phrase is that the dog is big as compared with other dogs, not merely as compared with other red dogs. In fact, the bigness and redness are independent properties of the dog, and only obscure rules of English adjective ordering prevent us from saying “red big dog”.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|in tanru}} The Lojban approach to this problem is to introduce the cmavo {{vla|je}}, which is one of the many equivalents of English “and”. A big red dog is one that is both big and red, and we can say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0UrF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0UrF}}
{{judri|c5e6d3}}
:'''barda je xunre gerku'''
:<code>(big and red) type-of dog</code>

Of course,

{{dsp|example-random-id-DzeP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DzeP}}
{{judri|c5e6d4}}
:'''xunre je barda gerku'''
:<code>(red and big) type-of dog</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives in tanru|effect on tanru grouping}} is equally satisfactory and means the same thing. As these examples indicate, joining two brivla with {{vla|je}} makes them a unit for tanru purposes. However, explicit grouping with {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} associates brivla more closely than {{vla|je}} does:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LES9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LES9}}
{{judri|c5e6d5}}
:'''barda je pelxu bo xunre gerku'''
:'''barda je ke pelxu xunre ke'e gerku'''
:<code>(big and (yellow type-of red)) dog</code>
:''big yellowish-red dog''

With no grouping indicators, we get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-fuhg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fuhg}}
{{judri|c5e6d6}}
:'''barda je pelxu xunre gerku'''
:<code>((big and yellow) type-of red) type-of dog</code>
:<code>biggish- and yellowish-red dog</code>

which again raises the question of {{lex|example-random-id-riAq}}: what does “biggish-red” mean?

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives in tanru|usefulness of}} Unlike {{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}}, {{vla|je}} is useful as well as merely legal within simple tanru. It may be used to partly resolve the ambiguity of simple tanru:

{{dsp|example-random-id-W56H}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-W56H}}
{{judri|c5e6d7}}
:'''ta blanu je zdani'''
:<code>that is-blue and is-a-house</code>

definitely refers to something which is both blue and is a house, and not to any of the other possible interpretations of simple 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}}. Furthermore, 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}} refers to something which is blue in the way that houses are blue; 
:{{jbo|blanu je zdani}} has no such implication &ndash; the blueness of a 
:{{jbo|blanu je zdani}} is independent of its houseness.

With the addition of {{vla|je}}, many more versions of “pretty little girls' school” are made possible: see 
{{ls|section-pretty-school-groupings}} for a complete list.

A subtle point in the semantics of tanru like {{lex|example-random-id-0UrF}} needs special elucidation. There are at least two possible interpretations of:

{{dsp|example-random-id-N5Bt}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-N5Bt}}
{{judri|c5e6d8}}
:'''ta melbi je nixli ckule'''
:<code>That is-a-(beautiful and girl) type-of school.</code>

It can be understood as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-FCDa}}
{{judri|c5e6d9}}
That is a girls' school and a beautiful school.

or as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aFxm}}
{{judri|c5e6d10}}
That is a school for things which are both girls and beautiful.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives in tanru|ambiguity of}} The interpretation specified by {{lex|example-random-id-FCDa}} treats the tanru as a sort of abbreviation for:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pHHw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pHHw}}
{{judri|c5e6d11}}
:'''ta ke melbi ckule ke'e je ke nixli ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>That is-a-( beautiful type-of school ) and ( girl type-of school )</code>

whereas the interpretation specified by {{lex|example-random-id-aFxm}} does not. This is a kind of semantic ambiguity for which Lojban does not compel a firm resolution. The way in which the school is said to be of type “beautiful and girl” may entail that it is separately a beautiful school and a girls' school; but the alternative interpretation, that the members of the school are beautiful and girls, is also possible. Still another interpretation is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2cjH}}
{{judri|c5e6d12}}
That is a school for beautiful things and also for girls.

so while the logical connectives help to resolve the meaning of tanru, they by no means compel a single meaning in and of themselves.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives in tanru|effect on formal logical manipulations}} In general, logical connectives within tanru cannot undergo the formal manipulations that are possible with the related logical connectives that exist outside tanru; See {{ls|section-tanru}} for further details.

The logical connective {{vla|je}} is only one of the fourteen logical connectives that Lojban provides. Here are a few examples of some of the others:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJse}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJse}}
{{judri|c5e6d13}}
:'''le bajra cu jinga ja te jinga'''
:''the runner(s) is/are winner(s) or loser(s).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJsg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJsg}}
{{judri|c5e6d14}}
:'''blanu naja lenku skapi'''
:<code>(blue only-if cold) skin</code>
:''skin which is blue only if it is cold''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjsy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjsy}}
{{judri|c5e6d15}}
:'''xamgu jo tordu nuntavla'''
:<code>(good if-and-only-if short) speech</code>
:''speech which is good if (and only if) it is short''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjtD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjtD}}
{{judri|c5e6d16}}
:'''vajni ju pluka nuntavla'''
:<code>(important whether-or-not pleasing) event-of-talking</code>
:''speech which is important, whether or not it is pleasing''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qJse}}, {{vla|ja}} is grammatically equivalent to {{vla|je}} but means “or” (more precisely, “and/or”). Likewise, {{vla|naja}} means “only if” in {{lex|example-random-id-qJsg}}, {{vla|jo}} means “if and only if” in {{lex|example-random-id-qjsy}}, and {{vla|ju}} means “whether or not” in {{lex|example-random-id-qjtD}}.

{{ind|general-imported|multiple logical connectives|within tanru}} Now consider the following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NuWM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NuWM}}
{{judri|c5e6d17}}
:'''ricfu je blanu jabo crino'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green)</code>

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping with JA+BO|effect on tanru grouping}} which illustrates a new grammatical feature: the use of both {{vla|ja}} and {{vla|bo}} between tanru components. The two cmavo combine to form a compound whose meaning is that of {{vla|ja}} but which groups more closely; {{vla|ja}}{{vla|bo}} is to 
{{vla|ja}} as plain {{vla|bo}} is to no cmavo at all. However, both {{vla|ja}} and {{vla|ja}}{{vla|bo}} group less closely than 
{{vla|bo}} does:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KxqX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KxqX}}
{{judri|c5e6d18}}
:'''ricfu je blanu jabo crino bo blanu'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green - blue)</code>
:<code>rich and (blue or greenish-blue)</code>

An alternative form of {{lex|example-random-id-NuWM}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2WtT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2WtT}}
{{judri|c5e6d19}}
:'''ricfu je ke blanu ja crino [ke'e]'''
:<code>rich and (blue or green)</code>

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|within tanru}} In addition to the logical connectives, there are also a variety of non-logical connectives, grammatically equivalent to the logical ones. The only one with a well-understood meaning in tanru contexts is {{vla|joi}}, which is the kind of “and” that denotes a mixture:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Hr1L}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Hr1L}}
{{judri|c5e6d20}}
:'''ti blanu joi xunre bolci'''
:<code>This is-a-(blue and red) ball.</code>

The ball described is neither solely red nor solely blue, but probably striped or in some other way exhibiting a combination of the two colors. {{lex|example-random-id-Hr1L}} is distinct from:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NAhT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NAhT}}
{{judri|c5e6d21}}
:'''ti blanu xunre bolci'''
:''This is a bluish-red ball''

which would be a ball whose color is some sort of purple tending toward red, since {{vla|xunre}} is the more important of the two components. On the other hand,

{{dsp|example-random-id-78C3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-78C3}}
{{judri|c5e6d22}}
:'''ti blanu je xunre bolci'''
:<code>This is a (blue and red) ball</code>

is probably self-contradictory, seeming to claim that the ball is independently both blue and red at the same time, although some sensible interpretation may exist.

{{ind|general-imported|forethought logical connectives|within tanru}} Finally, just as English “and” has the variant form “both ... and”, so {{vla|je}} between tanru components has the variant form {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}}, where {{vla|gu'e}} is placed before the components and {{vla|gi}} between them:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gLbh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gLbh}}
{{judri|c5e6d23}}
:'''gu'e barda gi xunre gerku'''
:<code>(both big and red) type-of dog</code>

is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-0UrF}}. For each logical connective related to {{vla|je}}, there is a corresponding connective related to {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} in a systematic way.

{{ind|general-imported|forethought logical connectives in tanru|effect on tanru grouping}} The portion of a {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} construction before the {{vla|gi}} is a full selbri, and may use any of the selbri resources including {{vla|je}} logical connections. After the {{vla|gi}}, logical connections are taken to be wider in scope than the {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}}, which has in effect the same scope as {{vla|bo}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ETVe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ETVe}}
{{judri|c5e6d24}}
:'''gu'e barda je xunre gi gerku ja mlatu'''
:<code>(both (big and red) and dog) or cat</code>
:''something which is either big, red, and a dog, or else a cat''

leaves {{vla|mlatu}} outside the {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} construction. The scope of the {{vla|gi}} arm extends only to a single brivla or to two or more brivla connected with {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}}.

{{ssp|section-be-sumti}}
==Linked sumti: {{vla|be}}-{{vla|bei}}-{{vla|be'o}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|be}}
:{{s|BE}}
:''description''

:{{c|bei}}
:{{s|BEI}}
:''description''

:{{c|be'o}}
:{{s|BEhO}}
:''description''

The question of the place structures of selbri has been glossed over so far. This chapter does not attempt to treat place structure issues in detail; they are discussed in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}}. One grammatical structure related to places belongs here, however. In simple sentences such as {{lex|example-do-mamta-mi}}, the place structure of the selbri is simply the defined place structure of the gismu{{vla|mamta}}. What about more complex selbri?

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|place structures of}} For tanru, the place structure rule is simple: the place structure of a tanru is always the place structure of its tertau. Thus, the place structure of 
:{{jbo|blanu zdani}} is that of {{vla|zdani}}: the x1 place is a house or nest, and the x2 place is its occupants.

What about the places of {{vla|blanu}}? Is there any way to get them into the act? In fact, {{vla|blanu}} has only one place, and this is merged, as it were, with the x1 place of {{vla|zdani}}. It is whatever is in the x1 place that is being characterized as blue-for-a-house. But if we replace {{vla|blanu}} with {{vla|xamgu}}, we get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-tffW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tffW}}
{{ind|example|good house|example}}
{{judri|c5e7d1}}
:'''ti xamgu zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good house.</code>
:''This is a good (for someone, by some standard) house.''

Since {{vla|xamgu}} has three places (x1, the good thing; x2, the person for whom it is good; and x3, the standard of goodness), {{lex|example-random-id-tffW}} necessarily omits information about the last two: there is no room for them. Room can be made, however!

{{dsp|example-random-id-Uuio}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Uuio}}
{{judri|c5e7d2}}
:'''ti xamgu be do bei mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good (for you by-standard me) house.</code>
:''This is a house that is good for you by my standards.''

{{ind|general-imported|linked sumti|in tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|seltau|filling sumti places in}} Here, the gismu {{vla|xamgu}} has been followed by the cmavo {{vla|be}} (of selma'o BE), which signals that one or more sumti follows. These sumti are not part of the overall bridi place structure, but fill the places of the brivla they are attached to, starting with x2. If there is more than one sumti, they are separated by the cmavo {{vla|bei}} (of selma'o BEI), and the list of sumti is terminated by the elidable terminator {{vla|be'o}} (of selma'o BEhO).

{{ind|general-imported|linked sumti|definition}} Grammatically, a brivla with sumti linked to it in this fashion plays the same role in tanru as a simple brivla. To illustrate, here is a fully fleshed-out version of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, with all places filled in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7vxB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7vxB}}
{{ind|example|Brooklyn|example}}
{{judri|c5e7d3}}
:'''ti cmalu be le ka canlu bei lo'e ckule be'o'''
:<code>This is a small (in-dimension the property-of volume by-standard the-typical school)</code>
:'''nixli be li mu bei lo merko be'o bo ckule'''
:<code>(girl (of-years the-number five by-standard some American-thing) school)</code>
:'''la bryklyn. loi pemci'''
:<code>in-Brooklyn with-subject poems</code>
:'''le mela nu,IORK. prenu le jecta'''
:<code>for-audience New-York persons with-operator the state.</code>
This is a school, small in volume compared to the typical school, pertaining to five-year-old girls (by American standards), in Brooklyn, teaching poetry to the New York community and operated by the state.

Here the three places of {{vla|cmalu}}, the three of {{vla|nixli}}, and the four of {{vla|ckule}} are fully specified. Since the places of {{vla|ckule}} are the places of the bridi as a whole, it was not necessary to link the sumti which follow {{vla|ckule}}. It would have been legal to do so, however:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YIty}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YIty}}
{{judri|c5e7d4}}
:'''mi klama be le zarci bei le zdani [be'o]'''
:<code>I go (to-the market from-the house).</code>

means the same as

{{dsp|example-random-id-UtBR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UtBR}}
{{judri|c5e7d5}}
:'''mi klama le zarci le zdani'''
:<code>I go to-the market from-the house.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|place structures of}} No matter how complex a tanru gets, the last brivla always dictates the place structure: the place structure of

{{dsp|example-random-id-Twmx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Twmx}}
{{judri|c5e7d6}}
:'''melbi je cmalu nixli bo ckule'''
:<code>a (pretty and little) (girl school)</code>
:''a school for girls which is both beautiful and small''

is simply that of {{vla|ckule}}. (The sole exception to this rule is discussed in {{ls|section-co-inversion}}.)

{{ind|general-imported|FA tags and linked sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|linked sumti and FA tags}} It is possible to precede linked sumti by the place structure ordering tags 
{{vla|fe}}, {{vla|fi}}, {{vla|fo}}, and {{vla|fu}} (of selma'o FA, discussed further in {{ls|section-FA}}), which serve to explicitly specify the x2, x3, x4, and x5 places respectively. Normally, the place following the {{vla|be}} is the x2 place and the other places follow in order. If it seems convenient to change the order, however, it can be accomplished as follows:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mhS7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mhS7}}
{{judri|c5e7d7}}
:'''ti xamgu be fi mi bei fe do [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good ( by-standard me for you ) house.</code>

which is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-Uuio}}. Note that the order of {{vla|be}}, {{vla|bei}}, and {{vla|be'o}} does not change; only the inserted {{vla|fi}} tells us that {{vla|mi}} is the x3 place (and correspondingly, the inserted {{vla|fe}} tells us that {{vla|do}} is the x2 place). Changing the order of sumti is often done to match the order of another language, or for emphasis or rhythm.

Of course, using FA cmavo makes it easy to specify one place while omitting a previous place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9b37}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9b37}}
{{judri|c5e7d8}}
:'''ti xamgu be fi mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>This is-a-good (by-standard me) house.</code>
:''This is a good house by my standards.''

{{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita and tense tags}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense tags and sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita and modal tags}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal tags and sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita and linked sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|linked sumti and sumti tcita}} Similarly, sumti labeled by modal or tense tags can be inserted into strings of linked sumti just as they can into bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GstI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GstI}}
{{judri|c5e7d9}}
:'''ta blanu be ga'a mi [be'o] zdani'''
:<code>That is-a-blue (to-observer me) house.</code>
:''That is a blue, as I see it, house.''

The meaning of {{lex|example-random-id-GstI}} is slightly different from:

{{dsp|example-random-id-63c5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-63c5}}
{{judri|c5e7d10}}
:'''ta blanu zdani ga'a mi'''
:<code>That is-a-blue house to-observer me.</code>
:''That is a blue house, as I see it.''

See discussions in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}} of modals and in {{lch|chapter-tenses}} of tenses for more explanations.

{{ind|general-imported|be'o|effect of relative clauses on elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|effect on elidability of be'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|be'o|elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|elidability of be'o}} The terminator {{vla|be'o}} is almost always elidable: however, if the selbri belongs to a description, then a relative clause following it will attach to the last linked sumti unless 
{{vla|be'o}} is used, in which case it will attach to the outer description:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJTI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJTI}}
{{judri|c5e7d11}}
:'''le xamgu be do noi barda cu zdani'''
:<code>The good-thing for you (who are-large) is-a-house.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjTj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjTj}}
{{judri|c5e7d12}}
:'''le xamgu be do be'o noi barda cu zdani'''
:<code>The (good-thing for you) (which is-large) is-a-house</code>

(Relative clauses are explained in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}.)

{{ind|general-imported|be'o|effect of ku on elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ku|effect on elidability of be'o}} In other cases, however, {{vla|be'o}} cannot be elided if {{vla|ku}} has also been elided:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zb4A}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zb4A}}
{{judri|c5e7d13}}
:'''le xamgu be le ctuca [ku] be'o zdani'''
:<code>the good (for the teacher) house</code>

requires either {{vla|ku}} or {{vla|be'o}}, and since there is only one occurrence of {{vla|be}}, the {{vla|be'o}} must match it, whereas it may be confusing which occurrence of {{vla|le}} the {{vla|ku}} terminates (in fact the second one is correct).

{{ssp|section-co-inversion}}
==Inversion of tanru: {{vla|co}}==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|co}}
:{{s|CO}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion}} The standard order of Lojban tanru, whereby the modifier precedes what it modifies, is very natural to English-speakers: we talk of “blue houses”, not of “houses blue”. In other languages, however, such matters are differently arranged, and Lojban supports this reverse order (tertau before seltau) by inserting the particle {{vla|co}}. {{lex|example-random-id-qjtV}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}} mean exactly the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjtV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjtV}}
{{judri|c5e8d1}}
:'''ta blanu zdani'''
:<code>That is-a-blue type-of-house.</code>
:''That is a blue house.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjty}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjty}}
{{judri|c5e8d2}}
:'''ta zdani co blanu'''
:<code>That is-a-house of-type blue.</code>
:''That is a blue house.''

{{ind|general-imported|seltau|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|tertau|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|definition}} This change is called “tanru inversion”. In tanru inversion, the element before 
{{vla|co}} ( {{vla|zdani}} in {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}}) is the tertau, and the element following {{vla|co}} ( {{vla|blanu}}) in {{lex|example-random-id-qjty}}) is the seltau.

{{ind|general-imported|place structure and tanru inversion}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion and place structure}} The meaning, and more specifically, the place structure, of a tanru is not affected by inversion: the place structure of 
:{{jbo|zdani co blanu}} is still that of {{vla|zdani}}. However, the existence of inversion in a selbri has a very special effect on any sumti which follow that selbri. Instead of being interpreted as filling places of the selbri, they actually fill the places (starting with x2) of the seltau. In {{ls|section-be-sumti}}, we saw how to fill interior places with {{vla|be}}&hellip;{{vla|bei}}&hellip;{{vla|be'o}}, and in fact {{lex|example-random-id-qjuc}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}} have the same meaning:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjuc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjuc}}
{{judri|c5e8d3}}
:'''mi klama be le zarci bei le zdani be'o troci'''
:<code>I am-a-(goer to the market from the house) type-of trier.</code>
:''I try to go to the market from the house.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjVx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjVx}}

{{ind|example|try to go|example}}
{{judri|c5e8d4}}
:'''mi troci co klama le zarci le zdani'''
:<code>I am-a-trier of-type (goer to-the market from-the house).</code>
:''I try to go to the market from the house.''
{{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}} is a less deeply nested construction, requiring fewer cmavo. As a result it is probably easier to understand.

Note that in Lojban “trying to go” is expressed using {{vla|troci}} as the tertau. The reason is that “trying to go” is a “going type of trying”, not a “trying type of going”. The trying is more fundamental than the going &ndash; if the trying fails, we may not have a going at all.

{{ind|general-imported|inverted tanru|effect on sumti after the selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|inverted tanru|effect on sumti before the selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|unfilled places of inverted tanru}} Any sumti which precede a selbri with an inverted tanru fill the places of the selbri (i.e., the places of the tertau) in the ordinary way. In {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}}, {{vla|mi}} fills the x1 place of 
:{{jbo|troci co klama}}, which is the x1 place of {{vla|troci}}. The other places of the selbri remain unfilled. The trailing sumti 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} and 
:{{jbo|le zdani}} do not occupy selbri places, despite appearances.

As a result, the regular mechanisms (involving selma'o VOhA and GOhI, explained in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}) for referring to individual sumti of a bridi cannot refer to any of the trailing places of {{lex|example-random-id-qjVx}}, because they are not really “sumti of the bridi” at all.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|where allowed}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|in complex tanru}} When inverting a more complex tanru, it is possible to invert it only at the most general modifier-modified pair. The only possible inversion of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}}, for instance, is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7uS2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7uS2}}
{{judri|c5e8d5}}
:'''ta nixli [bo] ckule co cmalu'''
:<code>That (is-a-girl type-of school) of-type little.</code>
:''That's a girls' school which is small.''

{{ind|general-imported|tanru grouping|effect of tanru inversion on}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|effect on tanru grouping}} 
Note that the {{vla|bo}} of {{lex|example-random-id-nwuU}} is optional in {{lex|example-random-id-7uS2}}, because {{vla|co}} groups more loosely than any other cmavo used in tanru, including none at all. Not even {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} parentheses can encompass a {{vla|co}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-y501}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-y501}}
{{judri|c5e8d6}}
:'''ta cmalu ke nixli ckule [ke'e] co melbi'''
:<code>That is-a-(little type-of (girl type-of school)) of-type pretty.</code>
:''That's a small school for girls which is beautiful.''

{{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|rule for removing}} In {{lex|example-random-id-y501}}, the {{vla|ke'e}} is automatically inserted before the {{vla|co}} rather than at its usual place at the end of the selbri. As a result, there is a simple and mechanical rule for removing {{vla|co}} from any selbri: change “A co B” to “ke B ke'e A”. (At the same time, any sumti following the selbri must be transformed into {{vla|be}}&hellip;{{vla|bei}}&hellip;{{vla|be'o}} form and attached following B.) Therefore,

{{dsp|example-random-id-4c0A}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4c0A}}
{{judri|c5e8d7}}
:'''ckule co melbi nixli'''
:<code>school of-type pretty girl</code>
:''school for beautiful girls''

means the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-w5cI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-w5cI}}
{{judri|c5e8d8}}
:'''ke melbi nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>(pretty girl) school</code>

{{ind|general-imported|multiple tanru inversion|effect on grouping}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru inversion|multiple}} Multiple {{vla|co}} cmavo can appear within a selbri, indicating multiple inversions: a right-grouping rule is employed, as for
