{{vla|bo}}. The above rule can be applied to interpret such selbri, but all {{vla|co}} cmavo must be removed simultaneously:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yLn5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yLn5}}
{{judri|c5e8d9}}
:'''ckule co nixli co cmalu'''
:<code>school of-type (girl of-type little)</code>

becomes formally

{{dsp|example-random-id-mM3Q}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mM3Q}}
{{judri|c5e8d10}}
:'''ke ke cmalu ke'e nixli ke'e ckule'''
:<code>( (little) girl ) school</code>

which by the left-grouping rule is simply

{{dsp|example-random-id-LGRz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LGRz}}
{{judri|c5e8d11}}
:'''cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>little girl school</code>
:''school for little girls''

As stated above, the selbri places, other than the first, of

{{dsp|example-random-id-Qcwd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Qcwd}}
{{judri|c5e8d12}}
:'''mi klama co sutra'''
:<code>I am-a-goer of-type quick</code>
:''I go quickly''

cannot be filled by placing sumti after the selbri, because any sumti in that position fill the places of {{vla|sutra}}, the seltau. However, the tertau places (which means in effect the selbri places) can be filled with {{vla|be}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PDAh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PDAh}}
{{judri|c5e8d13}}
:'''mi klama be le zarci be'o co sutra'''
:<code>I am-a-goer (to the store) of-type quick.</code>
:''I go to the store quickly.''

{{ssp|section-cmavo-selbri}}
==Other kinds of simple selbri==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|go'i}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|du}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|nu'a}}
:{{s|NUhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|moi}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|mei}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|nu}}
:{{s|NU}}
:''description''

:{{c|kei}}
:{{s|KEI}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|equivalents to brivla}}  {{ind|general-imported|brivla equivalents}} So far we have only discussed brivla and tanru built up from brivla as possible selbri. In fact, there are a few other constructions in Lojban which are grammatically equivalent to brivla: they can be used either directly as selbri, or as components in tanru. Some of these types of simple selbri are discussed at length in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}, {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}, and {{lch|chapter-mekso}}; but for completeness these types are mentioned here with a brief explanation and an example of their use in selbri.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|with GOhA}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|with GOhA}}  {{ind|general-imported|GOhA selma'o|as component in tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|GOhA selma'o|as selbri}} The cmavo of selma'o GOhA (with one exception) serve as pro-bridi, providing a reference to the content of other bridi; none of them has a fixed meaning. The most commonly used member of GOhA is probably {{vla|go'i}}, which amounts to a repetition of the previous bridi, or part of it. If I say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2UvG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2UvG}}
{{judri|c5e9d1}}
:'''la djan. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John goes-to the market.</code>

you may retort:

{{dsp|example-random-id-EvoD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-EvoD}}
{{judri|c5e9d2}}
:'''la djan. go'i troci'''
:<code>John [repeat last] are-a-tryer</code>
:''John tries to.''
{{lex|example-random-id-EvoD}} is short for:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nKQ3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nKQ3}}
{{judri|c5e9d3}}
:'''la djan. klama be le zarci be'o troci'''
:<code>John is-a-goer (to the market) type-of trier.</code>

because the whole bridi of {{lex|example-random-id-2UvG}} has been packaged up into the single word {{vla|go'i}} and inserted into {{lex|example-random-id-EvoD}}.

{{ind|general-imported|du|as an exception within GOhA selma'o}} The exceptional member of GOhA is {{vla|du}}, which represents the relation of identity. Its place structure is:
:''x1 is identical with x2, x3, ...''
for as many places as are given. More information on selma'o GOhA is available in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|containing mathematical expressions}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions in tanru}} Lojban mathematical expressions (mekso) can be incorporated into selbri in two different ways. Mathematical operators such as 
{{vla|su'i}}, meaning “plus”, can be transformed into selbri by prefixing them with {{vla|nu'a}} (of selma'o NUhA). The resulting place structure is:
:''x1 is the result of applying (the operator) to arguments x2, x3, etc.''
for as many arguments as are required. (The result goes in the x1 place because the number of following places may be indefinite.) For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pp6j}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pp6j}}
{{judri|c5e9d4}}
:'''li vo nu'a su'i li re li re'''
:<code>The-number 4 is-the-sum-of the-number 2 and-the-number 2.</code>

A possible tanru example might be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-K7yz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-K7yz}}
{{ind|example|addition problems|example}}
{{judri|c5e9d5}}
:'''mi jimpe tu'a loi nu'a su'i nabmi'''
:<code>I understand something-about the-mass-of is-the-sum-of problems.</code>
:''I understand addition problems.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|MOI selma'o}}   More usefully, it is possible to combine a mathematical expression with a cmavo of selma'o MOI to create one of various numerical selbri. Details are available in 
{{ls|section-mekso-selbri}}. Here are a few tanru:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjWh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjWh}}

{{ind|example|Preem Palver|example}}
{{judri|c5e9d6}}
:'''la prim. palvr. pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Preem Palver is-the-1-th speaker.</code>
:''Preem Palver is the first speaker.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJwU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJwU}}

{{ind|example|two brothers|example}}
{{judri|c5e9d7}}
:'''la an,iis. joi la .asun. bruna remei'''
:<code>Anyi massed-with Asun are-a-brother type-of-twosome.</code>
:''Anyi and Asun are two brothers.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|NU selma'o}}    Finally, an important type of simple selbri which is not a brivla is the abstraction. Grammatically, abstractions are simple: a cmavo of selma'o NU, followed by a bridi, followed by the elidable terminator {{vla|kei}} of selma'o KEI. Semantically, abstractions are an extremely subtle and powerful feature of Lojban whose full ramifications are documented in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}. A few examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5szz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5szz}}
{{judri|c5e9d8}}
:'''ti nu zdile kei kumfa'''
:<code>This is-an-event-of amusement room.</code>
:''This is an amusement room.''

{{ind|general-imported|abstraction bridi|contrasted with component non-abstraction bridi in meaning}} {{lex|example-random-id-5szz}} is quite distinct in meaning from:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yNSI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yNSI}}
{{judri|c5e9d9}}
:'''ti zdile kumfa'''
:<code>This is-an-amuser room.</code>

which suggests the meaning “a room that amuses someone”.

{{ssp|section-me-selbri}}
==selbri based on sumti: {{vla|me}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|me}}
:{{s|ME}}
:''description''

:{{c|me'u}}
:{{s|MEhU}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|me|place structure of}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of sumti into selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti into selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri from sumti}} A sumti can be made into a simple selbri by preceding it with {{vla|me}} (of selma'o ME) and following it with the elidable terminator {{vla|me'u}} (of selma'o MEhU). This makes a selbri with the place structure
:''x1 is one of the referents of “[the sumti]”''
which is true of the thing, or things, that are the referents of the sumti, and not of anything else. For example, consider the sumti

{{dsp|example-random-id-v6QW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-v6QW}}
{{ind|example|Three Kings|example}}
{{judri|c5e10d1}}
:'''le ci nolraitru'''
:<code>the three noblest-governors</code>
:''the three kings''

If these are understood to be the Three Kings of Christian tradition, who arrive every year on January 6, then we may say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-99r3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-99r3}}
{{judri|c5e10d2}}
:'''la BALtazar. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
<code>Balthazar is one-of-the-referents-of “the three kings”.</code>
:''Balthazar is one of the three kings.''

and likewise

{{dsp|example-random-id-gPnL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gPnL}}
{{judri|c5e10d3}}
:'''la kaspar. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
:''Caspar is one of the three kings.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-4827}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4827}}
{{judri|c5e10d4}}
:'''la melxi,or. cu me le ci nolraitru'''
:''Melchior is one of the three kings.''

{{ind|general-imported|du|compared with me in effect}}  {{ind|general-imported|me|compared with du in effect}}  {{ind|general-imported|me/du equivalence}} If the sumti refers to a single object, then the effect of {{vla|me}} is much like that of {{vla|du}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-HMHc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-HMHc}}
{{judri|c5e10d5}}
:'''do du la djan.'''
:<code>You are-identical-with the-one-called “John”.</code>
:''You are John.''

means the same as

{{dsp|example-random-id-GMCc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GMCc}}
{{judri|c5e10d6}}
:'''do me la djan.'''
<code>You are-the-referent-of “the-one-called "John”".</code>
:''You are John.''

{{ind|general-imported|me|used with names}} It is common to use {{vla|me}} selbri, especially those based on name sumti using {{vla|la}}, as seltau. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-raQG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-raQG}}
{{ind|example|Chrysler|example}}
{{judri|c5e10d7}}
:'''ta me lai kraislr. [me'u] karce'''
<code>That (is-a-referent of “the-mass-called "Chrysler"”) car.</code>
:''That is a Chrysler car.''

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|relative precedence with me'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|me'u|relative precedence with logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|elidability of me'u}} The elidable terminator {{vla|me'u}} can usually be omitted. It is absolutely required only if the {{vla|me}} selbri is being used in an indefinite description (a type of sumti explained in 
{{ls|section-indefinite-descriptions}}), and if the indefinite description is followed by a relative clause (explained in 
{{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}) or a sumti logical connective (explained in {{ls|section-sumti-connection}}). Without a {{vla|me'u}}, the relative clause or logical connective would appear to belong to the sumti embedded in the {{vla|me}} expression. Here is a contrasting pair of sentences:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJyi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJyi}}
{{judri|c5e10d8}}
:'''re me le ci nolraitru .e la djan. [me'u] cu blabi'''
:''Two of the group “the three kings and John” are white.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJyK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJyK}}
{{judri|c5e10d9}}
:'''re me le ci nolraitru me'u .e la djan. cu blabi'''
:''Two of the three kings, and John, are white.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qJyi}} the {{vla|me}} selbri covers the three kings plus John, and the indefinite description picks out two of them that are said to be white: we cannot say which two. In {{lex|example-random-id-qJyK}}, though, the {{vla|me}} selbri covers only the three kings: two of them are said to be white, and so is John.

Finally, here is another example requiring {{vla|me'u}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ygzq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ygzq}}
{{judri|c5e10d10}}
:'''ta me la'e le se cusku be do me'u cukta'''
:<code>That is-a-(what-you-said) type of book.</code>
:''That is the kind of book you were talking about.''

There are other sentences where either {{vla|me'u}} or some other elidable terminator must be expressed:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8yDj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8yDj}}
{{judri|c5e10d11}}
:'''le me le ci nolraitru [ku] me'u nunsalci'''
:<code>the (the three kings) type-of-event-of-celebrating</code>
:''the Three Kings celebration''

requires either {{vla|ku}} or {{vla|me'u}} to be explicit, and (as with {{vla|be'o}} in {{ls|section-be-sumti}}) the {{vla|me'u}} leaves no doubt which cmavo it is paired with.

{{ssp|section-place-conversion}}
==Conversion of simple selbri==
{{ind|lojban-word-imported|xe}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|ve}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|te}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|SE selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|place structure|re-ordering by conversion}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru and conversion}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion and tanru}} Conversion is the process of changing a selbri so that its places appear in a different order. This is not the same as labeling the sumti with the cmavo of FA, as mentioned in {{ls|section-be-sumti}}, and then rearranging the order in which the sumti are spoken or written. Conversion transforms the selbri into a distinct, though closely related, selbri with renumbered places.

In Lojban, conversion is accomplished by placing a cmavo of selma'o SE before the selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-29Gu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-29Gu}}
{{judri|c5e11d1}}
:'''mi prami do'''
:''I love you.''

is equivalent in meaning to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DWcN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DWcN}}
{{judri|c5e11d2}}
:'''do se prami mi'''
:<code>You [swap x1 and x2] love me.</code>
:''You are loved by me.''

Conversion is fully explained in {{ls|section-SE}}. For the purposes of this chapter, the important point about conversion is that it applies only to the following simple selbri. When trying to convert a tanru, therefore, it is necessary to be careful! Consider {{lex|example-random-id-mPX8}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mPX8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mPX8}}
{{ind|example|walk to market|example}}
{{judri|c5e11d3}}
:'''la .alis. cu cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>Alice is-a-walker type-of goer to-the market.</code>
:<code>Alice walkingly goes to the market.</code>
:''Alice walks to the market.''

To convert this sentence so that 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} is in the x1 place, one correct way is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4mbn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4mbn}}
{{judri|c5e11d4}}
:'''le zarci cu se ke cadzu klama [ke'e] la .alis.'''
:<code>The market is-a-[swap x1/x2] (walker type-of goer) Alice.</code>
:<code>The market is-walkingly gone-to by-Alice.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|ke|for conversion of tanru}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion with ke}} The {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} brackets cause the entire tanru to be converted by the {{vla|se}}, which would otherwise convert only {{vla|cadzu}}, leading to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-UNt0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UNt0}}
{{judri|c5e11d5}}
:'''le zarci cu se cadzu klama la .alis.'''
:<code>The market (is-a-[swap x1/x2] walker) type-of goer to Alice.</code>
:<code>The market is-a-walking-surface type-of goer to Alice.</code>

whatever that might mean. An alternative approach, since the place structure of 
:{{jbo|cadzu klama}} is that of {{vla|klama}} alone, is to convert only the latter:

{{dsp|example-random-id-U0fo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-U0fo}}
{{judri|c5e11d6}}
:'''le zarci cu cadzu se klama la .alis.'''
:<code>The market walkingly is-gone-to by-Alice.</code>

But the tanru in {{lex|example-random-id-U0fo}} may or may not have the same meaning as that in {{lex|example-random-id-mPX8}}; in particular, because {{vla|cadzu}} is not converted, there is a suggestion that although Alice is the goer, the market is the walker. With a different sumti as x1, this seemingly odd interpretation might make considerable sense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-XEnd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XEnd}}
{{judri|c5e11d7}}
:'''la djan. cu cadzu se klama la .alis'''
:<code>John walkingly is-gone-to by Alice</code>

suggests that Alice is going to John, who is a moving target.

{{ind|general-imported|tense conversion|with jai}}  {{ind|general-imported|jai|for modal conversion}} There is an alternative type of conversion, using the cmavo {{vla|jai}} of selma'o JAI optionally followed by a modal or tense construction. Grammatically, such a combination behaves exactly like conversion using SE. More details can be found in {{ls|section-modal-jai}}.

{{ssp|section-selbri-scalar-negation}}
==Scalar negation of selbri==
{{ind|general-imported|selbri|scalar negation of}}  {{ind|general-imported|scalar negation|effect on selbri}} Negation is too large and complex a topic to explain fully in this chapter; See {{lch|chapter-negation}}. In brief, there are two main types of negation in Lojban. This section is concerned with so-called “scalar negation”, which is used to state that a true relation between the sumti is something other than what the selbri specifies. Scalar negation is expressed by cmavo of selma'o NAhE:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4oxH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4oxH}}
{{judri|c5e12d1}}
:'''la .alis. cu na'e ke cadzu klama [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>Alice non- (walkingly goes) to-the market.</code>
:<code>Alice other-than (walkingly goes) to-the market.</code>
:''Alice doesn't walk to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|ke|for expanding scope of scalar negation}} meaning that Alice's relationship to the market is something other than that of walking there. But if the {{vla|ke}} were omitted, the result would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NL2Y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NL2Y}}
{{judri|c5e12d2}}
:'''la .alis. cu na'e cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>Alice non- walkingly goes to-the market.</code>
:''Alice doesn't walk to the market.''

meaning that Alice does go there in some way ( {{vla|klama}} is not negated), but by a means other than that of walking. {{lex|example-random-id-4oxH}} negates both {{vla|cadzu}} and {{vla|klama}}, suggesting that Alice's relation to the market is something different from walkingly-going; it might be walking without going, or going without walking, or neither.

Of course, any of the simple selbri types explained in {{ls|section-cmavo-selbri}} may be used in place of brivla in any of these examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YB00}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YB00}}
{{judri|c5e12d3}}
:'''la djonz. cu na'e pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Jones is non-1st speaker</code>
:''Jones is not the first speaker.''

Since only {{vla|pamoi}} is negated, an appropriate inference is that he is some other kind of speaker.

{{ind|general-imported|negation|complex examples}}  {{ind|general-imported|complex negation|examples}} Here is an assortment of more complex examples showing the interaction of scalar negation with {{vla|bo}} grouping, {{vla|ke}} and {{vla|ke'e}} grouping, logical connection, and sumti linked with {{vla|be}} and {{vla|bei}}:

{{ind|general-imported|na'e|contrasted with na'e ke}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-I1Rd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I1Rd}}
{{judri|c5e12d4}}
:'''mi na'e sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (non-quickly) ( walking using the arms) ) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, walking using my arms other than quickly.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-I1Rd}}, {{vla|na'e}} negates only {{vla|sutra}}. Contrast {{lex|example-random-id-KcK8}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KcK8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KcK8}}
{{judri|c5e12d5}}
:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I non- ( quickly (walking using the arms) ) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, other than by walking quickly on my arms.''

Now consider {{lex|example-random-id-qjyW}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjyy}}, which are equivalent in meaning, but use {{vla|ke}} grouping and {{vla|bo}} grouping respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjyW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjyW}}
{{judri|c5e12d6}}
:'''mi sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I (quickly &ndash; (walking using the arms) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both quickly walking using my arms and slowly.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjyy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjyy}}
{{judri|c5e12d7}}
:'''mi ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (quickly (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both quickly walking using my arms and slowly.''

However, if we place a {{vla|na'e}} at the beginning of the selbri in both {{lex|example-random-id-qjyW}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qjyy}}, we get different results:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjyz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjyz}}
{{judri|c5e12d8}}
:'''mi na'e sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I ( (non- quickly) - (walking using the arms) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both walking using my arms other than quickly, and also slowly.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qJzr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qJzr}}
{{judri|c5e12d9}}
:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka [be'o] ke'e je masno klama le zarci'''
:<code>I (non-(quickly (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market, both other than quickly walking using my arms, and also slowly.''

The difference arises because the {{vla|na'e}} in {{lex|example-random-id-qJzr}} negates the whole construction from {{vla|ke}} to {{vla|ke'e}}, whereas in {{lex|example-random-id-qjyz}} it negates {{vla|sutra}} alone.

{{ind|general-imported|perils of omitting terminators}}  {{ind|general-imported|omitting terminators|perils of}} Beware of omitting terminators in these complex examples! If the explicit 
{{vla|ke'e}} is left out in {{lex|example-random-id-qJzr}}, it is transformed into:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Y53U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Y53U}}
{{judri|c5e12d10}}
:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka be'o je masno klama [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>I non-(quickly ( (walking using the arms) ) and slowly) go-to) the market.</code>
:<code>I do something other than quickly both going to the market walking</code>
:''using my arms and slowly going to the market.''

And if both {{vla|ke'e}} and {{vla|be'o}} are omitted, the results are even sillier:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0WLq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0WLq}}
{{judri|c5e12d11}}
:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be fi le birka je masno klama [be'o] [ke'e] le zarci'''
:<code>I non-(quickly walk on my (arm-type and slow) goers) on the market.</code>
:''I do something other than quickly walking using the goers, both arm-type and slow, relative-to the market.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-0WLq}}, everything after {{vla|be}} is a linked sumti, so the place structure is that of 
{{vla|cadzu}}, whose x2 place is the surface walked upon. It is less than clear what an “arm-type goer” might be. Furthermore, since the x3 place has been occupied by the linked sumti, the 

:{{jbo|le zarci}} following the selbri falls into the nonexistent x4 place of {{vla|cadzu}}. As a result, the whole example, though grammatical, is complete nonsense. (The bracketed Lojban words appear where a fluent Lojbanist would understand them to be implied.)

{{ind|general-imported|na'e|before gu'e}} Finally, it is also possible to place {{vla|na'e}} before a {{vla|gu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} logically connected tanru construction. The meaning of this usage has not yet been firmly established.

{{ssp|section-bridi-negation-tenses}}
==Tenses and bridi negation==
A bridi can have cmavo associated with it which specify the time, place, or mode of action. For example, in

{{dsp|example-random-id-uz13}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uz13}}
{{judri|c5e13d1}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past] go to-the market.</code>
:''I went to the market.''

the cmavo {{vla|pu}} specifies that the action of the speaker going to the market takes place in the past. Tenses are explained in full detail in {{lch|chapter-tenses}}. Tense is semantically a property of the entire bridi; however, the usual syntax for tenses attaches them at the front of the selbri, as in {{lex|example-random-id-uz13}}. There are alternative ways of expressing tense information as well. Modals, which are explained in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}}, behave in the same way as tenses.

Similarly, a bridi may have the particle {{vla|na}} (of selma'o NA) attached to the beginning of the selbri to negate the bridi. A negated bridi expresses what is false without saying anything about what is true. Do not confuse this usage with the scalar negation of {{ls|section-selbri-scalar-negation}}. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PYSP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PYSP}}
{{judri|c5e13d2}}
:'''la djonz. na pamoi cusku'''
:<code>Jones (Not!) is-the-first speaker</code>
:<code>It is not true that Jones is the first speaker.</code>
:''Jones isn't the first speaker.''

Jones may be the second speaker, or not a speaker at all; {{lex|example-random-id-PYSP}} doesn't say. There are other ways of expressing bridi negation as well; the topic is explained fully in {{lch|chapter-negation}}.

{{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|relative order with tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|relative order with bridi negation}} Various combinations of tense and bridi negation cmavo are permitted. If both are expressed, either order is permissible with no change in meaning:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RV4C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RV4C}}
{{judri|c5e13d3}}
:'''mi na pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>mi pu na klama le zarci</code>
:<code>It is false that I went to the market.</code>
:''I didn't go to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|multiple}} It is also possible to have more than one {{vla|na}}, in which case pairs of {{vla|na}} cmavo cancel out:

{{dsp|example-random-id-TuP7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TuP7}}
{{judri|c5e13d4}}
:'''mi na na klama le zarci'''
:<code>It is false that it is false that I go to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|tense and na|multiple}}  {{ind|general-imported|na and tense|multiple}} It is even possible, though somewhat pointless, to have multiple {{vla|na}} cmavo and tense cmavo mixed together, subject to the limitation that two adjacent tense cmavo will be understood as a compound tense, and must fit the grammar of tenses as explained in 
{{lch|chapter-tenses}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-hw6g}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hw6g}}
{{judri|c5e13d5}}
:'''mi na pu na ca klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [not] [past] [not] [present] go to-the market</code>
:<code>It is not the case that in the past it was not the case that in the present I went to the market.</code>
:<code>I didn't not go to the market.</code>
:''I went to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|negation cmavo|position relative to selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal cmavo|position relative to selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense cmavo|position relative to selbri}} Tense, modal, and negation cmavo can appear only at the beginning of the selbri. They cannot be embedded within it.

{{ssp|section-asymmetric-tanru}}
==Some types of asymmetrical tanru==

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|asymmetrical}}  {{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru}} This section and {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}} contain some example tanru classified into groups based on the type of relationship between the modifying seltau and the modified tertau. All the examples are paralleled by compounds actually observed in various natural languages. In the tables which follow, each group is preceded by a brief explanation of the relationship. The tables themselves contain a tanru, a literal gloss, an indication of the languages which exhibit a compound analogous to this tanru, and (for those tanru with no English parallel) a translation.

{{ind|general-imported|languages|abbreviations for}} Here are the 3-letter abbreviations used for the various languages (it is presumed to be obvious whether a compound is found in English or not, so English is not explicitly noted):

;'''Aba'''
:Abazin

;'''Chi'''
:Chinese

;'''Ewe'''
:Ewe

;'''Fin'''
:Finnish

;'''Geo'''
:Georgian

;'''Gua'''
:Guarani

;'''Hop'''
:Hopi

;'''Hun'''
:Hungarian

;'''Imb'''
:Imbabura Quechua

;'''Kar'''
:Karaitic

;'''Kaz'''
:Kazakh

;'''Kor'''
:Korean

;'''Mon'''
:Mongolian

;'''Qab'''
:Qabardian

;'''Que'''
:Quechua

;'''Rus'''
:Russian

;'''Skt'''
:Sanskrit

;'''Swe'''
:Swedish

;'''Tur'''
:Turkish

;'''Udm'''
:Udmurt

Any lujvo or fu'ivla used in a group are glossed at the end of that group.

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru|definition}} The tanru discussed in this section are asymmetrical tanru; that is, ones in which the order of the terms is fundamental to the meaning of the tanru. For example, 

:{{jbo|junla dadysli}}, or “clock pendulum”, is the kind of pendulum used in a clock, whereas 
:{{jbo|dadysli junla}}, or “pendulum clock”, is the kind of clock that employs a pendulum. Most tanru are asymmetrical in this sense. Symmetrical tanru are discussed in {{ls|section-symmetric-tanru}}.

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object-of-action + action}} The tertau represents an action, and the seltau then represents the object of that action:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>{{jbo|pinsi nunkilbra}}	pencil sharpener	Hun
{{jbo|zgike nunctu}}	music instruction	Hun
{{jbo|mirli nunkalte}}	deer hunting	Hun
{{jbo|finpe nunkalte}}	fish hunting	Tur,Kor,Udm,Aba	fishing
{{jbo|smacu terkavbu}}	mousetrap	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|zdani turni}}	house ruler	Kar	host
{{jbo|zerle'a nunte'a}}	thief fear	Skt	fear of thieves
{{jbo|cevni zekri}}	god crime	Skt	offense against the gods
</tab>

;{{vla|nunkilbra}}
:sharpness-apparatus

;{{vla|nunctu}}
:event-of-teaching

;{{vla|nunkalte}}
:event-of-hunting

;{{vla|terkavbu}}
:trap

;{{vla|zerle'a}}
:crime-taker

;{{vla|nunte'a}}
:event-of-fearing

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|elements-in-set + set}} The tertau represents a set, and the seltau the type of the elements contained in that set:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|zdani lijgri}}	house row
{{jbo|selci lamgri}}	cell block
{{jbo|karda mulgri}}	card pack	Swe
{{jbo|rokci derxi}}	stone heap	Swe
{{jbo|tadni girzu}}	student group	Hun
{{jbo|remna girzu}}	human-being group	Qab	group of people
{{jbo|cpumi'i lijgri}}	tractor column	Qab
{{jbo|cevni jenmi}}	god army	Skt
{{jbo|cevni prenu}}	god folk	Skt
</tab>

;{{vla|lijgri}}
:line-group

;{{vla|lamgri}}
:adjacent-group

;{{vla|mulgri}}
:complete-group

;{{vla|cpumi'i}}
:pull-machine

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|set + element-of-set}} Conversely: the tertau is an element, and the seltau represents a set in which that element is contained. Implicitly, the meaning of the tertau is restricted from its usual general meaning to the specific meaning appropriate for elements in the given set. Note the opposition between 
:{{jbo|zdani linji}} in the previous group, and 
:{{jbo|linji zdani}} in this one, which shows why this kind of tanru is called “asymmetrical”.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|carvi dirgo}}	raindrop	Tur,Kor,Hun,Udm,Aba
{{jbo|linji zdani}}	row house
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object + component/detail}} The seltau specifies an object and the tertau a component or detail of that object; the tanru as a whole refers to the detail, specifying that it is a detail of that whole and not some other.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|junla dadysli}}	clock pendulum	Hun
{{jbo|purdi vorme}}	garden door	Qab
{{jbo|purdi bitmu}}	garden wall	Que
{{jbo|moklu skapi}}	mouth skin	Imb	lips
{{jbo|nazbi kevna}}	nose hole	Imb	nostril
{{jbo|karce xislu}}	automobile wheel	Chi
{{jbo|jipci pimlu}}	chicken feather	Chi
{{jbo|vinji rebla}}	airplane tail	Chi
</tab>

;{{vla|dadysli}}
:hang-oscillator

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|characteristic/detail + object}} Conversely: the seltau specifies a characteristic or important detail of the object described by the tertau; objects described by the tanru as a whole are differentiated from other similar objects by this detail.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|pixra cukta}}	picture book
{{jbo|kerfa silka}}	hair silk	Kar	velvet
{{jbo|plise tapla}}	apple cake	Tur
{{jbo|dadysli junla}}	pendulum clock	Hun
</tab>
;{{vla|dadysli}}
:hang-oscillator

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|general-class + sub-class}} The tertau specifies a general class of object (a genus), and the seltau specifies a sub-class of that class (a species):
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|ckunu tricu}}	pine tree	Hun,Tur,Hop
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|possessor + object}} The tertau specifies an object of possession, and the seltau may specify the possessor (the possession may be intrinsic or otherwise). In English, these compounds have an explicit possessive element in them: “lion's mane”, “child's foot”, “noble's cow”.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cinfo kerfa}}	lion mane	Kor,Tur,Hun,Udm,Qab
{{jbo|verba jamfu}}	child foot	Swe
{{jbo|nixli tuple}}	girl leg	Swe
{{jbo|cinfo jamfu}}	lion foot	Que
{{jbo|danlu skapi}}	animal skin	Ewe
{{jbo|ralju zdani}}	chief house	Ewe
{{jbo|jmive munje}}	living world	Skt
{{jbo|nobli bakni}}	noble cow	Skt
{{jbo|nolraitru ralju}}	king chief	Skt	emperor
</tab>


;{{vla|nolraitru}}
:nobly-superlative-ruler

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|inhabitant + habitat}} The tertau specifies a habitat, and the seltau specifies the inhabitant:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|lanzu tumla}}	family land
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|effect + causative agent}} The tertau specifies a causative agent, and the seltau specifies the effect of that cause:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kalselvi'i gapci}}	tear gas	Hun
{{jbo|terbi'a jurme}}	disease germ	Tur
{{jbo|fenki litki}}	crazy liquid	Hop	whisky
{{jbo|pinca litki}}	urine liquid	Hop	beer
</tab>


;{{vla|kalselvi'i}}
:eye-excreted-thing

;{{vla|terbi'a}}
:disease

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|cause + effect}} Conversely: the tertau specifies an effect, and the seltau specifies its cause.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|djacu barna}}	water mark	Chi
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|purpose-of-instrument + instrument}} The tertau specifies an instrument, and the seltau specifies the purpose of that instrument:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|taxfu dadgreku}}	garment rack	Chi
{{jbo|tergu'i ti'otci}}	lamp shade	Chi
{{jbo|xirma zdani}}	horse house	Chi	stall
{{jbo|nuzba tanbo}}	news board	Chi	bulletin board
</tab>


;{{vla|dadgreku}}
:hang-frame

;{{vla|tergu'i}}
:source of illumination

;{{vla|ti'otci}}
:shadow-tool

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object-of-purpose-of-instrument + instrument}} More vaguely: the tertau specifies an instrument, and the seltau specifies the object of the purpose for which that instrument is used:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cpina rokci}}	pepper stone	Que	stone for grinding pepper
{{jbo|jamfu djacu}}	foot water	Skt	water for washing the feet

{{jbo|lanme gerku}}	sheep dog		dog for working sheep
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|source + product}} The tertau specifies a product from some source, and the seltau specifies the source of the product:

{{jbo|ractu mapku}}	rabbit hat	Rus

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|product + source}} Conversely: the tertau specifies the source of a product, and the seltau specifies the product:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|silna jinto}}	salt well	Chi
{{jbo|kolme terkakpa}}	coal mine	Chi
{{jbo|ctile jinto}}	oil well	Chi
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|source-material + object}} The tertau specifies an object, and the seltau specifies the material from which the object is made. This case is especially interesting, because the referent of the tertau may normally be made from just one kind of material, which is then overridden in the tanru.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|rokci cinfo}}	stone lion
{{jbo|snime nanmu}}	snow man	Hun
{{jbo|kliti cipni}}	clay bird

{{jbo|blaci kanla}}	glass eye	Que	spectacles
{{jbo|solji sicni}}	gold coin	Tur
{{jbo|solji junla}}	gold watch	Tur,Kor,Hun
{{jbo|solji djine}}	gold ring	Udm,Aba,Que
{{jbo|rokci zdani}}	stone house	Imb
{{jbo|mudri zdani}}	wood house	Ewe	wooden house
{{jbo|rokci bitmu}}	stone wall	Ewe
{{jbo|solji carce}}	gold chariot	Skt
{{jbo|mudri xarci}}	wood weapon	Skt	wooden weapon
{{jbo|cmaro'i dargu}}	pebble road	Chi
{{jbo|sudysrasu cutci}}	straw shoe	Chi
</tab>

:small-rock

;{{vla|sudysrasu}}

Note: the two senses of 
:{{jbo|blaci kanla}} can be discriminated as:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|blaci kanla bo tarmi}}	glass (eye shape)	glass eye
{{jbo|blaci kanla bo sidju}}	glass (eye helper)	spectacles
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object-measured + standard-object}} The tertau specifies a typical object used to measure a quantity and the seltau specifies something measured. The tanru as a whole refers to a given quantity of the thing being measured. English does not have compounds of this form, as a rule.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|tumla spisa}}	land piece	Tur	piece of land
{{jbo|tcati kabri}}	tea cup	Kor,Aba	cup of tea
{{jbo|nanba spisa}}	bread piece	Kor	piece of bread
{{jbo|bukpu spisa}}	cloth piece	Udm,Aba	piece of cloth
{{jbo|djacu calkyguzme}}	water calabash	Ewe	calabash of water
</tab>


;{{vla|calkyguzme}}
:shell-fruit, calabash

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|overriding-property + object-with-implicit-properties}} The tertau specifies an object with certain implicit properties, and the seltau overrides one of those implicit properties:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kensa bloti}}	spaceship
{{jbo|bakni verba}}	cattle child	Ewe	calf
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|whole + part}} The seltau specifies a whole, and the tertau specifies a part which normally is associated with a different whole. The tanru then refers to a part of the seltau which stands in the same relationship to the whole seltau as the tertau stands to its typical whole.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|kosta degji}}	coat finger	Hun	coat sleeve
{{jbo|denci genja}}	tooth root	Imb
{{jbo|tricu stedu}}	tree head	Imb	treetop
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|product + producer}} The tertau specifies the producer of a certain product, and the seltau specifies the product. In this way, the tanru as a whole distinguishes its referents from other referents of the tertau which do not produce the product.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|silka curnu}}	silkworm	Tur,Hun,Aba
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object-giving-characteristic + other-object}} The tertau specifies an object, and the seltau specifies another object which has a characteristic property. The tanru as a whole refers to those referents of the tertau which possess the property.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|sonci manti}}	soldier ant
{{jbo|ninmu bakni}}	woman cattle	Imb	cow
{{jbo|mamta degji}}	mother finger	Imb	thumb
{{jbo|cifnu degji}}	baby finger	Imb	pinky
{{jbo|pacraistu zdani}}	hell house	Skt
{{jbo|fagri dapma}}	fire curse	Skt	curse destructive as fire
</tab>


;{{vla|pacraistu}}
:evil-superlative-site

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|similar-appearance-object + object}} As a particular case (when the property is that of resemblance): the seltau specifies an object which the referent of the tanru resembles.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|grutrceraso jbama}}	cherry bomb
{{jbo|solji kerfa}}	gold hair	Hun	golden hair
{{jbo|kanla djacu}}	eye water	Kar	spring

</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|typical-place + object}} The seltau specifies a place, and the tertau an object characteristically located in or at that place.

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|object + place-sold}} Specifically: the tertau is a place where the seltau is sold or made available to the public.

{{ind|general-imported|asymmetrical tanru types|miscellaneous}} Finally, some tanru which don't fall into any of the above categories.
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|ladru denci}}	milk tooth	Tur,Hun,Udm,Qab
{{jbo|kanla denci}}	eye tooth
</tab>
It is clear that “tooth” is being specified, and that “milk” and “eye” act as modifiers. However, the relationship between {{vla|ladru}} and {{vla|denci}} is something like “tooth which one has when one is drinking milk from one's mother”, a relationship certainly present nowhere except in this particular concept. As for 
:{{jbo|kanla denci}}, the relationship is not only not present on the surface, it is hardly possible to formulate it at all.

{{ssp|section-symmetric-tanru}}
==Some types of symmetrical tanru==

{{ind|general-imported|symmetrical tanru}} This section deals with symmetrical tanru, where order is not important. Many of these tanru can be expressed with a logical or non-logical connective between the components.

{{ind|general-imported|symmetrical tanru types|both separately true}} The tanru may refer to things which are correctly specified by both tanru components. Some of these instances may also be seen as asymmetrical tanru where the seltau specifies a material. The connective 
{{vla|je}} is appropriate:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
{{jbo|cipnrstrigi pacru'i}}	owl demon	Skt
{{jbo|nolraitru prije}}	royal sage	Skt
{{jbo|remna nakni}}	human-being male	Qab	man
{{jbo|remna fetsi}}	human-being female	Qab	woman
{{jbo|sonci tolvri}}	soldier coward	Que
{{jbo|panzi nanmu}}	offspring man	Ewe	son
{{jbo|panzi ninmu}}	offspring woman	Ewe	daughter
{{jbo|solji sicni}}	gold coin	Tur
{{jbo|solji junla}}	gold watch	Tur,Kor,Hun
{{jbo|solji djine}}	gold ring	Udm,Aba,Que
{{jbo|rokci zdani}}	stone house	Imb
{{jbo|mudri zdani}}	wooden house	Ewe
{{jbo|rokci bitmu}}	stone wall	Ewe
{{jbo|solji carce}}	gold chariot	Skt
{{jbo|mudri xarci}}	wooden weapon	Skt
{{jbo|zdani tcadu}}	home town	Chi
</tab>

:fu'ivla for “owl” based on Linnean name

;{{vla|pacru'i}}

;{{vla|tolvri}}
:opposite-of-brave

{{ind|general-imported|symmetrical tanru types|one or other true}} The tanru may refer to all things which are specified by either of the tanru components. The connective {{vla|ja}} is appropriate:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>

{{jbo|donri nicte}}	day night	Skt	day and night

{{jbo|bersa tixnu}}	son daughter	Chi	children
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|symmetrical tanru types|using more inclusive class}} Alternatively, the tanru may refer to things which are specified by either of the tanru components or by some more inclusive class of things which the components typify:

</tab>

{{ssp|section-pretty-school-groupings}}
==“Pretty little girls' school”: forty ways to say it==
{{ind|general-imported|pretty little girls' school|forty ways}} The following examples show every possible grouping arrangement of 
:{{jbo|melbi cmalu nixli ckule}} using {{vla|bo}} or {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} for grouping and {{vla|je}} or {{vla|je}}{{vla|bo}} for logical connection. Most of these are definitely not plausible interpretations of the English phrase “pretty little girls' school”, especially those which describe something which is both a girl and a school.

Examples {{lex|example-random-id-qjmr}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjNi}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjog}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qjop}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-tz0L}} are repeated here as Examples {{lex|example-random-id-qjzw}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKaM}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKfX}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKmg}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-qKPQ}} respectively.
<!-- was: Examples 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and 5.6 are repeated here as Examples 16.1, 16.9, 16.17, 16.25, and 16.33 respectively. -->
The seven examples following each of these share the same grouping pattern, but differ in the presence or absence of {{vla|je}} at each possible site. Some of the examples have more than one Lojban version. In that case, they differ only in grouping mechanism, and are always equivalent in meaning.

The logical connective {{vla|je}} is associative: that is, “A and (B and C)” is the same as “(A and B) and C”. Therefore, some of the examples have the same meaning as others. In particular, {{lex|example-random-id-qKAG}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKFA}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKLN}}, {{lex|example-random-id-qKpo}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-qKU6}} all have the same meaning because all four brivla are logically connected and the grouping is simply irrelevant.
<!-- was: In particular, 16.8, 16.16, 16.24, 16.32, and 16.40 all have the same meaning -->
Other equivalent forms are noted in the examples themselves. However, if 
{{vla|je}} were replaced by {{vla|naja}} or {{vla|jo}} or most of the other logical connectives, the meanings would become distinct.

It must be emphasized that, because of the ambiguity of all tanru, the English translations are by no means definitive &ndash; they represent only one possible interpretation of the corresponding Lojban sentence.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qjzw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qjzw}}
{{judri|c5e16d1}}
:'''melbi cmalu nixli ckule'''
:<code>((pretty type-of little) type-of girl) type-of school</code>
:''school for girls who are beautifully small''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qK2W}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qK2W}}

:''thing which is beautiful, a small girl, and a school''

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{csp|chapter-sumti}}
=To Speak Of Many Things: The Lojban sumti=
{{image|chapter-sumti-picture|The picture for chapter 6|CLL-chapter-sumti.gif}}
{{ssp|section-simple-sumti-kinds}}
==The five kinds of simple sumti==

{{ind|general-imported|sumti|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|simple sumti}} If you understand anything about Lojban, you know what a sumti is by now, right? An argument, one of those things that fills the places of simple Lojban sentences like:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VKU6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VKU6}}
{{judri|c6e1d1}}
:'''mi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I go-to the market</code>

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|contrasted with description}} In {{lex|example-random-id-VKU6}}, {{vla|mi}} and 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} are the sumti. It is easy to see that these two sumti are not of the same kind: {{vla|mi}} is a pro-sumti (the Lojban analogue of a pronoun) referring to the speaker, whereas 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} is a description which refers to something described as being a market.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti|kinds of}} There are five kinds of simple sumti provided by Lojban:
*{{ind|general-imported|gadri|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|descriptions as}} descriptions like 
:{{jbo|le zarci}}, which usually begin with a descriptor (called a {{vla|gadri}} in Lojban) such as 
{{vla|le}};
*{{ind|general-imported|sumti|pro-sumti as}} pro-sumti, such as {{vla|mi}};
*{{ind|general-imported|sumti|names as}} names, such as 
:{{jbo|la lojban.}}, which usually begin with {{vla|la}};
*{{ind|general-imported|sumti|quotations as}} quotations, which begin with {{vla|lu}}, {{vla|le'u}}, {{vla|zo}}, or {{vla|zoi}};
*{{ind|general-imported|sumti|numbers as}} pure numbers, which usually begin with {{vla|li}}.


Here are a few examples of each kind of sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Dx1s}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Dx1s}}
{{judri|c6e1d2}}
:'''e'osai ko sarji la lojban.'''
:''Please support Lojban!''
{{lex|example-random-id-Dx1s}} exhibits {{vla|ko}}, a pro-sumti; and 
:{{jbo|la lojban.}}, a name.

{{dsp|example-random-id-v1mS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-v1mS}}
{{judri|c6e1d3}}
:'''mi cusku lu e'osai li'u le tcidu'''
:''I express “Please!” to-the reader.''

<!-- FIXME: these three indexterms aren't tagged alone -->{{ind|lojban-word-imported|le}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|li'u}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|lu}}  {{lex|example-random-id-v1mS}} exhibits {{vla|mi}}, a pro-sumti; 
:{{jbo|lu e'osai li'u}}, a quotation; and 
:{{jbo|le tcidu}}, a description.

{{dsp|example-random-id-0YaH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0YaH}}
{{judri|c6e1d4}}
:'''ti mitre li ci'''
:<code>This measures-in-meters the-number three.</code>
:''This is three meters long.''

<!-- FIXME: this indexterm isn't tagged alone -->{{ind|lojban-word-imported|li}}  {{lex|example-random-id-0YaH}} exhibits {{vla|ti}}, a pro-sumti; and 
:{{jbo|li ci}}, a number.

Most of this chapter is about descriptions, as they have the most complicated syntax and usage. Some attention is also given to names, which are closely interwoven with descriptions. Pro-sumti, numbers, and quotations are described in more detail in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}, {{lch|chapter-mekso}}, and {{lch|chapter-structure}} respectively, so this chapter only gives summaries of their forms and uses. See {{ls|section-pro-sumti}} through {{ls|section-number-summary}} for these summaries.

{{ssp|section-basic-descriptors}}
==The three basic description types==
{{ind|general-imported|descriptions|types of}} The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|le}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lo}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|la}}
:{{s|LA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ku}}
:{{s|KU}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|selbri|as part of description}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptor|as part of description}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptions|components of}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptions|types of}} The syntax of descriptions is fairly complex, and not all of it can be explained within the confines of this chapter: relative clauses, in particular, are discussed in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}. However, most descriptions have just two components: a descriptor belonging to selma'o LE or LA, and a selbri. (The difference between selma'o LE and selma'o LA is not important until {{ls|section-names}}.) Furthermore, the selbri is often just a single brivla. Here is an elementary example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rBuQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rBuQ}}
{{judri|c6e2d1}}
:'''le zarci'''
:<code>one-or-more-specific-things-each-of-which-I-describe-as being-a-market</code>
:''the market''

{{ind|general-imported|le|compared with English the}} The long gloss for {{vla|le}} is of course far too long to use most of the time, and in fact 
{{vla|le}} is quite close in meaning to English “the”. It has particular implications, however, which “the” does not have.

{{ind|general-imported|descriptions|importance of selbri first place in}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptors|purpose of}} The general purpose of all descriptors is to create a sumti which might occur in the x1 place of the selbri belonging to the description. Thus 
:{{jbo|le zarci}} conveys something which might be found in the x1 place of {{vla|zarci}}, namely a market.

{{ind|general-imported|le|and truth of selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|and specificity}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|implications of}} The specific purpose of {{vla|le}} is twofold. First, it indicates that the speaker has one or more specific markets in mind (whether or not the listener knows which ones they are). Second, it also indicates that the speaker is merely describing the things he or she has in mind as markets, without being committed to the truth of that description.

{{dsp|example-random-id-ULGC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ULGC}}
{{judri|c6e2d2}}
:'''le zarci cu barda'''
:<code>One-or-more-specific-things-which-I-describe as “markets” is/are-big.</code>
:''The market is big.''
:''The markets are big.''

{{ind|general-imported|plurals|Lojban contrasted with English in necessity of marking}} Note that English-speakers must state whether a reference to markets is to just one ( “the market”) or to more than one ( “the markets”). Lojban requires no such forced choice, so both colloquial translations of {{lex|example-random-id-ULGC}} are valid. Only the context can specify which is meant. (This rule does not mean that Lojban has no way of specifying the number of markets in such a case: that mechanism is explained in {{ls|section-quantified-descriptions}}.)

Now consider the following strange-looking example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PutX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PutX}}
{{ind|example|The men are women|example}}
{{judri|c6e2d3}}
:'''le nanmu cu ninmu'''
:<code>One-or-more-specific-things-which-I-describe as “men” are women.</code>
:''The man is a woman.''
:''The men are women.''

{{ind|general-imported|le|in false-to-fact descriptions}} {{lex|example-random-id-PutX}} is not self-contradictory in Lojban, because 
:{{jbo|le nanmu}} merely means something or other which, for my present purposes, I choose to describe as a man, whether or not it really is a man. A plausible instance would be: someone we had assumed to be a man at a distance turned out to be actually a woman on closer observation. {{lex|example-random-id-PutX}} is what I would say to point out my observation to you.

{{ind|general-imported|descriptions|specific}}  {{ind|general-imported|specific descriptions}} In all descriptions with {{vla|le}}, the listener is presumed to either know what I have in mind or else not to be concerned at present (perhaps I will give more identifying details later). In particular, I might be pointing at the supposed man or men: {{lex|example-random-id-PutX}} would then be perfectly intelligible, since 
:{{jbo|le nanmu}} merely clarifies that I am pointing at the supposed man, not at a landscape, or a nose, which happens to lie in the same direction.

{{ind|general-imported|lo|implications of}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptions|non-specific}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-specific descriptions}} The second descriptor dealt with in this section is {{vla|lo}}. Unlike {{vla|le}}, {{vla|lo}} is nonspecific:

{{dsp|example-random-id-t11z}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-t11z}}
{{judri|c6e2d4}}
:'''lo zarci'''
:<code>one-or-more-of-all-the-things-which-really are-markets</code>
:''a market''
:''some markets''

{{ind|general-imported|lo|and truth of selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo|contrasted with le in truth requirement}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|contrasted with lo in truth requirement}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|contrasted with lo in specificity}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo|contrasted with le in specificity}} Again, there are two colloquial English translations. The effect of using {{vla|lo}} in {{lex|example-random-id-t11z}} is to refer generally to one or more markets, without being specific about which. Unlike 
:{{jbo|le zarci}}, 
:{{jbo|lo zarci}} must refer to something which actually is a market (that is, which can appear in the x1 place of a truthful bridi whose selbri is {{vla|zarci}}). Thus

{{dsp|example-random-id-fSxN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fSxN}}
{{judri|c6e2d5}}
:'''lo nanmu cu ninmu'''
:''Some man is a woman.''
:''Some men are women.''

must be false in Lojban, given that there are no objects in the real world which are both men and women. Pointing at some specific men or women would not make {{lex|example-random-id-fSxN}} true, because those specific individuals are no more both-men-and-women than any others. In general, {{vla|lo}} refers to whatever individuals meet its description.

{{ind|general-imported|la|use with descriptions contrasted with use before Lojbanized names}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|compared with la in specificity}}  {{ind|general-imported|la|compared with le in specificity}}  {{ind|general-imported|la|implications of}} The last descriptor of this section is {{vla|la}}, which indicates that the selbri which follows it has been dissociated from its normal meaning and is being used as a name. Like {{vla|le}} descriptions, {{vla|la}} descriptions are implicitly restricted to those I have in mind. (Do not confuse this use of {{vla|la}} with its use before regular Lojbanized names, which is discussed in {{ls|section-names}}.) For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PrGp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PrGp}}
{{ind|example|bear wrote story|example}}
{{judri|c6e2d6}}
:'''la cribe pu finti le lisri'''
<code>The-one-named “bear” [past] creates the story.</code>
:''Bear wrote the story.''

{{ind|general-imported|naming predicate}} In {{lex|example-random-id-PrGp}}, 
:{{jbo|la cribe}} refers to someone whose naming predicate is 
{{vla|cribe}}, i.e. “Bear”. In English, most names don't mean anything, or at least not anything obvious. The name “Frank” coincides with the English word “frank”, meaning “honest”, and so one way of translating “Frank ate some cheese” into Lojban would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yyBX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yyBX}}
{{judri|c6e2d7}}
:'''la stace pu citka lo cirla'''
:<code>The-one-called “Honest/Frank” [past] eats some cheese.</code>

English-speakers typically would not do this, as we tend to be more attached to the sound of our names than their meaning, even if the meaning (etymological or current) is known. Speakers of other languages may feel differently. (In point of fact, “Frank” originally meant “the free one” rather than “the honest one”.)

{{ind|general-imported|la|contrasted with le in implications}} It is important to note the differences between {{lex|example-random-id-PrGp}} and the following:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nXyo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nXyo}}
{{judri|c6e2d8}}
:'''le cribe pu finti le lisri'''
:<code>One-or-more-specific-things-which-I-describe-as a-bear [past] creates the story.</code>
:''The bear(s) wrote the story.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-93Yv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-93Yv}}
{{judri|c6e2d9}}
:'''lo cribe pu finti le lisri'''
:<code>One-or-more-of-the-things-which-really are-bears [past] creates the story.</code>
:''A bear wrote the story.''
:''Some bears wrote the story.''

{{ind|general-imported|la|contrasted with lo in implications}} {{lex|example-random-id-nXyo}} is about a specific bear or bearlike thing(s), or thing(s) which the speaker (perhaps whimsically or metaphorically) describes as a bear (or more than one); {{lex|example-random-id-93Yv}} is about one or more of the really existing, objectively defined bears. In either case, though, each of them must have contributed to the writing of the story, if more than one bear (or “bear”) is meant.

{{ind|general-imported|descriptions with lo|teddy bear contrasted with real bear}} (The notion of a “really existing, objectively defined bear” raises certain difficulties. Is a panda bear a “real bear”? How about a teddy bear? In general, the answer is “yes”. Lojban gismu are defined as broadly as possible, allowing tanru and lujvo to narrow down the definition. There probably are no necessary and sufficient conditions for defining what is and what is not a bear that can be pinned down with complete precision: the real world is fuzzy. In borderline cases, 
{{vla|le}} may communicate better than {{vla|lo}}.)

So while {{lex|example-random-id-PrGp}} could easily be true (there is a real writer named “Greg Bear”), and {{lex|example-random-id-nXyo}} could be true if the speaker is sufficiently peculiar in what he or she describes as a bear, {{lex|example-random-id-93Yv}} is certainly false.

Similarly, compare the following two examples, which are analogous to {{lex|example-random-id-nXyo}} and {{lex|example-random-id-93Yv}} respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qKw7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qKw7}}
{{judri|c6e2d10}}
:'''le remna pu finti le lisri'''
:''The human being(s) wrote the story.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qKYf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qKYf}}
{{judri|c6e2d11}}
:'''lo remna pu finti le lisri'''
:''A human being wrote the story.''
:''Some human beings wrote the story.''

{{ind|general-imported|lo|contrasted with le in implications}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|contrasted with lo in implications}} {{lex|example-random-id-qKw7}} says who the author of the story is: one or more particular human beings that the speaker has in mind. If the topic of conversation is the story, then {{lex|example-random-id-qKw7}} identifies the author as someone who can be pointed out or who has been previously mentioned; whereas if the topic is a person, then 
:{{jbo|le remna}} is in effect a shorthand reference to that person. {{lex|example-random-id-qKYf}} merely says that the author is human.

{{ind|general-imported|ku|uses of}}  {{ind|general-imported|cu|effect on elidability of ku}}  {{ind|general-imported|ku|effect of following selbri on elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ku|as elidable terminator for descriptions}} The elidable terminator for all descriptions is {{vla|ku}}. It can almost always be omitted with no danger of ambiguity. The main exceptions are in certain uses of relative clauses, which are discussed in {{ls|section-descriptors}}, and in the case of a description immediately preceding the selbri. In this latter case, using an explicit {{vla|cu}} before the selbri makes the {{vla|ku}} unnecessary. There are also a few other uses of {{vla|ku}}: in the compound negator 
:{{jbo|naku}} (discussed in {{lch|chapter-quantifiers}}) and to terminate place-structure, tense, and modal tags that do not have associated sumti (discussed in {{lch|chapter-sumti-tcita}} and {{lch|chapter-tenses}}).

{{ssp|section-masses}}
==Individuals and masses==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|lei}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|loi}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lai}}
:{{s|LA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|sumti|for set objects}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|for mass objects}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|for individual objects}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|classified by types of objects referred to}} All Lojban sumti are classified by whether they refer to one of three types of objects, known as “individuals”, “masses”, and “sets”. The term “individual” is misleading when used to refer to more than one object, but no less-confusing term has as yet been found. All the descriptions in {{ls|section-simple-sumti-kinds}} and {{ls|section-basic-descriptors}} refer to individuals, whether one or more than one. Consider the following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mwhq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mwhq}}
{{judri|c6e3d1}}
:'''le prenu cu bevri le pipno'''
:<code>One-or-more-of-those-I-describe-as persons carry the piano.</code>
:''The person(s) carry the piano.''

(Of course the second {{vla|le}} should really get the same translation as the first, but I am putting the focus of this discussion on the first {{vla|le}}, the one preceding {{vla|prenu}}. I will assume that there is only one piano under discussion.)

{{ind|general-imported|individual objects|multiple}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple individual objects|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|meaning of in the plural}}  {{ind|general-imported|plurals with le|meaning of}} Suppose the context of {{lex|example-random-id-mwhq}} is such that you can determine that I am talking about three persons. What am I claiming? I am claiming that each of the three persons carried the piano. This claim can be true if the persons carried the piano one at a time, or in turns, or in a variety of other ways. But in order for {{lex|example-random-id-mwhq}} to be true, I must be willing to assert that person 1 carried the piano, and that person 2 carried the piano, and that person 3 carried the piano.

But suppose I am not willing to claim that. For in fact pianos are heavy, and very few persons can carry a piano all by themselves. The most likely factual situation is that person 1 carried one end of the piano, and person 2 the other end, while person 3 either held up the middle or else supervised the whole operation without actually lifting anything. The correct way of expressing such a situation in Lojban is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eCsh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eCsh}}
{{ind|example|piano-moving|example}}
{{judri|c6e3d2}}
:'''lei prenu cu bevri le pipno'''
:<code>The-mass-of-one-or-more-of-those-I-describe-as persons carry the piano.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|mass object|and logical reasoning}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass object|properties of}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple individual objects|contrasted with mass object}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass object|contrasted with multiple individual objects}} Here the same three persons are treated not as individuals, but as a so-called “mass entity”, or just “mass”. A mass has the properties of each individual which composes it, and may have other properties of its own as well. This can lead to apparent contradictions. Thus suppose in the piano-moving example above that person 1 has fair skin, whereas person 2 has dark skin. Then it is correct to say that the person-mass has both fair skin and dark skin. Using the mass descriptor 
{{vla|lei}} signals that ordinary logical reasoning is not applicable: contradictions can be maintained, and all sorts of other peculiarities may exist. However, we can safely say that a mass inherits only the component properties that are relevant to it; it would be ludicrous to say that a mass of two persons is of molecular dimensions, simply because some of the parts (namely, the molecules) of the persons are that small.

{{ind|general-imported|lai|as mass counterpart of lai}}  {{ind|general-imported|loi|as mass counterpart of lo}} The descriptors {{vla|loi}} and {{vla|lai}} are analogous to {{vla|lo}} and {{vla|la}} respectively, but refer to masses either by property ( {{vla|loi}}) or by name ( {{vla|lai}}). A classic example of {{vla|loi}} use is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-T1pF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-T1pF}}
{{ind|example|lions in Africa|example}}
{{judri|c6e3d3}}
:'''loi cinfo cu xabju le fi'ortu'a'''
:<code>Part-of-the-mass-of-those-which-really are-lions dwell in-the African-land.</code>
:''The lion dwells in Africa.''
:''Lions dwell in Africa.''

{{ind|general-imported|loi|contrasted with lei in specificity}}  {{ind|general-imported|lei|contrasted with loi in specificity}} The difference between {{vla|lei}} and {{vla|loi}} is that 
:{{jbo|lei cinfo}} refers to a mass of specific individuals which the speaker calls lions, whereas 
:{{jbo|loi cinfo}} refers to some part of the mass of all those individuals which actually are lions. The restriction to “some part of the mass” allows statements like {{lex|example-random-id-T1pF}} to be true even though some lions do not dwell in Africa &ndash; they live in various zoos around the world. On the other hand, {{lex|example-random-id-T1pF}} doesn't actually say that most lions live in Africa: equally true is

{{dsp|example-random-id-JzXc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JzXc}}
{{ind|example|Englishman in Africa|example}}
{{judri|c6e3d4}}
:'''loi glipre cu xabju le fi'ortu'a'''
:<code>Part-of-the-mass-of-those-which-really are-English-persons dwell in-the African-land.</code>
:''The English dwell in Africa.''

since there is at least one English person living there. {{ls|section-sets}} explains another method of saying what is usually meant by “The lion lives in Africa” which does imply that living in Africa is normal, not exceptional, for lions.

{{ind|general-imported|mass objects|peculiarities of English translation of}} Note that the Lojban mass articles are sometimes translated by English plurals (the most usual case), sometimes by English singulars (when the singular is used to express typicalness or abstraction), and sometimes by singulars with no article:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yDCF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yDCF}}
{{ind|example|butter is soft|example}}
{{judri|c6e3d5}}
:'''loi matne cu ranti'''
:<code>Part-of-the-mass-of-that-which-really is-a-quantity-of-butter is-soft.</code>
:''Butter is soft.''

{{ind|general-imported|mass object|as dependent on intention}} Of course, some butter is hard (for example, if it is frozen butter), so the “part-of” implication of {{vla|loi}} becomes once again useful. The reason this mechanism works is that the English words like “butter”, which are seen as already describing masses, are translated in Lojban by non-mass forms. The place structure of {{vla|matne}} is “x1 is a quantity of butter from source x2”, so the single English word “butter” is translated as something like “a part of the mass formed from all the quantities of butter that exist”. (Note that the operation of forming a mass entity does not imply, in Lojban, that the components of the mass are necessarily close to one another or even related in any way other than conceptually. Masses are formed by the speaker's intention to form a mass, and can in principle contain anything.)

{{ind|general-imported|mass name|use of}} The mass name descriptor 
{{vla|lai}} is used in circumstances where we wish to talk about a mass of things identified by a name which is common to all of them. It is not used to identify a mass by a single name peculiar to it. Thus the mass version of {{lex|example-random-id-fSxN}},

{{dsp|example-random-id-H8z5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-H8z5}}
{{ind|example|Bears wrote book|example}}
{{judri|c6e3d6}}
:'''lai cribe pu finti le vi cukta'''
<code>The-mass-of-those-named “bear” [past] creates the nearby book.</code>
:''The Bears wrote this book.''

{{ind|general-imported|lai|contrasted with la in implications}}  {{ind|general-imported|la|contrasted with lai in implications}} in a context where 
:{{jbo|la cribe}} would be understood as plural, would mean that either Tom Bear or Fred Bear (to make up some names) might have written the book, or that Tom and Fred might have written it as collaborators. Using 
{{vla|la}} instead of {{vla|lai}} in {{lex|example-random-id-H8z5}} would give the implication that each of Tom and Fred, considered individually, had written it.

{{ssp|section-sets}}
==Masses and sets==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|le'i}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lo'i}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|la'i}}
:{{s|LA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|mass|compared with set as abstract of multiple individuals}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|compared with mass as abstract of multiple individuals}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass|contrasted with set in attribution of component properties}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|contrasted with mass in attribution of component properties}} Having said so much about masses, let us turn to sets. Sets are easier to understand than masses, but are more rarely used. Like a mass, a set is an abstract object formed from a number of individuals; however, the properties of a set are not derived from any of the properties of the individuals that compose it.

{{ind|general-imported|la'i|as set counterpart of lai}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo'i|as set counterpart of loi}}  {{ind|general-imported|le'i|as set counterpart of lei}}  {{ind|general-imported|sets|properties of}}  {{ind|general-imported|cardinality|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|cardinality|property of sets}}  {{ind|general-imported|membership|property of sets}}  {{ind|general-imported|inclusion|property of sets}} Sets have properties like cardinality (how many elements in the set), membership (the relationship between a set and its elements), and set inclusion (the relationship between two sets, one of which &ndash; the superset &ndash; contains all the elements of the other &ndash; the subset). The set descriptors 
{{vla|le'i}}, {{vla|lo'i}} and {{vla|la'i}} correspond exactly to the mass descriptors {{vla|lei}}, {{vla|loi}}, and {{vla|lai}} except that normally we talk of the whole of a set, not just part of it. Here are some examples contrasting {{vla|lo}}, {{vla|loi}}, and {{vla|lo'i}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qL1E}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qL1E}}

{{ind|example|rats are brown|example}}
{{judri|c6e4d1}}
:'''lo ratcu cu bunre'''
:<code>One-or-more-of-those-which-really-are rats are-brown.</code>
:''Some rats are brown.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qL2Y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qL2Y}}
{{judri|c6e4d2}}
:'''loi ratcu cu cmalu'''
:<code>Part-of-the-mass-of-those-which-really-are rats are-small.</code>
:''Rats are small.''

{{ind|general-imported|lo'i|contrasted with lo and loi}}  {{ind|general-imported|loi|contrasted with lo and lo'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo|contrasted with loi and lo'i}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qL3V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qL3V}}
{{judri|c6e4d3}}
:'''lo'i ratcu cu barda'''
:<code>The-set-of rats is-large.</code>
:''There are a lot of rats.''

The mass of rats is small because at least one rat is small; the mass of rats is also large; the set of rats, though, is unquestionably large &ndash; it has billions of members. The mass of rats is also brown, since some of its components are; but it would be incorrect to call the set of rats brown &ndash; brown-ness is not the sort of property that sets possess.

{{ind|general-imported|sets|use in Lojban place structure}} Lojban speakers should generally think twice before employing the set descriptors. However, certain predicates have places that require set sumti to fill them. For example, the place structure of {{vla|fadni}} is:
:''x1 is ordinary/common/typical/usual in property x2 among the members of set x3''
Why is it necessary for the x3 place of {{vla|fadni}} to be a set? Because it makes no sense for an individual to be typical of another individual: an individual is typical of a group. In order to make sure that the bridi containing {{vla|fadni}} is about an entire group, its x3 place must be filled with a set:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xIXo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xIXo}}
{{ind|example|typical Lojban user|example}}
{{judri|c6e4d4}}
:'''mi fadni zo'e lo'i lobypli'''
:<code>I am-ordinary among the-set-of Lojban-users.</code>
:''I am a typical Lojban user.''

Note that the x2 place has been omitted; I am not specifying in exactly which way I am typical &ndash; whether in language knowledge, or age, or interests, or something else. If {{vla|lo'i}} were changed to {{vla|lo}} in {{lex|example-random-id-xIXo}}, the meaning would be something like “I am typical of some Lojban user”, which is nonsense.

{{ssp|section-typicals}}
==Descriptors for typical objects==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|lo'e}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

:{{c|le'e}}
:{{s|LE}}
:''description''

As promised in {{ls|section-masses}}, Lojban has a method for discriminating between “the lion” who lives in Africa and “the Englishman” who, generally speaking, doesn't live in Africa even though some Englishmen do. The descriptor {{vla|lo'e}} means “the typical”, as in

{{dsp|example-random-id-AJKt}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AJKt}}
{{ind|example|lion in Africa|example}}
{{judri|c6e5d1}}
:'''lo'e cinfo cu xabju le fi'ortu'a'''
:<code>The-typical lion dwells-in the African-land.</code>
:''The lion dwells in Africa.''

{{ind|general-imported|typical objects|and instantiation}}  {{ind|general-imported|typical objects|determining characteristics of}} What is this “typical lion”? Surely it is not any particular lion, because no lion has all of the “typical” characteristics, and (worse yet) some characteristics that all real lions have can't be viewed as typical. For example, all real lions are either male or female, but it would be bizarre to suppose that the typical lion is either one. So the typical lion has no particular sex, but does have a color (golden brown), a residence (Africa), a diet (game), and so on. Likewise we can say that

{{dsp|example-random-id-8PoG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8PoG}}
{{ind|example|typical Englishman|example}}
{{judri|c6e5d2}}
:'''lo'e glipre cu xabju le fi'ortu'a na.e le gligugde'''
:<code>The-typical English-person dwells-in the African-land (Not!) and the English-country.</code>
:''The typical English person dwells not in Africa but in England.''

{{ind|general-imported|le'i|relationship to le'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|le'e|relationship to le'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo'i|relationship to lo'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo'e|relationship to lo'i}} The relationship between 
:{{jbo|lo'e cinfo}} and 
:{{jbo|lo'i cinfo}} may be explained thus: the typical lion is an imaginary lion-abstraction which best exemplifies the set of lions. There is a similar relationship between {{vla|le'e}} and {{vla|le'i}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-D88V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-D88V}}
{{judri|c6e5d3}}
:'''le'e xelso merko cu gusta ponse'''
:<code>The-stereotypical Greek-type-of American is-a-restaurant-type-of owner.</code>
:''Lots of Greek-Americans own restaurants.''

{{ind|general-imported|stereotypical|compared with typical}}  {{ind|general-imported|typical|compared with stereotypical}}  {{ind|general-imported|stereotypical|as not derogatory in Lojban}}  {{ind|general-imported|Greek-Americans own restaurants}}  {{ind|general-imported|stereotypical objects}} Here we are concerned not with the actual set of Greek-Americans, but with the set of those the speaker has in mind, which is typified by one (real or imaginary) who owns a restaurant. The word “stereotypical” is often derogatory in English, but 
{{vla|le'e}} need not be derogatory in Lojban: it simply suggests that the example is typical in the speaker's imagination rather than in some objectively agreed-upon way. Of course, different speakers may disagree about what the features of “the typical lion” are (some would include having a short intestine, whereas others would know nothing of lions' intestines), so the distinction between 
:{{jbo|lo'e cinfo}} and 
:{{jbo|le'e cinfo}} may be very fine.

Furthermore,

{{dsp|example-random-id-NVFy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NVFy}}
{{ind|example|Hollywood|example}}
{{judri|c6e5d4}}
:'''le'e skina cu se finti ne'i la xali,uyd.'''
:<code>The-stereotypical movie is-invented in Hollywood.</code>

is probably true to an American, but might be false (not the stereotype) to someone living in India or Russia.

{{ind|general|typical Smith|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|name equivalent for “typical”|rationale for lack of}} Note that there is no naming equivalent of {{vla|lo'e}} and {{vla|le'e}}, because there is no need, as a rule, for a “typical George” or a “typical Smith”. People or things who share a common name do not, in general, have any other common attributes worth mentioning.

{{ssp|section-quantified-sumti}}
==Quantified sumti==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ro}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|su'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''
