Quantifiers tell us how many: in the case of quantifiers with sumti, how many things we are talking about. In Lojban, quantifiers are expressed by numbers and mathematical expressions: a large topic discussed in some detail in 
{{lch|chapter-mekso}}. For the purposes of this chapter, a simplified treatment will suffice. Our examples will employ either the simple Lojban numbers {{vla|pa}}, {{vla|re}}, {{vla|ci}}, {{vla|vo}}, and {{vla|mu}}, meaning “one”, “two”, “three”, “four”, “five” respectively, or else one of four special quantifiers, two of which are discussed in this section and listed above. These four quantifiers are important because every Lojban sumti has either one or two of them implicitly present in it &ndash; which one or two depends on the particular kind of sumti. There is more explanation of implicit quantifiers later in this section. (The other two quantifiers, {{vla|piro}} and {{vla|pisu'o}}, are explained in 
{{ls|section-quantified-descriptions}}.)

Every Lojban sumti may optionally be preceded by an explicit quantifier. The purpose of this quantifier is to specify how many of the things referred to by the sumti are being talked about. Here are some simple examples contrasting sumti with and without explicit quantifiers:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qL61}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qL61}}
{{judri|c6e6d1}}
:'''do cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>You walk-on the ice.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLAH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLAH}}
{{judri|c6e6d2}}
:'''re do cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>Two-of you walk-on the ice.</code>

The difference between {{lex|example-random-id-qL61}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qLAH}} is the presence of the explicit quantifier {{vla|re}} in the latter example. Although {{vla|re}} by itself means “two”, when used as a quantifier it means “two-of”. Out of the group of listeners (the number of which isn't stated), two (we are not told which ones) are asserted to be “walkers on the ice”. Implicitly, the others (if any) are not walkers on the ice. In Lojban, you cannot say “I own three shoes” if in fact you own four shoes. Numbers need never be specified, but if they are specified they must be correct.

(This rule does not mean that there is no way to specify a number which is vague. The sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-gLpy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gLpy}}
{{judri|c6e6d3}}
:'''mi ponse su'o ci cutci'''
:<code>I possess at-least three shoes.</code>

is true if you own three shoes, or four, or indeed any larger number. More details on vague numbers appear in the discussion of mathematical expressions in 
{{lch|chapter-mekso}}.)

Now consider {{lex|example-random-id-qL61}} again. How many of the listeners are claimed to walk on the ice? The answer turns out to be: all of them, however many that is. So {{lex|example-random-id-qL61}} and {{lex|example-random-id-0qr0}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0qr0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0qr0}}
{{judri|c6e6d4}}
:'''ro do cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>All-of you walk-on the ice.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|sumti|as having implicit quantifiers}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantifiers|with sumti}} turn out to mean exactly the same thing. This is a safe strategy, because if one of my listeners doesn't turn out to be walking on the ice, I can safely claim that I didn't intend that person to be a listener! And in fact, all of the personal pro-sumti such as 
{{vla|mi}} and {{vla|mi'o}} and {{vla|ko}} obey the same rule. We say that personal pro-sumti have a so-called “implicit quantifier” of {{vla|ro}} (all). This just means that if no quantifier is given explicitly, the meaning is the same as if the implicit quantifier had been used.

{{ind|general-imported|implicit quantifier|on quotations|discussion of}} Not all sumti have {{vla|ro}} as the implicit quantifier, however. Consider the quotation in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3eMo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3eMo}}
{{judri|c6e6d5}}
:'''mi cusku lu do cadzu le bisli li'u'''
:<code>I express [quote] you walk-on the ice [unquote].</code>
:''I say, “You walk on the ice.”''

What is the implicit quantifier of the quotation 
:{{jbo|lu do cadzu le bisli li'u}}? Surely not {{vla|ro}}. If {{vla|ro}} were supplied explicitly, thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-h4SJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-h4SJ}}
{{judri|c6e6d6}}
:'''mi cusku ro lu do cadzu le bisli li'u'''
:''I express all-of [quote] you walk-on the ice [unquote].''

the meaning would be something like “I say every occurrence of the sentence 'You walk on the ice'”. Of course I don't say every occurrence of it, only some occurrences. One might suppose that {{lex|example-random-id-3eMo}} means that I express exactly one occurrence, but it is more Lojbanic to leave the number unspecified, as with other sumti. We can say definitely, however, that I say it at least once.

The Lojban cmavo meaning “at least” is {{vla|su'o}}, and if no ordinary number follows, {{vla|su'o}} means “at least once”. (See {{lex|example-random-id-gLpy}} for the use of {{vla|su'o}} with an ordinary number). Therefore, the explicitly quantified version of {{lex|example-random-id-3eMo}} is

{{ind|general-imported|implicit quantifier|for quotations}}  {{ind|general-imported|quotations|implicit quantifier for}}  {{ind|general-imported|su'o|as implicit quantifier for quotations}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-P558}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-P558}}
{{judri|c6e6d7}}
:'''mi cusku su'o lu do cadzu le bisli li'u'''
:<code>I express at-least-one-of [quote] you walk-on the ice [unquote].</code>
:<code>I say one or more instances of “You walk on the ice”.</code>
:''I say “You walk on the ice”.''

If an explicit ordinary number such as {{vla|re}} were to appear, it would have to convey an exact expression, so

{{dsp|example-random-id-59dF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-59dF}}
{{judri|c6e6d8}}
:'''mi cusku re lu do cadzu le bisli li'u'''
:<code>I express two-of [quote] you walk-on the ice [unquote].</code>

means that I say the sentence exactly twice, neither more nor less.

{{ssp|section-quantified-descriptions}}
==Quantified descriptions==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|piro}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''
{{c|pisu'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|quantification|before description sumti compared with before non-description sumti}} Like other sumti, descriptions can be quantified. When a quantifier appears before a description, it has the same meaning as one appearing before a non-description sumti: it specifies how many things, of all those referred to by the description, are being talked about in this particular bridi. Suppose that context tells us that 
:{{jbo|le gerku}} refers to three dogs. Then we can say that exactly two of them are white as follows:

{{dsp|example-random-id-WtUh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WtUh}}
{{ind|example|two dogs are white|example}}
{{judri|c6e7d1}}
:'''re le gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>Two-of the dogs are-white.</code>
:''Two of the dogs are white.''

{{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifier|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|contrasted with outer quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifier|contrasted with inner quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifier|definition}} When discussing descriptions, this ordinary quantifier is called an “outer quantifier”, since it appears outside the description. But there is another possible location for a quantifier: between the descriptor and the selbri. This quantifier is called an “inner quantifier”, and its meaning is quite different: it tells the listener how many objects the description selbri characterizes.

For example, the context of {{lex|example-random-id-WtUh}} supposedly told us that 
:{{jbo|le gerku}} referred to some three specific dogs. This assumption can be made certain with the use of an explicit inner quantifier:

{{dsp|example-random-id-X3iY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-X3iY}}
{{judri|c6e7d2}}
:'''re le ci gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>Two-of the three dogs are-white.</code>
:''Two of the three dogs are white.''

(As explained in the discussion of {{lex|example-random-id-gLpy}}, simple numbers like those in {{lex|example-random-id-X3iY}} must be exact: it therefore follows that the third dog cannot be white.)

{{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|explicit}} You may also specify an explicit inner quantifier and leave the outer quantifier implicit:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JxzV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JxzV}}
{{judri|c6e7d3}}
:'''le ci gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>The three dogs are-white.</code>
:''The three dogs are white.''

{{ind|general-imported|outer quantifier|implicit on descriptors}}  {{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|implicit on descriptors}}  {{ind|general-imported|descriptors|implicit quantifiers for}} There are rules for each of the 11 descriptors specifying what the implicit values for the inner and outer quantifiers are. They are meant to provide sensible default values when context is absent, not necessarily to prescribe hard and fast rules. The following table lists the implicit values:
<tab class=wikitable header=true>{{vla|le}}:	{{jbo|ro le su'o}}	all of the at-least-one described as{{vla|lo}}:	{{jbo|su'o lo ro}}	at least one of all of those which really are{{vla|la}}:	{{jbo|ro la su'o}}	all of the at least one named{{vla|lei}}:	{{jbo|pisu'o lei su'o}}	some part of the mass of the at-least-one described as{{vla|loi}}:	{{jbo|pisu'o loi ro}}	some part of the mass of all those that really are{{vla|lai}}:	{{jbo|pisu'o lai su'o}}	some part of the mass of the at-least-one named{{vla|le'i}}:	{{jbo|piro le'i su'o}}	the whole of the set of the at-least-one described as{{vla|lo'i}}:	{{jbo|piro lo'i ro}}	the whole of the set of all those that really are{{vla|la'i}}:	{{jbo|piro la'i su'o}}	the whole of the set of the at-least-one named{{vla|le'e}}:	{{jbo|ro le'e su'o}}	all the stereotypes of the at-least-one described as{{vla|lo'e}}:	{{jbo|su'o lo'e ro}}	at least one of the types of all those that really are
</tab>
{{ind|general-imported|le-series cmavo|as encompassing le-series and la-series descriptors for quantification discussion}}  {{ind|general-imported|le-series cmavo|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|la-series descriptors|compared with le-series in implicit quantification}}  {{ind|general-imported|le-series descriptors|compared with la-series in implicit quantification}} When examined for the first time, this table looks dreadfully arbitrary. In fact, there are quite a few regularities in it. First of all, the la-series (that is, the descriptors {{vla|la}}, {{vla|lai}}, and {{vla|la'i}}) and the le-series (that is, the descriptors {{vla|le}}, {{vla|lei}}, {{vla|le'i}}, and {{vla|le'e}}) always have corresponding implicit quantifiers, so we may subsume the la-series under the le-series for the rest of this discussion: “le-series cmavo” will refer to both the le-series proper and to the la-series.

{{ind|general-imported|le-series cmavo|rule for implicit inner quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo-series cmavo|rule for implicit inner quantifier}} The rule for the inner quantifier is very simple: the lo-series cmavo (namely, 
{{vla|lo}}, {{vla|loi}}, {{vla|lo'i}}, and {{vla|lo'e}}) all have an implicit inner quantifier of {{vla|ro}}, whereas the le-series cmavo all have an implicit inner quantifier of 
{{vla|su'o}}.

{{ind|general-imported|le-series cmavo|rationale for implicit inner quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo-series cmavo|rationale for implicit inner quantifier}} Why? Because lo-series descriptors always refer to all of the things which really fit into the x1 place of the selbri. They are not restricted by the speaker's intention. Descriptors of the le-series, however, are so restricted, and therefore talk about some number, definite or indefinite, of objects the speaker has in mind &ndash; but never less than one.

{{ind|general-imported|masses|rule for implicit outer quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|sets|rule for implicit outer quantifier}} Understanding the implicit outer quantifier requires rules of greater subtlety. In the case of mass and set descriptors, a single rule suffices for each: reference to a mass is implicitly a reference to some part of the mass; reference to a set is implicitly a reference to the whole set. Masses and sets are inherently singular objects: it makes no sense to talk about two distinct masses with the same components, or two distinct sets with the same members. Therefore, the largest possible outer quantifier for either a set description or a mass description is {{vla|piro}}, the whole of it.

{{ind|general-imported|plural masses|possible use for}} (Pedantically, it is possible that the mass of water molecules composing an ice cube might be thought of as different from the same mass of water molecules in liquid form, in which case we might talk about 
:{{jbo|re lei djacu}}, two masses of the water-bits I have in mind.)

{{ind|general-imported|pisu'o|explanation of meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|piro|explanation of meaning}} Why “{{vla|pi}}-”? It is the Lojban cmavo for the decimal point. Just as 

:{{jbo|pimu}} means “{{math|.5}}”, and when used as a quantifier specifies a portion consisting of five tenths of a thing, {{vla|piro}} means a portion consisting of the all-ness &ndash; the entirety &ndash; of a thing. Similarly, {{vla|pisu'o}} specifies a portion consisting of at least one part of a thing, i.e. some of it.

{{ind|general-imported|portion|on set contrasted with on individual}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifiers|for expressing subsets}}  {{ind|general-imported|subsets|expressing with outer quantifiers}} Smaller quantifiers are possible for sets, and refer to subsets. Thus 

:{{jbo|pimu le'i nanmu}} is a subset of the set of men I have in mind; we don't know precisely which elements make up this subset, but it must have half the size of the full set. This is the best way to say “half of the men”; saying 
:{{jbo|pimu le nanmu}} would give us a half-portion of one of them instead! Of course, the result of 
:{{jbo|pimu le'i nanmu}} is still a set; if you need to refer to the individuals of the subset, you must say so (see {{vla|lu'a}} in 
{{ls|section-sumti-qualifiers}}).

{{ind|general-imported|lo|implicit outer quantifier for}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|implicit outer quantifier for}}  {{ind|general-imported|individual descriptors|different implicit outer quantifiers among}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifiers|rationale for differences in implicit quantifier on descriptors}} The case of outer quantifiers for individual descriptors (including {{vla|le}}, {{vla|lo}}, {{vla|la}}, and the typical descriptors {{vla|le'e}} and {{vla|lo'e}}) is special. When we refer to specific individuals with {{vla|le}}, we mean to refer to all of those we have in mind, so {{vla|ro}} is appropriate as the implicit quantifier, just as it is appropriate for {{vla|do}}. Reference to non-specific individuals with {{vla|lo}}, however, is typically to only some of the objects which can be correctly described, and so {{vla|su'o}} is the appropriate implicit quantifier, just as for quotations.

{{ind|general-imported|lo|contrasted with le in implicit quantification}}  {{ind|general-imported|le|contrasted with lo in implicit quantification}} From the English-speaking point of view, the difference in structure between the following example using {{vla|le}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-f643}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-f643}}
{{judri|c6e7d4}}
:'''[ro] le ci gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>[All-of] those-described-as three dogs are-white.</code>
:''The three dogs are white.''

and the corresponding form with {{vla|lo}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gr7Y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gr7Y}}
{{judri|c6e7d5}}
:'''ci lo [ro] gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>Three-of those-which-are [all] dogs are-white.</code>
:''Three dogs are white.''

looks very peculiar. Why is the number {{vla|ci}} found as an inner quantifier in {{lex|example-random-id-f643}} and as an outer quantifier in {{lex|example-random-id-gr7Y}}? The number of dogs is the same in either case. The answer is that the {{vla|ci}} in {{lex|example-random-id-f643}} is part of the specification: it tells us the actual number of dogs in the group that the speaker has in mind. In {{lex|example-random-id-gr7Y}}, however, the dogs referred to by 
:{{jbo|... lo gerku}} are all the dogs that exist: the outer quantifier then restricts the number to three; which three, we cannot tell. The implicit quantifiers are chosen to avoid claiming too much or too little: in the case of {{vla|le}}, the implicit outer quantifier {{vla|ro}} says that each of the dogs in the restricted group is white; in the case of {{vla|lo}}, the implicit inner quantifier simply says that three dogs, chosen from the group of all the dogs there are, are white.

{{ind|general-imported|lo-series description|caution on exact numbers as inner quantifiers on}} Using exact numbers as inner quantifiers in lo-series descriptions is dangerous, because you are stating that exactly that many things exist which really fit the description. So examples like

{{dsp|example-random-id-uYH4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uYH4}}
{{judri|c6e7d6}}
:'''[so'o] lo ci gerku cu blabi'''
:<code>[some-of] those-which-really-are three dogs are-white</code>

are semantically anomalous; {{lex|example-random-id-uYH4}} claims that some dog (or dogs) is white, but also that there are just three dogs in the universe!

Nevertheless, inner quantifiers are permitted on {{vla|lo}} descriptors for consistency's sake, and may occasionally be useful.

Note that the inner quantifier of {{vla|le}}, even when exact, need not be truthful: 
:{{jbo|le ci nanmu}} means “what I describe as three men”, not “three of what I describe as men”. This follows from the rule that what is described by a {{vla|le}} description represents the speaker's viewpoint rather than the objective way things are.

{{ssp|section-indefinite-descriptions}}
==Indefinite descriptions==
{{ind|general-imported|descriptors|omission of}}  {{ind|general-imported|lo|omission of}} By a quirk of Lojban syntax, it is possible to omit the descriptor {{vla|lo}}, but never any other descriptor, from a description like that of {{lex|example-random-id-gr7Y}}; namely, one which has an explicit outer quantifier but no explicit inner quantifier. The following example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-EsVd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-EsVd}}
{{judri|c6e8d1}}
:'''ci gerku [ku] cu blabi'''
:''Three dogs are white.''

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite description|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|omission of descriptor|effect on ku}}  {{ind|general-imported|ku|effect on of omitting descriptor}} is equivalent in meaning to {{lex|example-random-id-gr7Y}}. Even though the descriptor is not present, the elidable terminator {{vla|ku}} may still be used. The name “indefinite description” for this syntactic form is historically based: of course, it is no more and no less indefinite than its counterpart with an explicit 
{{vla|lo}}. Indefinite descriptions were introduced into the language in order to imitate the syntax of English and other natural languages.

{{ind|general-imported|inner quantifier|in indefinite description}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer quantifier|in indefinite description}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite description|as prohibiting explicit inner quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite description|as needing explicit outer quantifier}} Indefinite descriptions must fit this mold exactly: there is no way to make one which does not have an explicit outer quantifier (thus 
:{{false|*gerku cu blabi}} is ungrammatical), or which has an explicit inner quantifier (thus 
:{{false|*reboi ci gerku cu blabi}} is also ungrammatical &ndash; 
:{{jbo|re ci gerku cu blabi}} is fine, but means “23 dogs are white”).

Note: {{lex|example-random-id-gLpy}} also contains an indefinite description, namely 

:{{jbo|su'o ci cutci}}; another version of that example using an explicit {{vla|lo}} would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-SMvA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-SMvA}}
{{judri|c6e8d2}}
:'''mi ponse su'o ci lo cutci'''
:<code>I possess at-least three things-which-really-are shoes</code>
:''I own three (or more) shoes.''

{{ssp|section-sumti-based-descriptions}}
==sumti-based descriptions==
As stated in {{ls|section-basic-descriptors}}, most descriptions consist of just a descriptor and a selbri. (In this chapter, the selbri have always been single gismu, but of course any selbri, however complex, can be employed in a description. The syntax and semantics of selbri are explained in {{lch|chapter-selbri}}.) In the intervening sections, inner and outer quantifiers have been added to the syntax. Now it is time to discuss a description of a radically different kind: the sumti-based description.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti-based description|outer quantifier on}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti-based description|inner quantifier on}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti-based description|definition}} A sumti-based description has a sumti where the selbri would normally be, and the inner quantifier is required &ndash; it cannot be implicit. An outer quantifier is permitted but not required.

A full theory of sumti-based descriptions has yet to be worked out. One common case, however, is well understood. Compare the following:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLaQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLaQ}}
<title>    

{{ind|example|the two of you|example}}
{{judri|c6e9d1}}
:'''re do cu nanmu'''
:<code>Two-of you are-men.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLAr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLAr}}
{{judri|c6e9d2}}
{{ind|example|the two of you|example}}
:'''le re do cu nanmu'''
:<code>The two-of you are men.</code>{{lex|example-random-id-qLaQ}} simply specifies that of the group of listeners, size unknown, two are men. {{lex|example-random-id-qLAr}}, which has the sumti-based description 

:{{jbo|le re do}}, says that of the two listeners, all (the implicit outer quantifier {{vla|ro}}) are men. So in effect the inner quantifier {{vla|re}} gives the number of individuals which the inner sumti 
{{vla|do}} refers to.

Here is another group of examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLbf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLbf}}
{{ind|example|three bears|example}}
{{judri|c6e9d3}}
:'''re le ci cribe cu bunre'''
:<code>Two-of the three bears are-brown.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLbh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLbh}}
{{judri|c6e9d4}}
{{ind|example|three bears|example}}
:'''le re le ci cribe cu bunre'''
:<code>The two-of the three bears are-brown.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLBq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLBq}}
{{judri|c6e9d5}}
{{ind|example|three bears|example}}
:'''pa le re le ci cribe cu bunre'''
:<code>One-of the two-of the three bears are-brown.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|sumti-based descriptions with le|as increasing restricting to in-mind}} In each case, 
:{{jbo|le ci cribe}} restricts the bears (or alleged bears) being talked of to some group of three which the speaker has in mind. {{lex|example-random-id-qLbf}} says that two of them (which two is not stated) are brown. {{lex|example-random-id-qLbh}} says that a specific pair of them are brown. {{lex|example-random-id-qLBq}} says that of a specific pair chosen from the original three, one or the other of that pair is brown.

{{ssp|section-sumti-qualifiers}}
==sumti qualifiers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

{{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|list of}}

:{{c|la'e}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lu'e}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|tu'a}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lu'a}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lu'i}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|lu'o}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|vu'i}}
:{{s|LAhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|na'ebo}}
:{{s|NAhE+BO}}
:''description''

:{{c|to'ebo}}
:{{s|NAhE+BO}}
:''description''

:{{c|no'ebo}}
:{{s|NAhE+BO}}
:''description''

:{{c|je'abo}}
:{{s|NAhE+BO}}
:''description''

:{{c|lu'u}}
:{{s|LUhU}}
:''description''

Well, that's quite a list of cmavo. What are they all about?

{{ind|general-imported|lu'u|as elidable terminator for qualified sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|elidable terminator for qualified sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|external syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|internal syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|NAhE selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|LAhE selma'o}} The above cmavo and compound cmavo are called the “sumti qualifiers”. All of them are either single cmavo of selma'o LAhE, or else compound cmavo involving a scalar negation cmavo of selma'o NAhE immediately followed by 
{{vla|bo}} of selma'o BO. Syntactically, you can prefix a sumti qualifier to any sumti and produce another simple sumti. (You may need to add the elidable terminator 
{{vla|lu'u}} to show where the qualified sumti ends.)

{{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|as short forms for common special cases}} Semantically, sumti qualifiers represent short forms of certain common special cases. Suppose you want to say “I see 'The Red Pony'”, where “The Red Pony” is the title of a book. How about:

{{ind|general-imported|unqualified sumti|contrasted with qualified sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|qualified sumti|contrasted with unqualified sumti}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-6W3v}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6W3v}}
{{ind|example|Red Pony|example}}
{{judri|c6e10d1}}
:'''mi viska lu le xunre cmaxirma li'u'''
:<code>I see [quote] the red small-horse [unquote].</code>

But {{lex|example-random-id-6W3v}} doesn't work: it says that you see a piece of text “The Red Pony”. That might be all right if you were looking at the cover of the book, where the words “The Red Pony” are presumably written. (More precisely, where the words 

:{{jbo|le xunre cmaxirma}} are written &ndash; but we may suppose the book has been translated into Lojban.)

What you really want to say is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MSVK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MSVK}}
{{judri|c6e10d2}}
{{ind|example|Red Pony|example}}
:'''mi viska le selsinxa be lu le xunre cmaxirma li'u'''
:<code>I see the thing-represented-by [quote] the red small-horse [unquote].</code>

The x2 place of 
:{{jbo|selsinxa}} (the x1 place of {{vla|sinxa}}) is a sign or symbol, and the x1 place of 
:{{jbo|selsinxa}} (the x2 place of {{vla|sinxa}}) is the thing represented by the sign. {{lex|example-random-id-MSVK}} allows us to use a symbol (namely the title of a book) to represent the thing it is a symbol of (namely the book itself).

This operation turns out to be needed often enough that it's useful to be able to say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ajty}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ajty}}
{{judri|c6e10d3}}
:'''mi viska la'e lu le xunre cmaxirma li'u [lu'u]'''

:<code>I see the-referent-of [quote] the red small-horse [unquote].</code>

{{ind|general-imported|referent|referring to with la'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|la'e|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|dereferencing a pointer|with la'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|la'e|as short for {{jbo|le selsinxa be}}}} So when {{vla|la'e}} is prefixed to a sumti referring to a symbol, it produces a sumti referring to the referent of that symbol. (In computer jargon, 
{{vla|la'e}} dereferences a pointer.)

By introducing a sumti qualifier, we correct a false sentence ( {{lex|example-random-id-6W3v}}), which too closely resembles its literal English equivalent, into a true sentence ( {{lex|example-random-id-Ajty}}), without having to change it overmuch; in particular, the structure remains the same. Most of the uses of sumti qualifiers are of this general kind.

{{ind|general-imported|symbol|referring to with lu'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|lu'e|effect of on meaning}} The sumti qualifier {{vla|lu'e}} provides the converse operation: it can be prefixed to a sumti referring to some thing to produce a sumti referring to a sign or symbol for the thing. For example,

{{ind|general-imported|lu'e|as short for {{jbo|le sinxa be}}}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-7ytm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7ytm}}
{{ind|example|title of book|example}}
{{judri|c6e10d4}}
:'''mi pu cusku lu'e le vi cukta'''
:<code>I [past] express a-symbol-for the nearby book.</code>
:''I said the title of this book.''

The equivalent form not using a sumti qualifier would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aC9Q}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-aC9Q}}
{{judri|c6e10d5}}
{{ind|example|title of book|example}}
:'''mi pu cusku le sinxa be le vi cukta'''
:<code>I [past] express the symbol-for the nearby book.</code>

which is equivalent to {{lex|example-random-id-7ytm}}, but longer.

{{ind|general-imported|sequence|contrasted with set}}  {{ind|general-imported|vu'i|use for creating sequence}}  {{ind|general-imported|tu'a|use for forming abstractions}}  {{ind|general-imported|vu'i|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|lu'o|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|lu'i|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|lu'a|effect of on meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|tu'a|effect of on meaning}} The other sumti qualifiers follow the same rules. The cmavo {{vla|tu'a}} is used in forming abstractions, and is explained more fully in {{ls|section-events-and-contours}}. The triplet {{vla|lu'a}}, 
{{vla|lu'i}}, and 
{{vla|lu'o}} convert between individuals, sets, and masses; 
{{vla|vu'i}} belongs to this group as well, but creates a sequence, which is similar to a set but has a definite order. (The set of John and Charles is the same as the set of Charles and John, but the sequences are different.) Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ioCu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ioCu}}
{{judri|c6e10d6}}
:'''mi troci tu'a le vorme'''
:<code>I try some-abstraction-about the door.</code>
:''I try (to open) the door.''

{{ind|general-imported|tu'a|as being deliberately vague}} {{lex|example-random-id-ioCu}} might mean that I try to do something else involving the door; the form is deliberately vague.

Most of the following examples make use of the cmavo {{vla|ri}}, belonging to selma'o KOhA. This cmavo means “the thing last mentioned”; it is equivalent to repeating the immediately previous sumti (but in its original context). It is explained in more detail in {{ls|section-ri-gohi-series}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLbv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLbv}}
{{ind|example|set of rats|example}}
{{judri|c6e10d7}}
:'''lo'i ratcu cu barda .iku'i lu'a ri cmalu'''
:<code>The-set-of rats is-large. But some-members-of it-last-mentioned is-small.</code>
:''The set of rats is large, but some of its members are small.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLCP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLCP}}
{{judri|c6e10d8}}
{{ind|example|set of rats|example}}
:'''lo ratcu cu cmalu .iku'i lu'i ri barda'''
:<code>Some rats are-small. But the-set-of them-last-mentioned is-large.</code>
:''Some rats are small, but the set of rats is large.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLcy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLcy}}
{{judri|c6e10d9}}
{{ind|example|set of rats|example}}
:'''mi ce do girzu .i lu'o ri gunma .i vu'i ri porsi'''
:<code>I in-a-set-with you are-a-set. The-mass-of it-last-mentioned is-a-mass. The-sequence-of it-last-mentioned is-a-sequence</code>
:''The set of you and me is a set. The mass of you and me is a mass. The sequence of you and me is a sequence.''

(Yes, I know these examples are a bit silly. This set was introduced for completeness, and practical examples are as yet hard to come by.)

{{ind|general-imported|negation sumti qualifiers|meanings of}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti qualifiers|for negation}} Finally, the four sumti qualifiers formed from a cmavo of NAhE and {{vla|bo}} are all concerned with negation, which is discussed in detail in {{lch|chapter-negation}}. Here are a few examples of negation sumti qualifiers:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4Mte}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4Mte}}
{{judri|c6e10d10}}
:'''mi viska na'ebo le gerku'''
:<code>I see something-other-than the dog.</code>

This compound, 
:{{jbo|na'ebo}}, is the most common of the four negation sumti qualifiers. The others usually only make sense in the context of repeating, with modifications, something already referred to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JwCb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JwCb}}
{{ind|example|lukewarm food|example}}
{{judri|c6e10d11}}
:'''mi nelci loi glare cidja .ije do nelci to'ebo ri .ije la djein. nelci no'ebo ra'''
:<code>I like part-of-the-mass-of hot-type-of food. And you like the-opposite-of the-last-mentioned. And Jane likes the-neutral-value-of something-mentioned.</code>
:''I like hot food, and you like cold food, and Jane likes lukewarm food.''

(In {{lex|example-random-id-JwCb}}, the sumti {{vla|ra}} refers to some previously mentioned sumti other than that referred to by {{vla|ri}}. We cannot use {{vla|ri}} here, because it would signify 
:{{jbo|la djein.}}, that being the most recent sumti available to {{vla|ri}}. See more detailed explanations in {{ls|section-ri-gohi-series}}.)

{{ssp|section-vocative-syntax}}
==The syntax of vocative phrases==
{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrases|as a “free modifier”}} Vocative phrases are not sumti, but are explained in this chapter because their syntax is very similar to that of sumti. Grammatically, a vocative phrase is one of the so-called “free modifiers” of Lojban, along with subscripts, parentheses, and various other constructs explained in 
{{lch|chapter-structure}}. They can be placed after many, but not all, constructions of the grammar: in general, after any elidable terminator (which, however, must not then be elided!), at the beginnings and ends of sentences, and in many other places.

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|purpose of}} The purpose of a vocative phrase is to indicate who is being addressed, or to indicate to that person that he or she ought to be listening. A vocative phrase begins with a cmavo of selma'o COI or DOI, all of which are explained in more detail in 
{{ls|section-vocative-scales}}. Sometimes that is all there is to the phrase:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLE3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLE3}}
{{judri|c6e11d1}}
:'''coi'''
:<code>[greetings]</code>
:''Hello.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLeB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLeB}}
{{judri|c6e11d2}}
:'''je'e'''
:<code>[acknowledgement]</code>
:''Uh-huh.''
:''Roger!''

{{ind|general-imported|vocative word|phrase following}} In these cases, the person being addressed is obvious from the context. However, a vocative word (more precisely, one or more cmavo of COI, possibly followed by {{vla|doi}}, or else just {{vla|doi}} by itself) can be followed by one of several kinds of phrases, all of which are intended to indicate the addressee. The most common case is a name:

<!-- FIXME: this indexterm isn't tagged alone -->{{ind|lojban-word-imported|coi}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-Bega}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Bega}}
{{judri|c6e11d3}}
:'''coi. djan.'''
:''Hello, John.''

A pause is required (for morphological reasons) between a member of COI and a name. You can use {{vla|doi}} instead of a pause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-QmzB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QmzB}}
{{judri|c6e11d4}}
:'''coi doi djan.'''
:''Hello, John.''

means exactly the same thing and does not require a pause. Using {{vla|doi}} by itself is like just saying someone's name to attract his or her attention:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ULHn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ULHn}}
{{judri|c6e11d5}}
:'''doi djan.'''
:''John!''

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|implicit descriptor on}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|with sumti without descriptor}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|forms of}} In place of a name, a description may appear, lacking its descriptor, which is understood to be {{vla|le}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-V530}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-V530}}
{{judri|c6e11d6}}
:'''coi xunre pastu nixli'''
:<code>Hello, (red-type-of dress)-type-of girl.</code>
:''Hello, girl with the red dress!''

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|explicit quantifiers prohibited on}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|implicit quantifiers on}} The listener need not really be a 
:{{jbo|xunre pastu nixli}}, as long as she understands herself correctly from the description. (Actually, only a bare selbri can appear; explicit quantifiers are forbidden in this form of vocative, so the implicit quantifiers 
:{{jbo|su'o le ro}} are in effect.)

Finally, a complete sumti may be used, the most general case.

{{dsp|example-random-id-tBTa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tBTa}}
{{judri|c6e11d7}}
:'''co'o la bab. .e la noras.'''
:''Goodbye, Bob and Nora.''

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|with complete sumti}} {{lex|example-random-id-V530}} is thus the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3Qac}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3Qac}}
{{judri|c6e11d8}}
:'''coi le xunre pastu nixli'''
:<code>Hello, the-one-described-as red-dress girl!</code>

and {{lex|example-random-id-ULHn}} is the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bx2C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bx2C}}
{{judri|c6e11d9}}
:'''doi la djan.'''
:<code>The-one-named John!</code>

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase terminator|elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|elidable terminator for}} Finally, the elidable terminator for vocative phrases is {{vla|do'u}} (of selma'o DOhU), which is rarely needed except when a simple vocative word is being placed somewhere within a bridi. It may also be required when a vocative is placed between a sumti and its relative clause, or when there are a sequence of so-called “free modifiers” (vocatives, subscripts, utterance ordinals &ndash; See {{lch|chapter-mekso}} &ndash; metalinguistic comments &ndash; See {{ls|section-parentheses}} &ndash; or reciprocals &ndash; see{{lch|chapter-structure}}) which must be properly separated.

{{ind|general-imported|vocative phrase|effect of position on meaning}} The meaning of a vocative phrase that is within a sentence is not affected by its position in the sentence: thus {{lex|example-random-id-bx2C}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qLFi}} mean the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLFi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLFi}}
{{judri|c6e11d10}}
:'''doi djan. ko klama mi'''
:''John, come to me!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLGC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLGC}}
{{judri|c6e11d11}}
:'''ko klama mi doi djan.'''
:''Come to me, John!''

As usual for this chapter, the full syntax of vocative phrases has not been explained: relative clauses, discussed in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}, make for more possibilities.

{{ssp|section-names}}
==Lojban names==
Names have been used freely as sumti throughout this chapter without too much explanation. The time for the explanation has now come.

{{ind|general-imported|name words|recognition of}}  {{ind|general-imported|names|two kinds of}} First of all, there are two different kinds of things usually called “names” when talking about Lojban. The naming predicates of {{ls|section-basic-descriptors}} are just ordinary predicates which are being used in a special sense. In addition, though, there is a class of Lojban words which are used only to name things: these can be recognized by the fact that they end in a consonant followed by a pause. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-u0zY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-u0zY}}
{{judri|c6e12d1}}
:'''djan. meris. djein. .alis.'''
:''John. Mary. Jane. Alice.''

(Note that 
{{cmevla|.alis.}} begins as well as ends with a pause, because all Lojban words beginning with a vowel must be preceded by a pause. See {{lch|chapter-morphology}} for more information.)

{{ind|general-imported|names|with LA descriptor}}  {{ind|general-imported|names|in vocative phrase}}  {{ind|general-imported|names|uses of}} Names of this kind have two basic uses in Lojban: when used in a vocative phrase (see 
{{ls|section-vocative-syntax}}) they indicate who the listener is or should be. When used with a descriptor of selma'o LA, namely {{vla|la}}, {{vla|lai}}, or {{vla|la'i}}, they form sumti which refer to the persons or things known by the name.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLgw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLgw}}
{{judri|c6e12d2}}
:'''la djonz. klama le zarci'''
:<code>Jones goes to-the store.</code>
:''The Joneses go to-the store.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLHn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLHn}}
{{judri|c6e12d3}}
:'''lai djonz. klama le zarci'''
:<code>The-mass-of Joneses go to-the store.</code>
:''The Joneses go to the store.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qLgw}}, the significance is that all the persons (perhaps only one) I mean to refer to by the name 
{{cmevla|djonz.}} are going to the store. In {{lex|example-random-id-qLHn}}, the Joneses are massified, and only some part of them needs to be going. Of course, by 
{{cmevla|djonz.}} I can mean whomever I want: that person need not use the name 
{{cmevla|djonz.}} at all.

{{ind|general-imported|LA selma'o|contrasted with LE in use of name-words}}  {{ind|general-imported|LE selma'o|contrasted with LA in use of name-words}} The sumti in {{lex|example-random-id-qLgw}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qLHn}} operate exactly like the similar uses of {{vla|la}} and {{vla|lai}} in {{lex|example-random-id-PrGp}} and {{lex|example-random-id-H8z5}} respectively. The only difference is that these descriptors are followed by Lojban name-words. And in fact, the only difference between descriptors of selma'o LA (these three) and of selma'o LE (all the other descriptors) is that the former can be followed by name-words, whereas the latter cannot.

{{ind|general-imported|doi|effect on necessity for pause before name-word}}  {{ind|general-imported|LA selma'o|effect on necessity for pause before name-word}}  {{ind|general-imported|name-words|pause requirements before}}  {{ind|general-imported|name-words|limitations on}} There are certain limitations on the form of name-words in Lojban. In particular, they cannot contain the letter-sequences (or sound-sequences) 
{{vla|la}}, {{vla|lai}}, or {{vla|doi}} unless a consonant immediately precedes within the name. Reciprocally, every name not preceded by {{vla|la}}, {{vla|lai}}, {{vla|la'i}}, or {{vla|doi}} must be preceded by a pause instead:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLiB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLiB}}
{{judri|c6e12d4}}
:'''coi .djan.'''
:''Hello, John.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLIJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLIJ}}
{{judri|c6e12d5}}
:'''zo .djan. cmene mi'''
:<code>The-word “John” is-the-name-of me.</code>
:''My name is John.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qLiB}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qLIJ}}, 
{{cmevla|.djan.}} appears with a pause before it as well as after it, because the preceding word is not one of the four special cases. These rules force names to always be separable from the general word-stream.

{{ind|general-imported|names|multiple}} Unless some other rule prevents it (such as the rule that {{vla|zo}} is always followed by a single word, which is quoted), multiple names may appear wherever one name is permitted, each with its terminating pause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cw3p}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cw3p}}
{{ind|example|Newport News|example}}
{{ind|example|John Paul Jones|example}}
{{judri|c6e12d6}}
:'''doi djan. pol. djonz. le bloti cu klama fi la niuport. niuz.'''
:''John Paul Jones, the boat comes (to somewhere) from Newport News.''

{{ind|general-imported|name-words|permissible consonant combinations}} A name may not contain any consonant combination that is illegal in Lojban words generally: the “impermissible consonant clusters” of Lojban morphology (explained in 
{{ls|section-clusters}}). Thus {{false|djeimz.}} is not a valid version of “James” (because '''mz''' is invalid): 
{{cmevla|djeimyz}} will suffice. Similarly, {{vla|la}} may be replaced by {{vla|ly}}, {{vla|lai}} by 
:{{jbo|ly'i}}, {{vla|doi}} by {{vla|do'i}} or {{vla|dai}}. Here are a few examples:

{{ind|example|Doyle|example}}
{{ind|example|Lyra|example}}  
{{ind|example|Lottie|example}}  
<tab class=wikitable header=true>
Doyle	{{false|*doi,l}}	{{cmevla|do'il}} or {{cmevla|dai,l}}
Lyra	{{false|*lairas}}	{{cmevla|ly'iras}}
Lottie	{{false|*latis}}	{{cmevla|LYtis.}} or {{cmevla|lotis.}}
(American pronunciation)
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|names|using rafsi}} Names may be borrowed from other languages or created arbitrarily. Another common practice is to use one or more rafsi, arranged to end with a consonant, to form a name: thus the rafsi 
{{raf|loj-}} for {{vla|logji}} (logical) and 
{{raf|ban-}} for {{vla|bangu}} (language) unite to form the name of this language:

{{dsp|example-random-id-uXAY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uXAY}}
{{judri|c6e12d7}}
:'''lojban.'''
:''Lojban''

{{ind|general-imported|names from vowel-final base|commonly used consonant endings}}  {{ind|general-imported|names|borrowing from other languages}} When borrowing names from another language which end in a vowel, or when turning a Lojban brivla (all of which end in vowels) into a name, the vowel may be removed or an arbitrary consonant added. It is common (but not required) to use the consonants 

{{raf|s}} or 
{{raf|n}} when borrowing vowel-final names from English; speakers of other languages may wish to use other consonant endings.

{{ind|general-imported|names with la|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for name sumti of the form {{vla|la}} followed by a name is {{vla|su'o}}, just as for {{vla|la}} followed by a selbri.

{{ssp|section-pro-sumti}}
==Pro-sumti summary==
{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|classes of}} The Lojban pro-sumti are the cmavo of selma'o KOhA. They fall into several classes: personal, definable, quantificational, reflexive, back-counting, indefinite, demonstrative, metalinguistic, relative, question. More details are given in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}; this section mostly duplicates information found there, but adds material on the implicit quantifier of each pro-sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|implicit quantifier for}} The following examples illustrate each of the classes. Unless otherwise noted below, the implicit quantification for pro-sumti is {{vla|ro}} (all). In the case of pro-sumti which refer to other sumti, the {{vla|ro}} signifies “all of those referred to by the other sumti”: thus it is possible to restrict, but not to extend, the quantification of the other sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|personal pro-sumti}} Personal pro-sumti ( {{vla|mi}}, {{vla|do}}, {{vla|mi'o}}, {{vla|mi'a}}, 
{{vla|ma'a}}, 
{{vla|do'o}}, 
{{vla|ko}}) refer to the speaker or the listener or both, with or without third parties:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PHPi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PHPi}}
{{judri|c6e13d1}}
:'''mi prami do'''
:''I love you.''

{{ind|general-imported|personal pro-sumti|implicit quantifier for}} The personal pro-sumti may be interpreted in context as either representing individuals or masses, so the implicit quantifier may be 
{{vla|pisu'o}} rather than 
{{vla|ro}}: in particular, {{vla|mi'o}}, {{vla|mi'a}}, 
{{vla|ma'a}}, and 
{{vla|do'o}} specifically represent mass combinations of the individuals (you and I, I and others, you and I and others, you and others) that make them up.

{{ind|general-imported|definable pro-sumti}} Definable pro-sumti ( {{vla|ko'a}}, {{vla|ko'e}}, {{vla|ko'i}}, {{vla|ko'o}}, {{vla|ko'u}}, {{vla|fo'a}}, 
{{vla|fo'e}}, {{vla|fo'i}}, {{vla|fo'o}}, {{vla|fo'u}}) refer to whatever the speaker has explicitly made them refer to. This reference is accomplished with {{vla|goi}} (of selma'o GOI), which means “defined-as”.

{{dsp|example-random-id-8whK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8whK}}
{{judri|c6e13d2}}
:'''le cribe goi ko'a cu xekri .i ko'a citka le smacu'''
:''The bear defined-as it-1 is-black. It-1 eats the mouse.''

{{ind|general-imported|quantificational pro-sumti}} Quantificational pro-sumti ( {{vla|da}}, {{vla|de}}, {{vla|di}}) are used as variables in bridi involving predicate logic:

{{dsp|example-random-id-FVj8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-FVj8}}
{{judri|c6e13d3}}
:'''ro da poi prenu cu prami pa de poi finpe'''
:<code>All somethings-1 which-are persons love one something-2 which-is a-fish.</code>
:''All persons love a fish (each his/her own).''

{{ind|general-imported|quantificational pro-sumti|implicit quantification rules}} (This is not the same as “All persons love a certain fish”; the difference between the two is one of quantifier order.) The implicit quantification rules for quantificational pro-sumti are particular to them, and are discussed in detail in 
{{lch|chapter-quantifiers}}. Roughly speaking, the quantifier is {{vla|su'o}} (at least one) when the pro-sumti is first used, and {{vla|ro}} (all) thereafter.

{{ind|general-imported|reflexive pro-sumti}} Reflexive pro-sumti ( {{vla|vo'a}}, {{vla|vo'e}}, {{vla|vo'i}}, {{vla|vo'o}}, {{vla|vo'u}}) refer to the same referents as sumti filling other places in the same bridi, with the effect that the same thing is referred to twice:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nMse}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nMse}}
{{judri|c6e13d4}}
:'''le cribe cu batci vo'a'''
:<code>The bear bites what-is-in-the-x1-place.</code>
:''The bear bites itself.''

{{ind|general-imported|back-counting pro-sumti}} Back-counting pro-sumti ( {{vla|ri}}, {{vla|ra}}, {{vla|ru}}) refer to the referents of previous sumti counted backwards from the pro-sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cjTj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cjTj}}
{{judri|c6e13d5}}
:'''mi klama la frankfurt. ri'''
:<code>I go to-Frankfurt from-the-referent-of-the-last-sumti</code>
:''I go from Frankfurt to Frankfurt (by some unstated route).''

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-sumti}} Indefinite pro-sumti ( {{vla|zo'e}}, {{vla|zu'i}}, 
{{vla|zi'o}}) refer to something which is unspecified:

{{dsp|example-random-id-d5Ee}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-d5Ee}}
{{judri|c6e13d6}}
:'''mi klama la frankfurt. zo'e zo'e zo'e'''
:<code>I go to-Frankfurt from-unspecified via-unspecified by-means-unspecified.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-sumti|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for indefinite pro-sumti is, well, indefinite. It might be 
{{vla|ro}} (all) or {{vla|su'o}} (at least one) or conceivably even {{vla|no}} (none), though {{vla|no}} would require a very odd context indeed.

{{ind|general-imported|demonstrative pro-sumti}} Demonstrative pro-sumti ( {{vla|ti}}, {{vla|ta}}, {{vla|tu}}) refer to things pointed at by the speaker, or when pointing is not possible, to things near or far from the speaker:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aqfJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-aqfJ}}
{{judri|c6e13d7}}
:'''ko muvgau ti ta tu'''
:<code>You [imperative] move this-thing from-that-nearby-place to-that-further-away-place.</code>
:''Move this from there to over there!''

{{ind|general-imported|metalinguistic pro-sumti}} Metalinguistic pro-sumti ( {{vla|di'u}}, {{vla|de'u}}, 
{{vla|da'u}}, 
{{vla|di'e}}, 
{{vla|de'e}}, 
{{vla|da'e}}, 
{{vla|dei}}, {{vla|do'i}}) refer to spoken or written utterances, either preceding, following, or the same as the current utterance.

{{dsp|example-random-id-8VYF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8VYF}}
{{judri|c6e13d8}}
:'''li re su'i re du li vo .i la'e di'u jetnu'''
:<code>The-number two plus two equals the-number four. The-referent-of the-previous-utterance is-true.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|metalinguistic pro-sumti|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for metalinguistic pro-sumti is 
{{vla|su'o}} (at least one), because they are considered analogous to {{vla|lo}} descriptions: they refer to things which really are previous, current, or following utterances.

{{ind|general-imported|relative pro-sumti}} The relative pro-sumti ( 
{{vla|ke'a}}) is used within relative clauses (See {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}} for a discussion of relative clauses) to refer to whatever sumti the relative clause is attached to.

{{dsp|example-random-id-sf2T}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sf2T}}
{{judri|c6e13d9}}
:'''mi viska le mlatu ku poi zo'e zbasu ke'a loi slasi'''
:<code>I see the cat(s) such-that something-unspecified makes it/them (the cats) from-a-mass-of plastic.</code>
:''I see the cat(s) made of plastic.''

{{ind|general-imported|question pro-sumti}} The question pro-sumti ( 
{{vla|ma}}) is used to ask questions which request the listener to supply a sumti which will make the question into a truth:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9tSb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9tSb}}
{{judri|c6e13d10}}
:'''do klama ma'''
:<code>You go to-what-sumti?</code>
:''Where are you going?''

{{ind|general-imported|question pro-sumti|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for the question pro-sumti is 
{{vla|su'o}} (at least one), because the listener is only being asked to supply a single answer, not all correct answers.

{{ind|general-imported|definable pro-sumti|sequences of lerfu words as}} In addition, sequences of lerfu words (of selma'o BY and related selma'o) can also be used as definable pro-sumti.

{{ssp|section-quotation}}
==Quotation summary==
{{ind|general-imported|quotation|four kinds}} There are four kinds of quotation in Lojban: text quotation, words quotation, single-word quotation, non-Lojban quotation. More information is provided in {{lch|chapter-structure}}.

{{ind|general-imported|text quotation|as internally grammatical}}  {{ind|general-imported|text quotation|syntax of}} Text quotations are preceded by {{vla|lu}} and followed by {{vla|li'u}}, and are an essential part of the surrounding text: they must be grammatical Lojban texts.

{{dsp|example-random-id-v1DE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-v1DE}}
{{judri|c6e14d1}}
:'''mi cusku lu mi'e djan. li'u'''
:<code>I say the-text [quote] I-am John [unquote].</code>
:''I say “I'm John”.''

{{ind|general-imported|word quotation|internal grammar of}}  {{ind|general-imported|word quotation|as morphologically valid}} Words quotations are quotations of one or more Lojban words. The words need not mean anything, but they must be morphologically valid so that the end of the quotation can be discerned.

<!-- FIXME: these indexterms aren't tagged alone -->{{ind|lojban-word-imported|le'u}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|lo'u}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-UMDQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UMDQ}}
{{judri|c6e14d2}}
:'''mi cusku lo'u li mi le'u'''
:<code>I say the-words [quote] {{false|li mi}} [unquote].</code>
:''I say “{{false|li mi}}”.''

Note that the translation of {{lex|example-random-id-UMDQ}} does not translate the Lojban words, because they are not presumed to have any meaning (in fact, they are ungrammatical).

{{ind|general-imported|single-word quotation}} Single-word quotation quotes a single Lojban word. Compound cmavo are not allowed.

{{dsp|example-random-id-XqKv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XqKv}}
{{judri|c6e14d3}}
:'''mi cusku zo .ai'''
:''I say the-word {{vla|ai}}.''

{{ind|general-imported|non-Lojban quotation}} Non-Lojban quotation can quote anything, Lojban or not, even non-speech such as drum talk, whistle words, music, or belching. A Lojban word which does not appear within the quotation is used before and after it to set it off from the surrounding Lojban text.

{{dsp|example-random-id-1Uey}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1Uey}}
{{judri|c6e14d4}}
:'''mi cusku zoi kuot. I'm John .kuot'''
:''I say “I'm John”.''

{{ind|general-imported|quotation|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for all types of quotation is {{vla|su'o}} (at least one), because quotations are analogous to {{vla|lo}} descriptions: they refer to things which actually are words or sequences of words.

{{ssp|section-number-summary}}
==Number summary==
{{ind|general-imported|number sumti|with li}}  {{ind|general-imported|number sumti|syntax of}} The sumti which refer to numbers consist of the cmavo {{vla|li}} (of selma'o LI) followed by an arbitrary Lojban mekso, or mathematical expression. This can be anything from a simple number up to the most complicated combination of numbers, variables, operators, and so on. Much more information on numbers is given in {{lch|chapter-mekso}}. Here are a few examples of increasing complexity:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLIm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLIm}}
{{judri|c6e15d1}}
:'''li vo'''
:<code>the-number four</code>
:{{math|4}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLis}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLis}}
{{judri|c6e15d2}}
:'''li re su'i re'''
:<code>the-number two plus two</code>
:{{math|2 + 2}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLiX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLiX}}
{{judri|c6e15d3}}
:'''li .abu bopi'i xy. bote'a re su'i by. bopi'i xy. su'i cy.'''
:<code>the-number a times x to-power 2 plus b times x plus c</code>
:{{math|ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c}}

{{ind|general-imported|number sumti|with li contrasted with me'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|number sumti|with me'o contrasted with li}}  {{ind|general-imported|LI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|me'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|number sumti|with me'o}} An alternative to {{vla|li}} is {{vla|me'o}}, also of selma'o LI. Number expressions beginning with {{vla|me'o}} refer to the actual expression, rather than its value. Thus {{lex|example-random-id-qLIm}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qLis}} above have the same meaning, the number four, whereas

{{dsp|example-random-id-sW7u}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sW7u}}
{{judri|c6e15d4}}
:'''me'o vo'''
:<code>the-expression four</code>
:''“{{math|4}}”''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-3s82}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3s82}}
{{judri|c6e15d5}}
:'''me'o re su'i re'''
:<code>the-expression two plus two</code>
:''“{{math|2+2}}”''

refer to different pieces of text.

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions|implicit quantifier for}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|implicit quantifier for}} The implicit quantifier for numbers and mathematical expressions is 
{{vla|su'o}}, because these sumti are analogous to {{vla|lo}} descriptions: they refer to things which actually are numbers or pieces of text. In the case of numbers (with {{vla|li}}), this is a distinction without a difference, as there is only one number which is 4; but there are many texts “4”, as many as there are documents in which that numeral appears.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{csp|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}
=Brevity Is The Soul Of Language: Pro-sumti And Pro-bridi=

{{image|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo-picture|The picture for chapter 7|CLL-chapter-anaphoric-cmavo.gif}}
{{ssp|section-anaphoric-cmavo-introduction}}
==What are pro-sumti and pro-bridi? What are they for?==
{{ind|general-imported|pronouns in English|as noun abbreviations}} Speakers of Lojban, like speakers of other languages, require mechanisms of abbreviation. If every time we referred to something, we had to express a complete description of it, life would be too short to say what we have to say. In English, we have words called “pronouns” which allow us to replace nouns or noun phrases with shorter terms. An English with no pronouns might look something like this:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KeL4}}
{{judri|c7e1d1}}
Speakers of Lojban, like speakers of other languages, require mechanisms of abbreviation. If every time speakers of Lojban referred to a thing to which speakers of Lojban refer, speakers of Lojban had to express a complete description of what speakers of Lojban referred to, life would be too short to say what speakers of Lojban have to say.

{{ind|general-imported|pronouns in English|as independent of abbreviations}} Speakers of this kind of English would get mightily sick of talking. Furthermore, there are uses of pronouns in English which are independent of abbreviation. There is all the difference in the world between:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VISf}}
{{ind|example|shook stick|example}}
{{judri|c7e1d2}}
John picked up a stick and shook it.

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-GoqJ}}
{{ind|example|shook stick|example}}
{{judri|c7e1d3}}
John picked up a stick and shook a stick.{{lex|example-random-id-GoqJ}} does not imply that the two sticks are necessarily the same, whereas {{lex|example-random-id-VISf}} requires that they are.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GOhA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|series}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|compared to pro-bridi as means of abbreviation}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi|compared to pro-sumti as means of abbreviation}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|compared to pronouns in usage as abbreviations}}  {{ind|general-imported|pronouns|compared to pro-sumti in usage as abbreviations}} In Lojban, we have sumti rather than nouns, so our equivalent of pronouns are called by the hybrid term “pro-sumti”. A purely Lojban term would be 
:{{jbo|sumti cmavo}}: all of the pro-sumti are cmavo belonging to selma'o KOhA. In exactly the same way, Lojban has a group of cmavo (belonging to selma'o GOhA) which serve as selbri or full bridi. These may be called “pro-bridi” or 
:{{jbo|bridi cmavo}}. This chapter explains the uses of all the members of selma'o KOhA and GOhA. They fall into a number of groups, known as series: thus, in selma'o KOhA, we have among others the mi-series, the ko'a-series, the da-series, and so on. In each section, a series of pro-sumti is explained, and if there is a corresponding series of pro-bridi, it is explained and contrasted. Many pro-sumti series don't have pro-bridi analogues, however.

{{ind|general-imported|antecedent of pro-bridi|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|referent of pro-bridi|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|antecedent of pro-sumti|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|referent of pro-sumti|definition}} A few technical terms: The term “referent” means the thing to which a pro-sumti (by extension, a pro-bridi) refers. If the speaker of a sentence is James, then the referent of the word “I” is James. On the other hand, the term “antecedent” refers to a piece of language which a pro-sumti (or pro-bridi) implicitly repeats. In

{{dsp|example-random-id-AnBS}}
{{judri|c7e1d4}}
John loves himself

the antecedent of “himself” is “John”; not the person, but a piece of text (a name, in this case). John, the person, would be the referent of “himself”. Not all pro-sumti or pro-bridi have antecedents, but all of them have referents.

{{ssp|section-mi-series}}
==Personal pro-sumti: the mi-series==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''mi'''	KOhA	mi-series	''I, me''
'''do'''	KOhA	mi-series	''you''
'''mi'o'''	KOhA	mi-series	''you and I''
'''mi'a'''	KOhA	mi-series	''I and others, we but not you''
'''ma'a'''	KOhA	mi-series	''you and I and others''
'''do'o'''	KOhA	mi-series	''you and others''
'''ko'''	KOhA	mi-series	''you-imperative''
</tab>

{{ind|general|foreman of a jury|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|personal pronouns|with mi-series for I/you}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|for listener(s)}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|for speaker(s)}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|mi-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|mi-series|of pro-sumti}} The mi-series of pro-sumti refer to the speaker, the listener, and others in various combinations. {{vla|mi}} refers to the speaker and perhaps others for whom the speaker speaks; it may be a Lojbanic mass. {{vla|do}} refers to the listener or listeners. Neither {{vla|mi}} nor {{vla|do}} is specific about the number of persons referred to; for example, the foreman of a jury may refer to the members of the jury as 
{{vla|mi}}, since in speaking officially he represents all of them.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|COI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|COI selma'o|effect on referent of &quot;do&quot;<!-- FIXME: what should these &quot;s become? -->}}  {{ind|general-imported|COI selma'o|effect on referent of &quot;mi&quot;}} The referents of {{vla|mi}} and {{vla|do}} are usually obvious from the context, but may be assigned by the vocative words of selma'o COI, explained in {{ls|section-vocative-scales}}. The vocative {{vla|mi'e}} assigns {{vla|mi}}, whereas all of the other vocatives assign {{vla|do}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-4dna}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4dna}}
{{judri|c7e2d1}}
:'''mi'e djan. doi frank. mi cusku lu mi bajra li'u do'''
:<code>I-am John, O Frank, I express [quote] I run [unquote] to-you</code>
:''I am John, Frank; I tell you “I run”.''

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|for listeners and/or speakers and/or others}} The cmavo {{vla|mi'o}}, {{vla|mi'a}}, 
{{vla|ma'a}}, and 
{{vla|do'o}} express various combinations of the speaker and/or the listener and/or other people:
*{{vla|mi'o}} includes only the speaker and the listener but no one else;
*{{vla|mi'a}} includes the speaker and others but excludes the listener;
*{{vla|do'o}} includes the listener and others but excludes the speaker;
*{{vla|ma'a}} includes all three: speaker, listener, others.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti for speaker/listener/others|as masses}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti for speaker/listener/others|relation to joi}} All of these pro-sumti represent masses. For example, {{vla|mi'o}} is the same as 
:{{jbo|mi joi do}}, the mass of me and you considered jointly.

<!-- FIXME: what should these &quot;s become? -->{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti for &quot;we&quot;|contrasted with English &quot;we&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|English &quot;we&quot;|contrasted with Lojban pro-sumti for &quot;we&quot;}} In English, “we” can mean {{vla|mi}} or {{vla|mi'o}} or {{vla|mi'a}} or even 
{{vla|ma'a}}, and English-speakers often suffer because they cannot easily distinguish 
{{vla|mi'o}} from {{vla|mi'a}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-22dg}}
{{judri|c7e2d2}}
We're going to the store.

Does this include the listener or not? There's no way to be sure.

{{ind|general-imported|ko|use for commands}}  {{ind|general-imported|ko|use for imperatives}}  {{ind|general-imported|imperatives|with ko}}  {{ind|general-imported|commands|with ko}} Finally, the cmavo {{vla|ko}} is logically equivalent to {{vla|do}}; its referent is the listener. However, its use alters an assertion about the listener into a command to the listener to make the assertion true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-n1Rv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-n1Rv}}
{{judri|c7e2d3}}
:'''do klama le zarci'''
:<code>You go to-the store.</code>

becomes:

{{dsp|example-random-id-uwDI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uwDI}}
{{judri|c7e2d4}}
:'''ko klama le zarci'''
:<code>You [imperative] go to-the store.</code>
:<code>Make “you go to the store” true!</code>
:''Go to the store!''

{{ind|general-imported|ko|in later selbri place in imperative}}  {{ind|general-imported|imperatives|English contrasted with Lojban in presence of subject of command}} In English, the subject of a command is omitted, but in Lojban, the word {{vla|ko}} must be used. However, {{vla|ko}} does not have to appear in the x1 place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5Jbi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5Jbi}}
{{judri|c7e2d5}}
:'''mi viska ko'''
:<code>I see you [imperative]</code>
<code>Make “I see you” true!</code>
:''Be seen by me!''

{{ind|general-imported|ko|in sub-clause of main bridi}} In {{lex|example-random-id-5Jbi}}, it is necessary to make the verb passive in English in order to convey the effect of {{vla|ko}} in the x2 place. Indeed, {{vla|ko}} does not even have to be a sumti of the main bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VTRG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VTRG}}
{{judri|c7e2d6}}
:'''mi viska le prenu poi prami ko'''
:<code>I see the person that loves you [imperative]</code>
<code>Make “I see the person that loves you” true!</code>
:<code>Be such that the person who loves you is seen by me!</code>
:''Show me the person who loves you!''

{{ind|general-imported|mi-series pro-sumti|lack of pro-bridi equivalent}} As mentioned in {{ls|section-anaphoric-cmavo-introduction}}, some pro-sumti series have corresponding pro-bridi series. However, there is no equivalent of the mi-series among pro-bridi, since a person isn't a relationship.

{{ssp|section-ti-series}}
==Demonstrative pro-sumti: the ti-series==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ti'''	KOhA	ti-series	''this here, a nearby object''
'''ta'''	KOhA	ti-series	''that there, a medium-distant object''
'''tu'''	KOhA	ti-series	''that yonder, a far-distant object''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|ti-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|as pointing referents only}}  {{ind|general-imported|this/that in English|compared with ti-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|compared with English this/that}}  {{ind|general-imported|demonstrative pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|pointing|reference by}} It is often useful to refer to things by pointing to them or by some related non-linguistic mechanism. In English, the words “this” and “that” serve this function among others: “this” refers to something pointed at that is near the speaker, and “that” refers to something further away. The Lojban pro-sumti of the ti-series serve the same functions, but more narrowly. The cmavo {{vla|ti}}, {{vla|ta}}, and {{vla|tu}} provide only the pointing function of “this” and “that”; they are not used to refer to things that cannot be pointed at.

{{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|3 degrees of distance with}}  {{ind|general-imported|tu|archaic English yon as equivalent of}}  {{ind|general-imported|yon|as archaic English equivalent of tu}} There are three pro-sumti of the ti-series rather than just two because it is often useful to distinguish between objects that are at more than two different distances. Japanese, among other languages, regularly does this. Until the 16th century, English did too; the pronoun “that” referred to something at a medium distance from the speaker, and the now-archaic pronoun “yon” to something far away.

{{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|problems in written text}}  {{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|conversational convention for}} In conversation, there is a special rule about {{vla|ta}} and {{vla|tu}} that is often helpful in interpreting them. When used contrastingly, {{vla|ta}} refers to something that is near the listener, whereas {{vla|tu}} refers to something far from both speaker and listener. This makes for a parallelism between {{vla|ti}} and {{vla|mi}}, and {{vla|ta}} and {{vla|do}}, that is convenient when pointing is not possible; for example, when talking by telephone. In written text, on the other hand, the meaning of the ti-series is inherently vague; is the writer to be taken as pointing to something, and if so, to what? In all cases, what counts as “near” and “far away” is relative to the current situation.

{{ind|general-imported|this|pronoun expression with ti}}  {{ind|general-imported|ti|as pronoun expression for English this}}  {{ind|general-imported|this|adjective usage contrasted with pronoun usage}}  {{ind|general-imported|this|pronoun usage contrasted with adjective usage}} It is important to distinguish between the English pronoun “this” and the English adjective “this” as in “this boat”. The latter is not represented in Lojban by 
{{vla|ti}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-IWi7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-IWi7}}
{{ind|example|this boat|example}}
{{judri|c7e3d1}}
:'''le ti bloti'''
:<code>the this boat</code>

{{ind|general-imported|this|adjective expression with vi}}  {{ind|general-imported|vi|as adjective expression for English this}} does not mean “this boat” but rather “this one's boat”, “the boat associated with this thing”, as explained in {{ls|section-possessive-sumti}}. A correct Lojban translation of {{lex|example-random-id-IWi7}} is

{{dsp|example-random-id-rfUc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rfUc}}
{{judri|c7e3d2}}
{{ind|example|this boat|example}}
:'''le vi bloti'''
:<code>the here boat</code>
:''the nearby boat''

using a spatial tense before the selbri {{vla|bloti}} to express that the boat is near the speaker. (Tenses are explained in full in {{lch|chapter-tenses}}.) Another correct translation would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pRLq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pRLq}}
{{judri|c7e3d3}}
{{ind|example|this boat|example}}
:'''ti noi bloti'''
:<code>this-thing which-incidentally is-a-boat</code>

{{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|lack of pro-bridi equivalent}}  {{ind|general-imported|this|adjective expression with ti noi}}  {{ind|general-imported|ti noi|as adjective expression for this}} There are no demonstrative pro-bridi to correspond to the ti-series: you can't point to a relationship.

{{ssp|section-dihu-series}}
==Utterance pro-sumti: the di'u-series==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''di'u'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''the previous utterance''
'''de'u'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''an earlier utterance''
'''da'u'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''a much earlier utterance''
'''di'e'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''the next utterance''
'''de'e'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''a later utterance''
'''da'e'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''a much later utterance''
'''dei'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''this very utterance''
'''do'i'''	KOhA	di'u-series	''some utterance''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|di'u-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|this|as utterance reference in English}}  {{ind|general-imported|di'u-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|utterance pro-sumti (see also di'u-series pro-sumti)}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti for utterances}} The cmavo of the di'u-series enable us to talk about things that have been, are being, or will be said. In English, it is normal to use “this” and “that” for this (indeed, the immediately preceding “this” is an example of such a usage):

{{dsp|example-random-id-KNih}}
{{judri|c7e4d1}}
You don't like cats.

That is untrue.

Here “that” does not refer to something that can be pointed to, but to the preceding sentence “You don't like cats”. In Lojban, therefore, {{lex|example-random-id-KNih}} is rendered:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nTou}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nTou}}
{{judri|c7e4d2}}
:'''do na nelci loi mlatu .i di'u jitfa jufra'''
:<code>You (Not!) like the-mass-of cats. The-previous-utterance is-a-false-sentence.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|ti-series pro-sumti|contrasted with di'u-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|di'u|contrasted with ta}}  {{ind|general-imported|ta|contrasted with di'u}} Using {{vla|ta}} instead of {{vla|di'u}} would cause the listener to look around to see what the speaker of the second sentence was physically pointing to.

As with {{vla|ti}}, {{vla|ta}}, and {{vla|tu}}, the cmavo of the di'u-series come in threes: a close utterance, a medium-distance utterance, and a distant utterance, either in the past or in the future. It turned out to be impossible to use the {{lerfu|i}}/ {{lerfu|a}}/ {{lerfu|u}} vowel convention of the demonstratives in {{ls|section-ti-series}} without causing collisions with other cmavo, and so the di'u-series has a unique {{lerfu|i}}/ {{lerfu|e}}/ {{lerfu|a}} convention in the first vowel of the cmavo.

Most references in speech are to the past (what has already been said), so {{vla|di'e}}, 
{{vla|de'e}}, and 
{{vla|da'e}} are not very useful when speaking. In writing, they are frequently handy:

{{dsp|example-random-id-erEL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-erEL}}
{{ind|example|Simon says|example}}
{{judri|c7e4d3}}
:'''la saimn. cusku di'e'''
:<code>Simon expresses the-following-utterance.</code>
:''Simon says:''
{{lex|example-random-id-erEL}} would typically be followed by a quotation. Note that although presumably the quotation is of something Simon has said in the past, the quotation utterance itself would appear after {{lex|example-random-id-erEL}}, and so {{vla|di'e}} is appropriate.

The remaining two cmavo, {{vla|dei}} and {{vla|do'i}}, refer respectively to the very utterance that the speaker is uttering, and to some vague or unspecified utterance uttered by someone at some time:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLmA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLmA}}
{{judri|c7e4d4}}
:'''dei jetnu jufra'''
:<code>This-utterance is-a-true-sentence.</code>
:''What I am saying (at this moment) is true.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLmV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLmV}}
{{judri|c7e4d5}}
:'''do'i jetnu jufra'''
:<code>Some-utterance is-a-true-sentence.</code>
:''That's true (where “that” is not necessarily what was just said).''

The cmavo of the di'u-series have a meaning that is relative to the context. The referent of {{vla|dei}} in the current utterance is the same as the referent of {{vla|di'u}} in the next utterance. The term “utterance” is used rather than “sentence” because the amount of speech or written text referred to by any of these words is vague. Often, a single bridi is intended, but longer utterances may be thus referred to.

Note one very common construction with {{vla|di'u}} and the cmavo {{vla|la'e}} (of selma'o LAhE; See {{ls|section-sumti-qualifiers}}) which precedes a sumti and means “the thing referred to by (the sumti)”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MsUd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MsUd}}
{{judri|c7e4d6}}
:'''mi prami la djein. .i mi nelci la'e di'u'''
:<code>I love Jane. And I like the-referent-of the-last-utterance.</code>
:''I love Jane, and I like that.''

{{ind|general-imported|la'edi'u|contrasted with di'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|di'u|contrasted with la'edi'u}} The effect of 
:{{jbo|la'e di'u}} in {{lex|example-random-id-MsUd}} is that the speaker likes, not the previous sentence, but rather the state of affairs referred to by the previous sentence, namely his loving Jane. This cmavo compound is often written as a single word: {{vla|la'edi'u}}. It is important not to mix up 
{{vla|di'u}} and {{vla|la'edi'u}}, or the wrong meaning will generally result:

{{dsp|example-random-id-68ru}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-68ru}}
{{judri|c7e4d7}}
:'''mi prami la djein. .i mi nelci di'u'''
:''I love Jane. And I like the-last-utterance.''

says that the speaker likes one of his own sentences.
