There are no pro-bridi corresponding to the di'u-series.

{{ssp|section-koha-broda-series}}
==Assignable pro-sumti and pro-bridi: the ko'a-series and the broda-series==
The following cmavo and gismu are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ko'a'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-1''
'''ko'e'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-2''
'''ko'i'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-3''
'''ko'o'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-4''
'''ko'u'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-5''
'''fo'a'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-6''
'''fo'e'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-7''
'''fo'i'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-8''
'''fo'o'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-9''
'''fo'u'''	KOhA'''	KO'a-series	''it-10''
'''broda'''	BRIVLA	broda-series	''is-thing-1''
'''brode'''	BRIVLA	broda-series	''is-thing-2''
'''brodi'''	BRIVLA	broda-series	''is-thing-3''
'''brodo'''	BRIVLA	broda-series	''is-thing-4''
'''brodu'''	BRIVLA	broda-series	''is-thing-5''
'''goi'''	GOI	pro-sumti assignment''
'''cei'''	CEI	pro-bridi assignment''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|ko'a-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|personal pronouns|with ko'a-series for he/she/it/they}} The discussion of personal pro-sumti in 
{{ls|section-mi-series}} may have seemed incomplete. In English, the personal pronouns include not only “I” and “you” but also “he”, “she”, “it”, and “they”. Lojban does have equivalents of this latter group: in fact, it has more of them than English does. However, they are organized and used very differently.

{{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series pro-sumti|as assignable}}  {{ind|general-imported|personal pronouns for he/she/it/they|English contrasted with Lojban in organization}} There are ten cmavo in the ko'a-series, and they may be assigned freely to any sumti whatsoever. The English word “he” can refer only to males, “she” only to females (and ships and a few other things), “it” only to inanimate things, and “they” only to plurals; the cmavo of the ko'a-series have no restrictions at all. Therefore, it is almost impossible to guess from the context what ko'a-series cmavo might refer to if they are just used freely:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdCR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdCR}}
{{judri|c7e5d1}}
:'''la .alis. klama le zarci .i ko'a blanu'''
:''Alice goes-to the store. It-1 is-blue.''

The English gloss “it-1”, plus knowledge about the real world, would tend to make English-speakers believe that 
{{vla|ko'a}} refers to the store; in other words, that its antecedent is 
:{{jbo|le zarci}}. To a Lojbanist, however, 
:{{jbo|la .alis.}} is just as likely an antecedent, in which case {{lex|example-random-id-qdCR}} means that Alice, not the store, is blue.

{{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series pro-sumti|assigning with goi}} To avoid this pitfall, Lojban employs special syntax, using the cmavo {{vla|goi}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-duGR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-duGR}}
{{judri|c7e5d2}}
:'''la .alis. klama le zarci .i ko'a goi la .alis. cu blanu'''
:<code>Alice goes-to the store. It-1, also-known-as Alice, is-blue.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series pro-sumti|assignment with goi as symmetrical}} Syntactically, 
:{{jbo|goi la .alis.}} is a relative phrase (relative phrases are explained in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}). Semantically, it says that {{vla|ko'a}} and 
:{{jbo|la .alis.}} refer to the same thing, and furthermore that this is true because {{vla|ko'a}} is being defined as meaning 
:{{jbo|la .alis.}}. It is equally correct to say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-oKaM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-oKaM}}
{{judri|c7e5d3}}
:'''la .alis. klama le zarci .i la .alis. goi ko'a cu blanu'''
:<code>Alice goes-to the store. Alice, also-known-as it-1, is-blue.</code>

in other words, {{vla|goi}} is symmetrical. There is a terminator, {{vla|ge'u}} (of selma'o GEhU), which is almost always elidable. The details are in {{ls|section-relative-phrases}}.

{{ind|general-imported|goi assignment of ko'a-series pro-sumti|use in speech contrasted with writing}} The afterthought form of {{vla|goi}} shown in {{lex|example-random-id-duGR}} and {{lex|example-random-id-oKaM}} is probably most common in speech, where we do not know until part way through our utterance that we will want to refer to Alice again. In writing, though, {{vla|ko'a}} may be assigned at the point where Alice is first mentioned. An example of this forethought form of {{vla|goi}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1FJV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1FJV}}
{{judri|c7e5d4}}
:'''la .alis. goi ko'a klama le zarci .i ko'a cu blanu'''
:<code>Alice, also-known-as it-1, goes-to the store. It-1 is-blue.</code>

{{ind|general|hereafter known as|example}}
{{ind|general|legal jargon|example}} 

Again, {{jbo|ko'a goi la .alis.}} would have been entirely acceptable in {{lex|example-random-id-1FJV}}. This last form is reminiscent of legal jargon: “The party of the first part, hereafter known as Buyer, ...”.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi|as abbreviation for bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|broda-series for pro-bridi|compared with ko'a-series for pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series for pro-sumti|compared with broda-series for pro-bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi|broda-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi}} Just as the ko'a-series of pro-sumti allows a substitute for a sumti which is long or complex, or which for some other reason we do not want to repeat, so the broda-series of pro-bridi allows a substitute for a selbri or even a whole bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yXYT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yXYT}}
{{ind|example|thingy|example}}
{{judri|c7e5d5}}
:'''ti slasi je mlatu bo cidja lante gacri cei broda .i le crino broda cu barda .i le xunre broda cu cmalu'''
:''These are plastic cat-food can covers or thingies. The green thingy is large. The red thingy is small.''

{{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi|word-form rationale}}  {{ind|general-imported|cei|for broda-series pro-bridi assignment}}  {{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi|assigning with cei}}  {{ind|general-imported|goi for ko'a-series assignment|compared with cei for broda-series assignment}}  {{ind|general-imported|cei for broda-series assignment|compared with goi for ko'a-series assignment}}  {{ind|general-imported|antecedent|for pro-bridi}} The pro-bridi {{vla|broda}} has as its antecedent the selbri 
:{{jbo|slasi je mlatu bo cidja lante gacri}}. The cmavo {{vla|cei}} performs the role of 
{{vla|goi}} in assigning {{vla|broda}} to this long phrase, and {{vla|broda}} can then be used just like any other brivla. (In fact, {{vla|broda}} and its relatives actually 
<u>are</u> brivla: they are gismu in morphology, although they behave exactly like the members of selma'o GOhA. The reasons for using gismu rather than cmavo are buried in the Loglan Project's history.)

{{ind|general-imported|antecedent|for pro-bridi as full bridi}} Note that pro-bridi are so called because, even though they have the grammar of selbri, their antecedents are whole bridi. In the following rather contrived example, the antecedent of {{vla|brode}} is the whole bridi 
:{{jbo|mi klama le zarci}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-UFJf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UFJf}}
{{judri|c7e5d6}}
:'''mi klama cei brode le zarci .i do brode'''
:<code>I go-to (which-is claim-1) the store. You claim-1.</code>
:''I go to the store. You, too.''

{{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi|overriding sumti of antecedent bridi for}} In the second bridi, 
:{{jbo|do brode}} means 
:{{jbo|do klama le zarci}}, because {{vla|brode}} carries the x2 sumti of 
:{{jbo|mi klama le zarci}} along with it. It also potentially carries the x1 sumti as well, but the explicit x1 sumti {{vla|do}} overrides the {{vla|mi}} of the antecedent bridi. Similarly, any tense or negation that is present in the antecedent is also carried, and can be overridden by explicit tense or negation cmavo on the pro-bridi. These rules hold for all pro-bridi that have antecedents.

{{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi|with no assignment}}  {{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi|use as abstract pattern}}  {{ind|general-imported|broda-series pro-bridi|use as sample gismu}} Another use of {{vla|broda}} and its relatives, without assignment, is as “sample gismu”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AYYA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AYYA}}
{{judri|c7e5d7}}
:'''broda ke brode brodi'''
:<code>a thing-1 type of (thing-2 type-of thing-3)</code>

represents an abstract pattern, a certain kind of tanru. (Historically, this use was the original one.)

{{ind|general-imported|lerfu as pro-sumti|implicit assignment of antecedent}}  {{ind|general-imported|ko'a-series pro-sumti|contrasted with lerfu as pro-sumti in explicit assignment of}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu as pro-sumti|contrasted with ko'a-series in explicit assignment of}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|lerfu as}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu|as assignable pro-sumti}} As is explained in {{ls|section-lerfu-pro-sumti}}, the words for Lojban letters, belonging to selma'o BY and certain related selma'o, are also usable as assignable pro-sumti. The main difference between letter pro-sumti and ko'a-series pro-sumti is that, in the absence of an explicit assignment, letters are taken to refer to the most recent name or description sumti beginning with the same letter:

{{dsp|example-random-id-x1gh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-x1gh}}
{{judri|c7e5d8}}
:'''mi viska le gerku .i gy. cusku zo arf.'''
<code>I see the dog. D expresses the-word “Arf!”.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|goi|use in assigning lerfu as pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu as pro-sumti|explicit assignment of antecedent}} The Lojban word {{vla|gerku}} begins with {{lerfu|g}}, so the antecedent of {{vla|gy.}}, the cmavo for the letter {{lerfu|g}}, must be 
:{{jbo|le gerku}}. In the English translation, we use the same principle to refer to the dog as “D”. Of course, in case of ambiguity, {{vla|goi}} can be used to make an explicit assignment.

{{ind|general-imported|names|assigning with goi}}  {{ind|general-imported|goi|use in assigning name}} Furthermore, {{vla|goi}} can even be used to assign a name:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rbPr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rbPr}}
{{judri|c7e5d9}}
:'''le ninmu goi la sam. cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>The woman also-known-as Sam goes to-the store.</code>
:''The woman, whom I'll call Sam, goes to the store.''

This usage does not imply that the woman's name is Sam, or even that the speaker usually calls the woman “Sam”. “Sam” is simply a name chosen, as if at random, for use in the current context only.

{{ssp|section-ri-gohi-series}}
==Anaphoric pro-sumti and pro-bridi: the ri-series and the go'i-series==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ri'''	KOhA	ri-series	''(repeats last sumti)''
'''ra'''	KOhA	ri-series	''(repeats previous sumti)''
'''ru'''	KOhA	ri-series	''(repeats long-ago sumti)''

'''go'i'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats last bridi)''
'''go'a'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats previous bridi)''
'''go'u'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats long-ago bridi)''
'''go'e'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats last-but-one bridi)''
'''go'o'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats future bridi)''
'''nei'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats current bridi)''
'''no'a'''	GOhA'''	GO'i-series	''(repeats outer bridi)''

'''ra'o	'''RAhO'''	''pro-cmavo update''
</tab>

The term “anaphora” literally means “repetition”, but is used in linguistics to refer to pronouns whose significance is the repetition of earlier words, namely their antecedents. Lojban provides three pro-sumti anaphora, 
{{vla|ri}}, {{vla|ra}}, and {{vla|ru}}; and three corresponding pro-bridi anaphora, 
{{vla|go'i}}, {{vla|go'a}}, and 
{{vla|go'u}}. These cmavo reveal the same vowel pattern as the ti-series, but the “distances” referred to are not physical distances, but distances from the anaphoric cmavo to its antecedent.

The cmavo {{vla|ri}} is the simplest of these; it has the same referent as the last complete sumti appearing before the {{vla|ri}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3som}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3som}}
{{judri|c7e6d1}}
:'''la .alis. sipna le ri kumfa'''
:<code>Alice sleeps-in the of-[repeat last sumti] room.</code>
:''Alice sleeps in her room.''

The {{vla|ri}} in {{lex|example-random-id-3som}} is equivalent to repeating the last sumti, which is 
:{{jbo|la .alis.}}, so {{lex|example-random-id-3som}} is equivalent to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bs5R}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bs5R}}
{{judri|c7e6d2}}
:'''la .alis. sipna le la .alis. kumfa'''
:<code>Alice sleeps-in the of-Alice room.</code>
:''Alice sleeps in Alice's room.''

Note that {{vla|ri}} does not repeat 
:{{jbo|le ri kumfa}}, because that sumti is not yet complete when {{vla|ri}} appears. This prevents {{vla|ri}} from getting entangled in paradoxes of self-reference. (There are plenty of other ways to do that!) Note also that sumti within other sumti, as in quotations, abstractions, and the like, are counted in the order of their beginnings; thus a lower level sumti like 
:{{jbo|la alis.}} in {{lex|example-random-id-bs5R}} is considered to be more recent than a higher level sumti that contains it.

Certain sumti are ignored by {{vla|ri}}; specifically, most of the other cmavo of KOhA, and the almost-grammatically-equivalent lerfu words of selma'o BY. It is simpler just to repeat these directly:

{{dsp|example-random-id-CVmN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-CVmN}}
{{judri|c7e6d3}}
:'''mi prami mi'''
:<code>I love me.</code>
:''I love myself.''

However, the cmavo of the ti-series can be picked up by {{vla|ri}}, because you might have changed what you are pointing at, so repeating {{vla|ti}} may not be effective. Likewise, {{vla|ri}} itself (or rather its antecedent) can be repeated by a later {{vla|ri}}; in fact, a string of {{vla|ri}} cmavo with no other intervening sumti always all repeat the same sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eXsN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eXsN}}
{{judri|c7e6d4}}
:'''la djan. viska le tricu .i ri se jadni le ri jimca'''
:<code>John sees the tree. [repeat last] is-adorned-by the of-[repeat last] branch.</code>
:''John sees the tree. It is adorned by its branches.''

Here the second {{vla|ri}} has as antecedent the first {{vla|ri}}, which has as antecedent 
:{{jbo|le tricu}}. All three refer to the same thing: a tree.

To refer to the next-to-last sumti, the third-from-last sumti, and so on, {{vla|ri}} may be subscripted (subscripts are explained in {{ls|section-subscripts-general}}):

{{dsp|example-random-id-Lc2y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Lc2y}}
{{judri|c7e6d5}}
:'''lo smuci .i lo forca .i la rik. pilno rixire .i la .alis. pilno riximu'''
:<code>A spoon. A fork. Rick uses [repeat next-to-last]. Alice uses [repeat fifth-from-last].</code>

Here 
:{{jbo|rixire}}, or “ri-sub-2”, skips 
:{{jbo|la rik.}} to reach 
:{{jbo|lo forca}}. In the same way, 
:{{jbo|riximu}}, or “ri-sub-5”, skips 
:{{jbo|la .alis.}}, 
:{{jbo|rixire}}, 
:{{jbo|la rik.}}, and 
:{{jbo|lo forca}} to reach 
:{{jbo|lo smuci}}. As can clearly be seen, this procedure is barely practicable in writing, and would break down totally in speech.

Therefore, the vaguer {{vla|ra}} and {{vla|ru}} are also provided. The cmavo {{vla|ra}} repeats a recently used sumti, and {{vla|ru}} one that was further back in the speech or text. The use of {{vla|ra}} and {{vla|ru}} forces the listener to guess at the referent, but makes life easier for the speaker. Can {{vla|ra}} refer to the last sumti, like {{vla|ri}}? The answer is no if {{vla|ri}} has also been used. If {{vla|ri}} has not been used, then {{vla|ra}} might be the last sumti. Likewise, if {{vla|ra}} has been used, then any use of {{vla|ru}} would repeat a sumti earlier than the one {{vla|ra}} is repeating. A more reasonable version of Example {{lex|example-random-id-Lc2y}}, but one that depends more on context, is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-N89g}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-N89g}}
{{judri|c7e6d6}}
:'''lo smuci .i lo forca .i la rik. pilno ra .i la .alis. pilno ru'''
:<code>A spoon. A fork. Rick uses [some previous thing]. Alice uses [some more remote thing].</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-N89g}}, the use of {{vla|ra}} tells us that something other than 
:{{jbo|la rik.}} is the antecedent; 
:{{jbo|lo forca}} is the nearest sumti, so it is probably the antecedent. Similarly, the antecedent of {{vla|ru}} must be something even further back in the utterance than 
:{{jbo|lo forca}}, and 
:{{jbo|lo smuci}} is the obvious candidate.

The meaning of {{vla|ri}} must be determined every time it is used. Since {{vla|ra}} and {{vla|ru}} are more vaguely defined, they may well retain the same meaning for a while, but the listener cannot count on this behavior. To make a permanent reference to something repeated by {{vla|ri}}, {{vla|ra}}, or {{vla|ru}}, use {{vla|goi}} and a ko'a-series cmavo:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xIRG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xIRG}}
{{judri|c7e6d7}}
:'''la .alis. klama le zarci .i ri goi ko'a blanu'''
:<code>Alice goes-to the store. It-last-mentioned also-known-as it-1 is-blue.</code>

allows the store to be referred to henceforth as {{vla|ko'a}} without ambiguity. {{lex|example-random-id-xIRG}} is equivalent to {{lex|example-random-id-qdCR}} and eliminates any possibility of {{vla|ko'a}} being interpreted by the listener as referring to Alice.

{{ind|general-imported|answers|go'i for yes/no questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|questions|answering with go'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i|as affirmative answer to yes/no question}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|effect of sumti of referent bridi on}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|as main-bridi anaphora only}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|effect of sub-clauses on}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|referent of}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|compared with ri-series pro-sumti in rules of reference}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|ri-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|anaphora|pro-bridi go'i-series as}}  {{ind|general-imported|anaphora|pro-sumti ri-series as}}  {{ind|general-imported|pronouns|as anaphora}}  {{ind|general-imported|anaphora|definition}} The cmavo {{vla|go'i}}, {{vla|go'a}}, and 
{{vla|go'u}} follow exactly the same rules as 
{{vla|ri}}, {{vla|ra}}, and {{vla|ru}}, except that they are pro-bridi, and therefore repeat bridi, not sumti &ndash; specifically, main sentence bridi. Any bridi that are embedded within other bridi, such as relative clauses or abstractions, are not counted. Like the cmavo of the broda-series, the cmavo of the go'i-series copy all sumti with them. This makes {{vla|go'i}} by itself convenient for answering a question affirmatively, or for repeating the last bridi, possibly with new sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLN4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLN4}}
{{judri|c7e6d8}}
:'''xu zo djan. cmene do .i go'i'''
<code>[True-false?] The-word “John” is-the-name of you? [repeat last bridi].</code>
:''Is John your name? Yes.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLn5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLn5}}
{{judri|c7e6d9}}
:'''mi klama le zarci .i do go'i'''
:<code>I go-to the store. You [repeat last bridi].</code>
:''I go to the store. You, too.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|cei}}  {{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|assigning for permanent reference}} Note that {{lex|example-random-id-qLn5}} means the same as {{lex|example-random-id-UFJf}}, but without the bother of assigning an actual broda-series word to the first bridi. For long-term reference, use 
:{{jbo|go'i cei broda}} or the like, analogously to 

:{{jbo|ri goi ko'a}} in {{lex|example-random-id-xIRG}}.

The remaining four cmavo of the go'i-series are provided for convenience or for achieving special effects. The cmavo {{vla|go'e}} means the same as 

:{{jbo|go'ixire}}: it repeats the last bridi but one. This is useful in conversation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9hf5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9hf5}}
{{judri|c7e6d10}}
:'''A: mi ba klama le zarci B: mi nelci le si'o mi go'i A: do go'e'''
:<code>A: I [future] go-to the store. B: I like the concept-of I [repeat last bridi]. A: You [repeat last bridi but one].</code>
:''A: I am going to the store. B: I like the idea of my going. A: You'll go, too.''

Here B's sentence repeats A's within an abstraction (explained in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}): 
:{{jbo|le si'o mi go'i}} means 
:{{jbo|le si'o mi klama le zarci}}. Why must B use the word {{vla|mi}} explicitly to replace the x1 of 
:{{jbo|mi klama le zarci}}, even though it looks like {{vla|mi}} is replacing {{vla|mi}}? Because B's {{vla|mi}} refers to B, whereas A's {{vla|mi}} refers to A. If B said:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2uS7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2uS7}}
{{judri|c7e6d11}}
:'''mi nelci le si'o go'i'''
that would mean:
:''I like the idea of your going to the store.''

The repetition signalled by {{vla|go'i}} is not literally of words, but of concepts. Finally, A repeats her own sentence, but with the x1 changed to {{vla|do}}, meaning B. Note that in {{lex|example-random-id-9hf5}}, the tense {{vla|ba}} (future time) is carried along by both {{vla|go'i}} and {{vla|go'e}}.

Descriptions based on go'i-series cmavo can be very useful for repeating specific sumti of previous bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hwau}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hwau}}
{{judri|c7e6d12}}
:'''le xekri mlatu cu klama le zarci .i le go'i cu cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The black cat goes-to the store. That-described-as-the-x1-place-of [repeat last bridi] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The black cat goes to the store. It walks on the ice.''

Here the {{vla|go'i}} repeats 
:{{jbo|le xekri mlatu cu klama le zarci}}, and since {{vla|le}} makes the x1 place into a description, and the x1 place of this bridi is 
:{{jbo|le xekri mlatu}}, 
:{{jbo|le go'i}} means 
:{{jbo|le xekri mlatu}}.

The cmavo {{vla|go'o}}, 
{{vla|nei}}, and 
{{vla|no'a}} have been little used so far. They repeat respectively some future bridi, the current bridi, and the bridi that encloses the current bridi ( 
{{vla|no'a}}, unlike the other members of the go'i- series, can repeat non-sentence bridi). Here are a few examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-EUmV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-EUmV}}
{{judri|c7e6d13}}
:'''mi nupre le nu mi go'o .i ba dunda le djini le bersa .i ba dunda le zdani le tixnu'''
:<code>I promise the event-of I [repeat future bridi] [Future] give the money to-the son [Future] give the house to-the daughter</code>
:''I promise to do the following: Give the money to my son. Give the house to my daughter.''

(Note: The Lojban does not contain an equivalent of the {{vla|my}} in the colloquial English; it leaves the fact that it is the speaker's son and daughter that are referred to implicit. To make the fact explicit, use 
:{{jbo|le bersa}}/{{jbo|tixnu be mi}}.)

For good examples of {{vla|nei}} and 
{{vla|no'a}}, we need nested bridi contexts:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLo1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLo1}}
{{judri|c7e6d14}}
:'''mi se pluka le nu do pensi le nu nei kei pu le nu do zukte'''
:<code>I am-pleased-by the event-of (you think-about (the event-of [main bridi]) before the-event of (your acting).</code>
:''I am pleased that you thought about whether I would be pleased (about ...) before you acted.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLop}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLop}}
{{judri|c7e6d15}}
:'''mi ba klama ca le nu do no'a'''
:<code>I [future] go [present] the event-of you [repeats outer bridi]</code>
:''I will go when you do.''

{{ind|general-imported|go'i ra'o|contrasted with go'i}} Finally, {{vla|ra'o}} is a cmavo that can be appended to any go'i-series cmavo, or indeed any cmavo of selma'o GOhA, to signal that pro-sumti or pro-bridi cmavo in the antecedent are to be repeated literally and reinterpreted in their new context. Normally, any pro-sumti used within the antecedent of the pro-bridi keep their meanings intact. In the presence of {{vla|ra'o}}, however, their meanings must be reinterpreted with reference to the new environment. If someone says to you:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9Uq6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9Uq6}}
{{judri|c7e6d16}}
:'''mi ba lumci lemi karce'''
:''I will wash my car.''

you might reply either:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1fK3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1fK3}}
{{judri|c7e6d17}}
:'''mi go'i'''
:''I will wash your car.''

or:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qW1B}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qW1B}}
{{judri|c7e6d18}}
:'''mi go'i ra'o'''
:''I will wash my car.''

The {{vla|ra'o}} forces the second {{vla|mi}} from the original bridi to mean the new speaker rather than the former speaker. This means that 
:{{jbo|go'e ra'o}} would be an acceptable alternative to 

:{{jbo|do go'e}} in B's statement in {{lex|example-random-id-9hf5}}.

{{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|in quotations}}  {{ind|general-imported|ri-series pro-sumti|in quotations}} The anaphoric pro-sumti of this section can be used in quotations, but never refer to any of the supporting text outside the quotation, since speakers presumably do not know that they may be quoted by someone else.

{{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|in quotation series}}  {{ind|general-imported|ri-series pro-sumti|in quotation series}} However, a 
:{{jbo|ri-}} series or 
:{{jbo|go'a-}} series reference within a quotation can refer to something mentioned in an earlier quotation if the two quotations are closely related in time and context. This allows a quotation to be broken up by narrative material without interfering with the pro-sumti within it. Here's an example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LWyE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LWyE}}
{{judri|c7e6d19}}
:'''la djan. cusku lu mi klama le zarci li'u .i la .alis. cusku lu mi go'i li'u'''
:<code>John says [quote] I go-to the store [unquote]. Alice says [quote] I [repeat] [unquote].</code>
:''John says, “I am going to the store.” Alice says, “Me too.”''

{{ind|general-imported|go'i-series pro-bridi|in narrative about quotation}}  {{ind|general-imported|ri-series pro-sumti|in narrative about quotation}} Of course, there is no problem with narrative material referring to something within a quotation: people who quote, unlike people who are quoted, are aware of what they are doing.

{{ssp|section-zohe-cohe-series}}
==Indefinite pro-sumti and pro-bridi: the zo'e-series and the co'e-series==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''zo'e'''	KOhA	zo'e-series	''the obvious value''
'''zu'i'''	KOhA	zo'e-series	''the typical value''
'''zi'o'''	KOhA	zo'e-series	''the nonexistent value''

'''co'e'''	GOhA	co'e-series	''has the obvious relationship''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|typical value|contrasted with elliptical value for sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|elliptical value|contrasted with typical value for sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|elliptical sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|zo'e|as place-holder for sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|elliptical pro-bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|unspecified}}  {{ind|general-imported|elliptical pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|co'e-series pro-bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|zo'e-series pro-sumti}} The cmavo of the zo'e-series represent indefinite, unspecified sumti. The cmavo 
{{vla|zo'e}} represents an elliptical value for this sumti place; it is the optional spoken place holder when a sumti is skipped without being specified. Note that the elliptical value is not always the typical value. The properties of ellipsis lead to an elliptical sumti being defined as “whatever I want it to mean but haven't bothered to figure out, or figure out how to express”.

{{ind|general-imported|typical sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|typical}} The cmavo {{vla|zu'i}}, on the other hand, represents the typical value for this place of this bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VScg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VScg}}
{{judri|c7e7d1}}
:'''mi klama le bartu be le zdani le nenri be le zdani zu'i zu'i'''
:<code>I go to-the outside of the house from-the inside of the house [by-typical-route] [by-typical-means]</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-VScg}}, the first {{vla|zu'i}} probably means something like “by the door”, and the second {{vla|zu'i}} probably means something like “on foot”, those being the typical route and means for leaving a house. On the other hand, if you are at the top of a high rise during a fire, neither {{vla|zu'i}} is appropriate. It's also common to use 
{{vla|zu'i}} in “by standard” places.

{{ind|general-imported|irrelevant|specifying of sumti place}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|irrelevant to relationship}}  {{ind|general-imported|zi'o}} Finally, the cmavo {{vla|zi'o}} represents a value which does not even exist. When a bridi fills one of its places with {{vla|zi'o}}, what is really meant is that the selbri has a place which is irrelevant to the true relationship the speaker wishes to express. For example, the place structure of 
{{vla|zbasu}} is:

:''actor x1 makes x2 from materials x3''

{{ind|example|living things|example}}
Consider the sentence

:''Living things are made from cells.''
This cannot be correctly expressed as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ipCV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ipCV}}
{{judri|c7e7d2}}
:'''loi jmive cu se zbasu [zo'e] fi loi selci'''
:<code>The-mass-of living-things is-made [by-something] from the-mass-of cells</code>

because the {{vla|zo'e}}, expressed or understood, in {{lex|example-random-id-ipCV}} indicates that there is still a “maker” in this relationship. We do not generally suppose, however, that someone “makes” living things from cells. The best answer is probably to find a different selbri, one which does not imply a “maker”: however, an alternative strategy is to use {{vla|zi'o}} to eliminate the maker place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xxm1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xxm1}}
{{judri|c7e7d3}}
:'''loi jmive cu se zbasu zi'o loi selci'''
:<code>The-mass-of living-things is-made [without-maker] from the-mass-of cells.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|zi'o|as creating new selbri}} Note: The use of {{vla|zi'o}} to block up, as it were, one place of a selbri actually creates a new selbri with a different place structure. Consider the following examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLoY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLoY}}
{{judri|c7e7d4}}
:'''mi zbasu le dinju loi mudri'''
:<code>I make the building from-some-of-the-mass-of wood.</code>
:''I make the building out of wood.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLPI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLPI}}
{{judri|c7e7d5}}
:'''zi'o zbasu le dinju loi mudri'''
:<code>[without-maker] makes the building from-some-of-the-mass-of wood.</code>
:''The building is made out of wood.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLpy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLpy}}
{{judri|c7e7d6}}
:'''mi zbasu zi'o loi mudri'''
:<code>I make [without-thing-made] from-some-of-the-mass-of wood.</code>
:''I build using wood.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLqE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLqE}}
{{judri|c7e7d7}}
:'''mi zbasu le dinju zi'o'''
:<code>I make the building [without-material].</code>
:''I make the building.''

If {{lex|example-random-id-qLoY}} is true, then {{lex|example-random-id-qLPI}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qLqE}} must be true also. However, {{lex|example-random-id-xxm1}} does not correspond to any sentence with three regular (non-{{vla|zi'o}}) sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|co'e|as selbri place-holder}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|omitting with co'e}} The pro-bridi {{vla|co'e}} (which by itself constitutes the co'e-series of selma'o GOhA) represents the elliptical selbri. Lojban grammar does not allow the speaker to merely omit a selbri from a bridi, although any or all sumti may be freely omitted. Being vague about a relationship requires the use of 
{{vla|co'e}} as a selbri place-holder:

{{dsp|example-random-id-uy9R}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uy9R}}
{{judri|c7e7d8}}
:'''mi troci le nu mi co'e le vorme'''
:<code>I try the event-of my [doing-the-obvious-action] to-the door.</code>
:''I try the door.''

The English version means, and the Lojban version probably means, that I try to open the door, but the relationship of opening is not actually specified; the Lojbanic listener must guess it from context. Lojban, unlike English, makes it clear that there is an implicit action that is not being expressed.

{{ind|general-imported|co'e|rationale for word form}} The form of {{vla|co'e}} was chosen to resemble 
{{vla|zo'e}}; the cmavo {{vla|do'e}} of selma'o BAI (see 
{{ls|section-BAI}}) also belongs to the same group of cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|zo'e-series|compared with do'i as indefinite pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|do'i|compared with zo'e-series as indefinite pro-sumti}} Note that {{vla|do'i}}, of the di'u-series, is also a kind of indefinite pro-sumti: it is indefinite in referent, but is restricted to referring only to an utterance.

{{ssp|section-voha-series}}
==Reflexive and reciprocal pro-sumti: the vo'a-series==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''vo'a'''	KOhA	vo'a-series	''x1 of this bridi''
'''vo'e'''	KOhA	vo'a-series	''x2 of this bridi''
'''vo'i'''	KOhA	vo'a-series	''x3 of this bridi''
'''vo'o'''	KOhA	vo'a-series	''x4 of this bridi''
'''vo'u'''	KOhA	vo'a-series	''x5 of this bridi''

'''soi'''	SOI		''reciprocity''

'''se'u'''	SEhU		''soi terminator''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|reciprocal pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|reflexive pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|referring to place of same bridi with vo'a-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|vo'a-series}}  {{ind|general-imported|anaphora|pro-sumti vo'a-series as}} The cmavo of the vo'a-series are pro-sumti anaphora, like those of the ri-series, but have a specific function. These cmavo refer to the other places of the same bridi; the five of them represent up to five places. The same vo'a-series cmavo mean different things in different bridi. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLqT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLqT}}

{{ind|example|wash self|example}}
{{judri|c7e8d1}}
:'''mi lumci vo'a'''
:''I wash myself''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLqV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLqV}}
{{judri|c7e8d2}}
:'''mi klama le zarci vo'e'''
:''I go to the store from itself [by some route unspecified].''

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|referring to place of different bridi with go'i-series}} To refer to places of neighboring bridi, constructions like 
:{{jbo|le se go'i ku}} do the job: this refers to the 2nd place of the previous main bridi, as explained in {{ls|section-ri-gohi-series}}.

{{ind|general-imported|vice versa|English|expressing with vo'a-series pro-sumti and soi}}  {{ind|general-imported|vo'a-series pro-sumti|use in expressing reciprocity with soi}}  {{ind|general-imported|soi|use in expressing reciprocity with vo'a-series pro-sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|reciprocity|expressing with vo'a-series pro-sumti and soi}} The cmavo of the vo'a-series are also used with {{vla|soi}} (of selma'o SOI) to precisely express reciprocity, which in English is imprecisely expressed with a discursive phrase like “vice versa”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-vpb3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-vpb3}}
{{ind|example|vice versa|example}}
{{judri|c7e8d3}}
:'''mi prami do soi vo'a vo'e'''
:<code>I love you [reciprocity] [x1 of this bridi] [x2 of this bridi].</code>
:''I love you and vice versa (swapping “I” and “you”).''

{{ind|general-imported|soi with one following sumti|convention}} The significance of 
:{{jbo|soi vo'a vo'e}} is that the bridi is still true even if the x1 (specified by {{vla|vo'a}}) and the x2 (specified by {{vla|vo'e}}) places are interchanged. If only a single sumti follows {{vla|soi}}, then the sumti immediately preceding {{vla|soi}} is understood to be one of those involved:

{{dsp|example-random-id-CMQ1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-CMQ1}}
{{judri|c7e8d4}}
{{ind|example|vice versa|example}}
:'''mi prami do soi vo'a'''
:<code>I love you [reciprocity] [x1 of this bridi].</code>

again involves the x1 and x2 places.

{{ind|general-imported|soi|use in expressing reciprocity}}  {{ind|general-imported|reciprocity|expressing with soi}} Of course, other places can be involved, and other sumti may be used in place of vo'a-series cmavo, provided those other sumti can be reasonably understood as referring to the same things mentioned in the bridi proper. Here are several examples that mean the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rqNJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rqNJ}}
{{judri|c7e8d5}}
{{ind|example|vice versa|example}}
<!-- FIXME: I bet this looks bad; this isn't quite an
interlinear gloss situation -->
:'''mi bajykla ti ta soi vo'e'''
:'''mi bajykla ti ta soi vo'e vo'i'''
:'''soi vo'e vo'i mi bajykla ti ta'''
:<code>I runningly-go to this from that and vice versa (to that from this).</code>

{{ind|general-imported|se'u|elidability considerations}}  {{ind|general-imported|se'u|as elidable terminator for soi}} The elidable terminator for {{vla|soi}} is {{vla|se'u}} (selma'o SEhU), which is normally needed only if there is just one sumti after the {{vla|soi}}, and the {{vla|soi}} construction is not at the end of the bridi. Constructions using {{vla|soi}} are free modifiers, and as such can go almost anywhere. Here is an example where 
{{vla|se'u}} is required:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RFBV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RFBV}}
{{judri|c7e8d6}}
{{ind|example|vice versa|example}}
:'''mi bajykla ti soi vo'i se'u ta'''
:<code>I runningly-go to-this [reciprocity] [x3 of this bridi] from-that</code>
:''I run to this from that and vice versa.''

{{ssp|section-sumti-and-bridi-questions}}
==sumti and bridi questions: {{vla|ma}} and {{vla|mo}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ma}}
:{{s|KOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|mo}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|questions|sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|ma|as sumti question}} Lojban questions are more fully explained in {{ls|section-questions-and-answers}}, but {{vla|ma}} and {{vla|mo}} are listed in this chapter for completeness. The cmavo {{vla|ma}} asks for a sumti to make the bridi true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Csod}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Csod}}
{{judri|c7e9d1}}
:'''do klama ma'''
:<code>You go to-what-destination?</code>
:''Where are you going?''

{{ind|general-imported|go'i|compared with mo in overriding of arguments}}  {{ind|general-imported|mo|compared with go'i in overriding of arguments}}  {{ind|general-imported|questions|selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|mo|as selbri question}} The cmavo {{vla|mo}}, on the other hand, asks for a selbri which makes the question bridi true. If the answer is a full bridi, then the arguments of the answer override the arguments in the question, in the same manner as the go'i-series cmavo. A simple example is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ih10}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ih10}}
{{judri|c7e9d2}}
:'''do mo'''
:<code>What predicate is true as applied to you?</code>
:''How are you?''
:''What are you doing?''
:''What are you?''
{{lex|example-random-id-8HKo}} is a truly pregnant question that will have several meanings depending on context.

(One thing it probably does not mean is “Who are you?” in the sense “What is your name/identity?”, which is better expressed by:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8HKo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8HKo}}
{{ind|example|what is your name|example}}
{{judri|c7e9d3}}
:'''ma cmene do'''
:<code>What sumti is-the-name-of you?</code>
:''What is your name?''

or even

{{dsp|example-random-id-y4Yi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-y4Yi}}
{{judri|c7e9d4}}
:'''doi ma'''
:<code>O [what sumti?]</code>

which uses the vocative {{vla|doi}} to address someone, and simultaneously asks who the someone is.)

A further example of {{vla|mo}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PP7r}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PP7r}}
{{judri|c7e9d5}}
:'''lo mo prenu cu darxi do .i barda'''
:<code>A [what selbri?] type-of person hit you? (Observative:) A big thing.</code>
:''Which person hit you? The big one.''

{{ind|general-imported|multiple mo|as multiple questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple ma|as multiple questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple questions in one bridi|expressing}} When {{vla|ma}} or {{vla|mo}} is repeated, multiple questions are being asked simultaneously:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2KPQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2KPQ}}
{{judri|c7e9d6}}
:'''ma djuno ma'''
:<code>[What sumti] knows [what sumti]?</code>
:''Who knows what?''

{{ssp|section-keha}}
==Relativized pro-sumti: {{vla|ke'a}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ke'a}}
:{{s|KOhA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|use of ke'a for referral to relativized sumti in}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|for relativized sumti in relative clauses}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|for relativized sumti in relative clauses}} This pro-sumti is used in relative clauses (explained in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}) to indicate how the sumti being relativized fits within the clause. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-UNBb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-UNBb}}
{{ind|example|cat of plastic|example}}
{{judri|c7e10d1}}
:'''mi catlu lo mlatu poi [zo'e] zbasu ke'a lei slasi'''
:<code>I see a cat such-that something-unspecified makes the-thing-being-relativized [the cat] from-some-mass-of plastic.</code>
:''I see a cat made of plastic.''

{{ind|general-imported|ke'a|ambiguity when omitted}} If {{vla|ke'a}} were omitted from {{lex|example-random-id-UNBb}}, it might be confused with:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0EWp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0EWp}}
{{judri|c7e10d2}}
:'''mi catlu lo mlatu poi [ke'a] zbasu lei slasi'''
:<code>I see a cat such-that the-thing-being-relativized [the cat] makes a-mass-of plastic</code>
:''I see a cat that makes plastic.''

{{ind|general-imported|ri|contrasted with ke'a in relative clauses}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|contrasted with ri in relative clauses}} The anaphora cmavo 
{{vla|ri}} cannot be used in place of {{vla|ke'a}} in {{lex|example-random-id-UNBb}} and {{lex|example-random-id-0EWp}}, because the relativized sumti is not yet complete when the 
{{vla|ke'a}} appears.

{{ind|general-imported|subscripts|on ke'a for nested relative clauses}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|subscripting for nested relative clauses}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|and abstract descriptions}} Note that {{vla|ke'a}} is used only with relative clauses, and not with other embedded bridi such as abstract descriptions. In the case of relative clauses within relative clauses, {{vla|ke'a}} may be subscripted to make the difference clear (See {{ls|section-nesting}}).

{{ssp|section-cehu}}
==Abstraction focus pro-sumti: {{vla|ce'u}}==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ce'u}}
:{{s|KOhA}}
:''description''

The cmavo {{vla|ce'u}} is used within abstraction bridi, particularly property abstractions introduced by the cmavo 
{{vla|ka}}. Abstractions, including the uses of {{vla|ce'u}}, are discussed in full in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}.

{{ind|general-imported|ce'u|use in specifying sumti place of property in abstraction}}  {{ind|general-imported|property abstraction|specifying sumti place of property with ce'u}} In brief: Every property abstraction specifies a property of one of the sumti in it; that sumti place is filled by using 
{{vla|ce'u}}. This convention enables us to distinguish clearly between:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ELxF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ELxF}}
{{ind|example|happiness|example}}
{{judri|c7e11d1}}
:'''le ka ce'u gleki'''
:<code>the property-of (X being-happy)</code>
:<code>the property of being happy</code>
:''happiness''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-VSw3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VSw3}}
{{judri|c7e11d2}}
:'''le ka gleki ce'u'''
:<code>the property-of (being-happy about-X)</code>
:''the property of being that which someone is happy about''

{{ssp|section-da-buha-series}}
==Bound variable pro-sumti and pro-bridi: the da-series and the bu'a-series==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''da'''	KOhA	da-series	''something-1''
'''de'''	KOhA	da-series	''something-2''
'''di'''	KOhA	da-series	''something-3''

'''bu'a'''	GOhA	bu'a-series	''some-predicate-1''
'''bu'e'''	GOhA	bu'a-series	''some-predicate-2''
'''bu'i'''	GOhA	bu'a-series	''some-predicate-3''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|bu'a-series pro-sumti|for bound variables}}  {{ind|general-imported|da-series pro-sumti|for bound variables}} Bound variables belong to the predicate-logic part of Lojban, and are listed here for completeness only. Their semantics is explained in {{lch|chapter-quantifiers}}. It is worth mentioning that the Lojban translation of {{lex|example-random-id-VISf}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-6vxz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6vxz}}
{{judri|c7e12d1}}
:'''la djan. cu lafti da poi grana ku'o gi'e desygau da'''
:<code>John raised something-1 which is-a-stick and shake-did something-1.</code>
:''John picked up a stick and shook it.''

{{ssp|section-daho}}
==Pro-sumti and pro-bridi cancelling==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''da'o'''	DAhO		''cancel all pro-sumti/pro-bridi''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi assignment|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti assignment|stability of}} How long does a pro-sumti or pro-bridi remain stable? In other words, once we know the referent of a pro-sumti or pro-bridi, how long can we be sure that future uses of the same cmavo have the same referent? The answer to this question depends on which series the cmavo belongs to.

{{ind|general-imported|bound variable pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|assignable pro-sumti|explicit cancellation of by rebinding}}  {{ind|general-imported|assignable pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|personal pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|personal pro-sumti|implicit cancellation of by change of speaker/listener}} Personal pro-sumti are stable until there is a change of speaker or listener, possibly signaled by a vocative. Assignable pro-sumti and pro-bridi last indefinitely or until rebound with {{vla|goi}} or {{vla|cei}}. Bound variable pro-sumti and pro-bridi also generally last until re-bound; details are available in 
{{ls|section-notes-on-variables}}.

{{ind|general-imported|anaphoric pro-bridi|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|anaphoric pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|reflexive pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|utterance pro-sumti|stability of}} Utterance pro-sumti are stable only within the utterance in which they appear; similarly, reflexive pro-sumti are stable only within the bridi in which they appear; and 
{{vla|ke'a}} is stable only within its relative clause. Anaphoric pro-sumti and pro-bridi are stable only within narrow limits depending on the rules for the particular cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-bridi|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite pro-sumti|stability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|demonstrative pro-sumti|stability of}} Demonstrative pro-sumti, indefinite pro-sumti and pro-bridi, and sumti and bridi questions potentially change referents every time they are used.

{{ind|general-imported|da'o|syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|da'o|for cancellation of pro-sumti/pro-bridi assignment}}  {{ind|general-imported|cancellation of pro-sumti/pro-bridi assignment|with da'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi assignment|explicit cancellation of with da'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti assignment|explicit cancellation of with da'o}} However, there are ways to cancel all pro-sumti and pro-bridi, so that none of them have known referents. (Some, such as {{vla|mi}}, will acquire the same referent as soon as they are used again after the cancellation.) The simplest way to cancel everything is with the cmavo {{vla|da'o}} of selma'o DAhO, which is used solely for this purpose; it may appear anywhere, and has no effect on the grammar of texts containing it. One use of 
{{vla|da'o}} is when entering a conversation, to indicate that one's pro-sumti assignments have nothing to do with any assignments already made by other participants in the conversation.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi assignment|no'i effect on}}  {{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti assignment|no'i effect on}}  {{ind|general-imported|no'i|effect on pro-sumti/pro-bridi assignments}}  {{ind|general-imported|ni'o|effect on pro-sumti/pro-bridi assignments}} In addition, the cmavo {{vla|ni'o}} and {{vla|no'i}} of selma'o NIhO, which are used primarily to indicate shifts in topic, may also have the effect of canceling pro-sumti and pro-bridi assignments, or of reinstating ones formerly in effect. More explanations of NIhO can be found in {{ls|section-niho}}.

{{ssp|section-du}}
==The identity predicate: du==

The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''du'''	GOhA		''identity''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|identity predicate}} The cmavo {{vla|du}} has the place structure:

:''x1 is identical with x2, x3, ...''
{{ind|general-imported|du|rationale for selection of selma'o for}} and appears in selma'o GOhA for reasons of convenience: it is not a pro-bridi. {{vla|du}} serves as mathematical “=”, and outside mathematical contexts is used for defining or identifying. Mathematical examples may be found in {{lch|chapter-mekso}}.

{{ind|general-imported|mintu|contrasted with du}}  {{ind|general-imported|du|contrasted with mintu}} The main difference between

{{dsp|example-random-id-GGoH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GGoH}}
{{judri|c7e14d1}}
:'''ko'a du le nanmu'''
:<code>It-1 is-identical-to the man</code>

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-prfu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-prfu}}
{{judri|c7e14d2}}
:'''ko'a mintu le nanmu'''
:<code>It-1 is-the-same-as the man</code>

{{ind|general-imported|du|meaning of}} is this defining nature. {{lex|example-random-id-GGoH}} presumes that the speaker is responding to a request for information about what {{vla|ko'a}} refers to, or that the speaker in some way feels the need to define {{vla|ko'a}} for later reference. A bridi with {{vla|du}} is an identity sentence, somewhat metalinguistically saying that all attached sumti are representations for the same referent. There may be any number of sumti associated with {{vla|du}}, and all are said to be identical.{{lex|example-random-id-prfu}}, however, predicates; it is used to make a claim about the identity of {{vla|ko'a}}, which presumably has been defined previously.

{{ind|general-imported|dunli|contrasted with du}}  {{ind|general-imported|du|contrasted with dunli}}  {{ind|general-imported|du|derivation of}} Note: {{vla|du}} historically is derived from {{vla|dunli}}, but 
{{vla|dunli}} has a third place which 
{{vla|du}} lacks: the standard of equality.

{{ssp|section-anaphoric-rafsi}}
==lujvo based on pro-sumti==
{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti|rafsi for}}  {{ind|general-imported|rafsi|based on pro-sumti}} There exist rafsi allocated to a few cmavo of selma'o KOhA, but they are rarely used. (See {{ls|section-koha-summary}} for a complete list.) The obvious way to use them is as internal sumti, filling in an appropriate place of the gismu or lujvo to which they are attached; as such, they usually stand as the first rafsi in their lujvo.

{{ind|general|you-talk|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti rafsi|effect of on place structure of lujvo}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|pro-sumti rafsi effect on place structure of}} Thus {{vla|donta'a}}, meaning “you-talk”, would be interpreted as 
:{{jbo|tavla be do}}, and would have the place structure

{{dsp|example-random-id-unmV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-unmV}}
{{judri|c7e15d1}}
:''t1 talks to you about subject t3 in language t4''

since t2 (the addressee) is already known to be {{vla|do}}.

{{ind|general|you-cmavo|example}}
On the other hand, the lujvo {{vla|donma'o}}, literally “you-cmavo”, which means “a second person personal pronoun”, would be interpreted as 
:{{jbo|cmavo be zo do}}, and have the place structure:

{{dsp|example-random-id-H5NB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-H5NB}}
{{judri|c7e15d2}}
:''c1 is a second person pronoun in language c4''

since both the c2 place (the grammatical class) and the c3 place (the meaning) are obvious from the context {{vla|do}}.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-sumti rafsi|anticipated use of for abbreviating inconvenient forms}} An anticipated use of rafsi for cmavo in the 
{{vla|fo'a}} series is to express lujvo which can't be expressed in a convenient rafsi form, because they are too long to express, or are formally inconvenient (fu'ivla, cmene, and so forth.) An example would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-tH6w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tH6w}}
{{judri|c7e15d3}}
:'''fo'a goi le kulnrsu,omi .i lo fo'arselsanga'''
:<code>x6 stands for Finnish-culture. An x6-song.</code>

{{ind|general|beverage|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|zi'o rafsi|effect of on place structure of lujvo}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|zi'o rafsi effect on place structure of}} Finally, lujvo involving {{vla|zi'o}} are also possible, and are fully discussed in {{lch|chapter-lujvo}}. In brief, the convention is to use the rafsi for <!-- FIXME: chapter 12 does not talk about zi'o, it's probably supposed to -->{{vla|zi'o}} as a prefix immediately followed by the rafsi for the number of the place to be deleted. Thus, if we consider a beverage (something drunk without considering who, if anyone, drinks it) as a 

:{{jbo|se pinxe be zi'o}}, the lujvo corresponding to this is {{vla|zilrelselpinxe}} (deleting the second place of 
:{{jbo|se pinxe}}). Deleting the x1 place in this fashion would move all remaining places up by one. This would mean that {{vla|zilpavypinxe}} has the same place structure as {{vla|zilrelselpinxe}}, and 
:{{jbo|lo zilpavypinxe}}, like 
:{{jbo|lo zilrelselpinxe}}, refers to a beverage, and not to a non-existent drinker.

{{ind|general-imported|pro-bridi rafsi|as producing context-dependent meanings}} The pro-bridi {{vla|co'e}}, 
{{vla|du}}, and {{vla|bu'a}} also have rafsi, which can be used just as if they were gismu. The resulting lujvo have (except for 
:{{jbo|du-}} based lujvo) highly context-dependent meanings.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{csp|chapter-relative-clauses}}
=Relative Clauses, Which Make sumti Even More Complicated=
{{image|chapter-relative-clauses-picture|The picture for chapter 8|CLL-chapter-relative-clauses.gif}}
{{ssp|section-poi}}
==What are you pointing at?==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''poi'''	NOI	''restrictive relative clause introducer''
'''ke'a'''	GOhA	''relative pro-sumti''
'''ku'o'''	KUhO	''relative clause terminator''
</tab>

Let us think about the problem of communicating what it is that we are pointing at when we are pointing at something. In Lojban, we can refer to what we are pointing at by using the pro-sumti {{vla|ti}} if it is nearby, or {{vla|ta}} if it is somewhat further away, or {{vla|tu}} if it is distant. (Pro-sumti are explained in full in {{lch|chapter-anaphoric-cmavo}}.)

{{ind|general-imported|reference|ambiguity of ti/ta/tu}} However, even with the assistance of a pointing finger, or pointing lips, or whatever may be appropriate in the local culture, it is often hard for a listener to tell just what is being pointed at. Suppose one is pointing at a person (in particular, in the direction of his or her face), and says:

{{dsp|example-random-id-QzhK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QzhK}}
{{judri|c8e1d1}}
:'''ti cu barda'''
:<code>This-one is-big.</code>

What is the referent of {{vla|ti}}? Is it the person? Or perhaps it is the person's nose? Or even (for {{vla|ti}} can be plural as well as singular, and mean “these ones” as well as “this one”) the pores on the person's nose?

{{ind|general-imported|reference|use of relative clause for}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clause|use for reference}} To help solve this problem, Lojban uses a construction called a “relative clause”. Relative clauses are usually attached to the end of sumti, but there are other places where they can go as well, as explained later in this chapter. A relative clause begins with a word of selma'o NOI, and ends with the elidable terminator {{vla|ku'o}} (of selma'o KUhO). As you might suppose, {{vla|noi}} is a cmavo of selma'o NOI; however, first we will discuss the cmavo {{vla|poi}}, which also belongs to selma'o NOI.

{{ind|general-imported|ke'a|as referent for relativized sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|reference|to relativized sumti with ke'a}}  {{ind|general-imported|relativized sumti|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|poi|syntax of}} In between the {{vla|poi}} and the {{vla|ku'o}} appears a full bridi, with the same syntax as any other bridi. Anywhere within the bridi of a relative clause, the pro-sumti {{vla|ke'a}} (of selma'o KOhA) may be used, and it stands for the sumti to which the relative clause is attached (called the “relativized sumti”). Here are some examples before we go any further:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLt8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLt8}}
{{judri|c8e1d2}}
{{ind|example|big person|example}}  
:'''ti poi ke'a prenu ku'o cu barda'''
:<code>This-thing such-that-(IT is-a-person) is-large.</code>
:<code>This thing which is a person is big.</code>
:''This person is big.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLtX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLtX}}
<title>  
{{ind|example|big nose|example}}
{{judri|c8e1d3}}
:'''ti poi ke'a nazbi ku'o cu barda'''
:<code>This-thing such-that-(IT is-a-nose) is-large.</code>
:<code>This thing which is a nose is big.</code>
:''This nose is big.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLuj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLuj}}
{{ind|example|big nose-pores|example}}
{{judri|c8e1d4}}
:'''ti poi ke'a nazbi kapkevna ku'o cu barda'''
:<code>This-thing such-that-(IT is-a-nose-type-of skin-hole) is-big.</code>
:<code>These things which are nose-pores are big.</code>
:''These nose-pores are big.''

{{ind|general-imported|IT|as notation convention in relative clause chapter}} In the literal translations throughout this chapter, the word “IT”, capitalized, is used to represent the cmavo {{vla|ke'a}}. In each case, it serves to represent the sumti (in {{lex|example-random-id-qLt8}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qLuj}}, the cmavo {{vla|ti}}) to which the relative clause is attached.

{{ind|general-imported|ke'a|non-initial place use in relative clause}} Of course, there is no reason why {{vla|ke'a}} needs to appear in the x1 place of a relative clause bridi; it can appear in any place, or indeed even in a sub-bridi within the relative clause bridi. Here are two more examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLUV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLUV}}
{{judri|c8e1d5}}
:'''tu poi le mlatu pu lacpu ke'a ku'o cu ratcu'''
:<code>That-distant-thing such-that (the cat [past] drags IT) is-a-rat.</code>
:<code>That thing which the cat dragged is a rat.</code>
:''What the cat dragged is a rat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLxF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLxF}}
{{judri|c8e1d6}}
:'''ta poi mi djica le nu mi ponse ke'a [kei] ku'o cu bloti'''
:<code>That-thing such-that( I desire the event-of( I own IT ) ) is-a-boat.</code>
:''That thing that I want to own is a boat.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qLxF}}, {{vla|ke'a}} appears in an abstraction clause (abstractions are explained in {{lch|chapter-abstractions}}) within a relative clause.

{{ind|general-imported|relative clause|effect of omission of {{vla|ke'a}} on}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'a|effect of omission of}} Like any sumti, {{vla|ke'a}} can be omitted. The usual presumption in that case is that it then falls into the x1 place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sMHH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sMHH}}
{{judri|c8e1d7}}
:'''ti poi nazbi cu barda'''
:<code>This-thing which is-a-nose is-big.</code>

almost certainly means the same thing as {{lex|example-random-id-qLtX}}. However, {{vla|ke'a}} can be omitted if it is clear to the listener that it belongs in some place other than x1:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cUsJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cUsJ}}
{{judri|c8e1d8}}
:'''tu poi le mlatu pu lacpu cu ratcu'''
:<code>That-distant-thing which the cat [past] drags is-a-rat</code>

is equivalent to {{lex|example-random-id-qLuj}}.

{{ind|general-imported|ku'o|elidability for relative clauses}} As stated before, {{vla|ku'o}} is an elidable terminator, and in fact it is almost always elidable. Throughout the rest of this chapter, {{vla|ku'o}} will not be written in any of the examples unless it is absolutely required: thus, {{lex|example-random-id-qLt8}} can be written:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MtNs}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MtNs}}
{{judri|c8e1d9}}
:'''ti poi prenu cu barda'''
:<code>That which is-a-person is-big.</code>
:''That person is big.''

{{ind|general-imported|poi|discussion of translation}} without any change in meaning. Note that {{vla|poi}} is translated “which” rather than “such-that” when {{vla|ke'a}} has been omitted from the x1 place of the relative clause bridi. The word “which” is used in English to introduce English relative clauses: other words that can be used are “who” and “that”, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-j5ym}}
{{judri|c8e1d10}}
I saw a man who was going to the store.

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-J9yC}}
{{judri|c8e1d11}}
The building that the school was located in is large.

In {{lex|example-random-id-j5ym}} the relative clause is “who was going to the store”, and in {{lex|example-random-id-J9yC}} it is “that the school was located in”. Sometimes “who”, “which”, and “that” are used in literal translations in this chapter in order to make them read more smoothly.

{{ssp|section-noi}}
==Incidental relative clauses==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''noi'''	NOI	''incidental relative clause introducer''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|restricted contrasted with incidental}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-restrictive relative clause|definition (see also incidental relative clause)}}  {{ind|general-imported|incidental relative clause|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|restrictive relative clause|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clause|restrictive (see also restrictive relative clause)}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|kinds of}} There are two basic kinds of relative clauses: restrictive relative clauses introduced by 
{{vla|poi}}, and incidental (sometimes called simply “non-restrictive”) relative clauses introduced by {{vla|noi}}. The difference between restrictive and incidental relative clauses is that restrictive clauses provide information that is essential to identifying the referent of the sumti to which they are attached, whereas incidental relative clauses provide additional information which is helpful to the listener but is not essential for identifying the referent of the sumti. All of the examples in {{ls|section-poi}} are restrictive relative clauses: the information in the relative clause is essential to identification. (The title of this chapter, though, uses an incidental relative clause.)

Consider the following examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLXK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLXK}}
{{judri|c8e2d1}}
:'''le gerku poi blanu cu barda'''
:<code>The dog which is-blue is-large.</code>
:''The dog which is blue is large.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qLys}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qLys}}
{{judri|c8e2d2}}
:'''le gerku noi blanu cu barda'''
:<code>The dog incidentally-which is-blue is-large.</code>
:''The dog, which is blue, is large.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qLXK}}, the information conveyed by 
:{{jbo|poi blanu}} is essential to identifying the dog in question: it restricts the possible referents from dogs in general to dogs that are blue. This is why {{vla|poi}} relative clauses are called restrictive. In {{lex|example-random-id-qLys}}, on the other hand, the dog which is referred to has presumably already been identified clearly, and the relative clause 
:{{jbo|noi blanu}} just provides additional information about it. (If in fact the dog hasn't been identified clearly, then the relative clause does not help identify it further.)

{{ind|general-imported|incidental relative clause|as a parenthetical device}}  {{ind|general-imported|comma|effect on relative clause in English}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|effect of commas in English}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|restricted contrasted with incidental in English expression}} In English, the distinction between restrictive and incidental relative clauses is expressed in writing by surrounding incidental, but not restrictive, clauses with commas. These commas are functioning as parentheses, because incidental relative clauses are essentially parenthetical. This distinction in punctuation is represented in speech by a difference in tone of voice. In addition, English restrictive relative clauses can be introduced by “that” as well as “which” and “who”, whereas incidental relative clauses cannot begin with “that”. Lojban, however, always uses the cmavo {{vla|poi}} and {{vla|noi}} rather than punctuation or intonation to make the distinction.

Here are more examples of incidental relative clauses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-WxJo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WxJo}}
{{judri|c8e2d3}}
:'''mi noi jdice cu zvati'''
:<code>I who-incidentally am-a-judge am-at [some-place].</code>
:''I, a judge, am present.''

In this example, {{vla|mi}} is already sufficiently restricted, and the additional information that I am a judge is being provided solely for the listener's edification.

{{dsp|example-random-id-pR53}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pR53}}
{{judri|c8e2d4}}
:'''xu do viska le mi karce noi blabi'''
:<code>[True?] You see my car incidentally-which is-white.</code>
:''Do you see my car, which is white?''

In {{lex|example-random-id-pR53}}, the speaker is presumed to have only one car, and is providing incidental information that it is white. (Alternatively, he or she might have more than one car, since 
:{{jbo|le karce}} can be plural, in which case the incidental information is that each of them is white.) Contrast {{lex|example-random-id-0qU1}} with a restrictive relative clause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-0qU1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0qU1}}
{{judri|c8e2d5}}
:'''xu do viska le mi karce poi blabi'''
:<code>[True?] You see my car which is-white.</code>
:<code>Do you see my car that is white?</code>
:''Do you see my white car?''

{{ind|general-imported|relative clause|compared with tanru}} Here the speaker probably has several cars, and is restricting the referent of the sumti 
:{{jbo|le mi karce}} (and thereby the listener's attention) to the white one only. {{lex|example-random-id-0qU1}} means much the same as {{lex|example-random-id-zsQ6}}, which does not use a relative clause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zsQ6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zsQ6}}
{{judri|c8e2d6}}
:'''xu do viska le mi blabi karce'''
:<code>[True?] You see my white car.</code>
:''Do you see my car, the white one?''

{{ind|general-imported|relative clause|contrasted with tanru}} So a restrictive relative clause attached to a description can often mean the same as a description involving a tanru. However, 

:{{jbo|blabi karce}}, like all tanru, is somewhat vague: in principle, it might refer to a car which carries white things, or even express some more complicated concept involving whiteness and car-ness; the restrictive relative clause of {{lex|example-random-id-0qU1}} can only refer to a car which is white, not to any more complex or extended concept.

{{ssp|section-relative-phrases}}
==Relative phrases==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''pe'''	GOI	''restrictive association''
'''po'''	GOI	''restrictive possession''
'''po'e'''	GOI	''restrictive intrinsic possession''
'''po'u'''	GOI	''restrictive identification''
'''ne'''	GOI	''incidental association''
'''no'u'''	GOI	''incidental identification''

'''ge'u'''	GEhU	''relative phrase terminator''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|relative phrase|as an abbreviation of a common relative clause}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative phrase|syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative phrase|rationale for}} There are types of relative clauses (those which have a certain selbri) which are frequently wanted in Lojban, and can be expressed using a shortcut called a relative phrase. Relative phrases are introduced by cmavo of selma'o GOI, and consist of a GOI cmavo followed by a single sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|loose association|expressing with pe}}  {{ind|general-imported|pe|as loose association}}  {{ind|general-imported|pe|compared with {{jbo|poi ke'a srana}}}} Here is an example of {{vla|pe}}, plus an equivalent sentence using a relative clause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qM04}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qM04}}
{{judri|c8e3d1}}
:'''le stizu pe mi cu blanu'''
:<code>The chair associated-with me is-blue.</code>
:''My chair is blue.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qM1W}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qM1W}}
{{judri|c8e3d2}}
:'''le stizu poi ke'a srana mi cu blanu'''
:<code>The chair such-that( IT is-associated-with me) is-blue.</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-qM04}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qM1W}}, the link between the chair and the speaker is of the loosest kind.

{{ind|general-imported|specificity|expressing with po}}  {{ind|general-imported|possession|expressing with po}}  {{ind|general-imported|po|as restrictive possession}}  {{ind|general-imported|po|compared with {{jbo|poi ke'a se steci srana}}}} Here is an example of {{vla|po}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qM3D}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qM3D}}
{{judri|c8e3d3}}
:'''le stizu po mi cu xunre'''
:<code>The chair specific-to me is red.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qm3I}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qm3I}}
{{judri|c8e3d4}}
:'''le stizu poi ke'a se steci srana mi cu xunre'''
:<code>The chair such-that (IT is-specifically associated-with me) is-red.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|po|contrasted with pe}}  {{ind|general-imported|pe|contrasted with po}} {{lex|example-random-id-qM3D}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qm3I}} contrast with {{lex|example-random-id-qM04}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qM1W}}: the chair is more permanently connected with the speaker. A plausible (though not the only possible) contrast between {{lex|example-random-id-qM04}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qM3D}} is that 
:{{jbo|pe mi}} would be appropriate for a chair the speaker is currently sitting on (whether or not the speaker owned that chair), and 
:{{jbo|po mi}} for a chair owned by the speaker (whether or not he or she was currently occupying it).

{{ind|general-imported|po|contrasted with English “possession”}} As a result, the relationship expressed between two sumti by {{vla|po}} is usually called “possession”, although it does not necessarily imply ownership, legal or otherwise. The central concept is that of specificity ( 
{{vla|steci}} in Lojban).

{{ind|general-imported|inalienable possession|expressing with po'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|intrinsic possession|expressing with po'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|possession|intrinsic|expressing with po'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|po'e|as intrinsic possession}}  {{ind|general-imported|po'e|compared with {{jbo|poi ke'a jinzi ke se steci srana}}}} Here is an example of {{vla|po'e}}, as well as another example of 
{{vla|po}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qM3Q}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qM3Q}}
{{judri|c8e3d5}}
:'''le birka po'e mi cu spofu'''
:<code>The arm intrinsically-possessed-by me is-broken</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qm5E}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qm5E}}
{{ind|example|person's arm|example}}
{{judri|c8e3d6}}
:'''le birka poi jinzi ke se steci srana mi cu spofu'''
:<code>The arm which is-intrinsically (specifically associated-with) me is-broken.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qm7W}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qm7W}}
{{judri|c8e3d7}}
:'''le botpi po mi cu spofu'''
:<code>The bottle specific-to me is-broken</code>

{{ind|general-imported|alienable possession|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|extrinsic possession|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|inalienable possession|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|intrinsic possession|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|po|contrasted with po'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|po'e|contrasted with po}} {{lex|example-random-id-qM3Q}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qm5E}} on the one hand, and {{lex|example-random-id-qm7W}} on the other, illustrate the contrast between two types of possession called “intrinsic” and “extrinsic”, or sometimes “inalienable” and “alienable”, respectively. Something is intrinsically (or inalienably) possessed by someone if the possession is part of the possessor, and cannot be changed without changing the possessor. In the case of {{lex|example-random-id-qM3Q}}, people are usually taken to intrinsically possess their arms: even if an arm is cut off, it remains the arm of that person. (If the arm is transplanted to another person, however, it becomes intrinsically possessed by the new user, though, so intrinsic possession is a matter of degree.)

{{ind|general-imported|inalienable|distinguishing from alienable}} By contrast, the bottle of {{lex|example-random-id-qm7W}} can be given away, or thrown away, or lost, or stolen, so it is possessed extrinsically (alienably). The exact line between intrinsic and extrinsic possession is culturally dependent. The U.S. Declaration of Independence speaks of the “inalienable rights” of men, but just what those rights are, and even whether the concept makes sense at all, varies from culture to culture.

Note that {{lex|example-random-id-qM3Q}} can also be expressed without a relative clause:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bF0U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bF0U}}
{{judri|c8e3d8}}
:'''le birka be mi cu spofu'''
:<code>The arm of-body me is broken</code>

{{ind|general-imported|intrinsic possession|expressing by using place in some selbri}} reflecting the fact that the gismu {{vla|birka}} has an x2 place representing the body to which the arm belongs. Many, but not all, cases of intrinsic possession can be thus covered without using 
{{vla|po'e}} by placing the possessor into the appropriate place of the description selbri.

Here is an example of {{vla|po'u}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qM8u}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qM8u}}
{{judri|c8e3d9}}
:'''le gerku po'u le mi pendo cu cinba mi'''
:<code>The dog which-is my friend kisses me.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qm90}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qm90}}
{{judri|c8e3d10}}
:'''le gerku poi du le mi pendo cu cinba mi'''
:<code>The dog which = my friend kisses me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|identity|expressing with po'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|po'u|as identity}}  {{ind|general-imported|po'u|compared with {{jbo|poi ke'a du}}}} The cmavo {{vla|po'u}} does not represent possession at all, but rather identity. (Note that it means 
:{{jbo|poi du}} and its form was chosen to suggest the relationship.)

In {{lex|example-random-id-qM8u}}, the use of {{vla|po'u}} tells us that 
:{{jbo|le gerku}} and 
:{{jbo|le mi pendo}} represent the same thing. Consider the contrast between {{lex|example-random-id-qM8u}} and:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wARJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wARJ}}
{{judri|c8e3d11}}
:'''le mi pendo po'u le gerku cu cinba mi'''
:<code>My friend which-is the dog kisses me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|po'u|relative phrase of contrasted with relativized sumti of}} The facts of the case are the same, but the listener's knowledge about the situation may not be. In {{lex|example-random-id-qM8u}}, the listener is presumed not to understand which dog is meant by 
:{{jbo|le gerku}}, so the speaker adds a relative phrase clarifying that it is the particular dog which is the speaker's friend.{{lex|example-random-id-wARJ}}, however, assumes that the listener does not know which of the speaker's friends is referred to, and specifies that it is the friend that is the dog (which dog is taken to be obvious). Here is another example of the same contrast:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMAd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMAd}}
{{ind|example|New York city|example}}
{{judri|c8e3d12}}
:'''le tcadu po'u la nu,iork'''
:''The city of New York [not another city]''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmaY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmaY}}
{{ind|example|New York state|example}}
{{ind|example|New York city|example}}
{{judri|c8e3d13}}
:'''la nu,iork po'u le tcadu'''
:''New York the city (not the state or some other New York)''

{{ind|general-imported|possessed in relative phrases|compared with possessor}}  {{ind|general-imported|possessor in relative phrases|compared with possessed}} The principle that the possessor and the possessed may change places applies to all the GOI cmavo, and allows for the possibility of odd effects:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMb2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMb2}}
{{judri|c8e3d14}}
{{ind|example|friend's cup|example}} 
:'''le kabri pe le mi pendo cu cmalu'''
:<code>The cup associated-with my friend is small.</code>
:''My friend's cup is small''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmbn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmbn}}
{{judri|c8e3d15}}
{{ind|example|cup's friend|example}}
:'''le mi pendo pe le kabri cu cmalu'''
:<code>My friend associated-with the cup is small.</code>
:''My friend, the one with the cup, is small.''
