Consider {{lex|example-random-id-BSAc}} again. Another way to view the situation is to consider the speaker's left eye as a tool, a tool for seeing. The relevant selbri then becomes {{vla|pilno}}, whose place structure is
{{vla|pilno}} :''x1 uses x2 as a tool for purpose x3''

and we can rewrite {{lex|example-random-id-BSAc}} as

{{dsp|example-random-id-Lu15}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Lu15}}
{{judri|c9e5d2}}
:'''mi viska do fi'o se pilno le zunle kanla'''
:<code>I see you [modal] [conversion] use: the left eye.</code>
:''I see you using my left eye.''

Here the selbri belonging to the modal is 
:{{jbo|se pilno}}. The conversion of {{vla|pilno}} is necessary in order to get the “tool” place into x1, since only x1 can be the modal sumti. The “tool user” place is the x2 of 
:{{jbo|se pilno}} (because it is the x1 of {{vla|pilno}}) and remains unspecified. The tag 
:{{jbo|fi'o pilno}} would mean “with tool user”, leaving the tool unspecified.

{{ssp|section-BAI}}
==Modal tags: BAI==
There are certain selbri which seem particularly useful in constructing modal tags. In particular, {{vla|pilno}} is one of them. The place structure of {{vla|pilno}} is:
{{vla|pilno}} :''x1 uses x2 as a tool for purpose x3''

{{ind|general-imported|BAI modal tags|rationale for}} and almost any selbri which represents an action may need to specify a tool. Having to say 
:{{jbo|fi'o se pilno}} frequently would make many Lojban sentences unnecessarily verbose and clunky, so an abbreviation is provided in the language design: the compound cmavo {{vla|sepi'o}}.

{{ind|general-imported|conversion|of BAI cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal tags|short forms as BAI cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|fi'o constructs|short forms as BAI cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|BAI selma'o|as short forms for fi'o constructs}} Here {{vla|se}} is used before a cmavo, namely {{vla|pi'o}}, rather than before a brivla. The meaning of this cmavo, which belongs to selma'o BAI, is exactly the same as that of 

:{{jbo|fi'o pilno fe'u}}. Since what we want is a tag based on 
:{{jbo|se pilno}} rather than 
:{{jbo|pilno-}} the tool, not the tool user &ndash; the grammar allows a BAI cmavo to be converted using a SE cmavo. {{lex|example-random-id-Lu15}} may therefore be rewritten as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-N32m}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-N32m}}
{{judri|c9e6d1}}
:'''mi viska do sepi'o le zunle kanla'''
:<code>I see you with-tool: the left eye</code>
:''I see you using my left eye.''

The compound cmavo {{vla|sepi'o}} is much shorter than 

:{{jbo|fi'o se pilno [fe'u]}} and can be thought of as a single word meaning “with-tool”. The modal tag {{vla|pi'o}}, with no 
{{vla|se}}, similarly means “with-tool-user”, probably a less useful concept. Nevertheless, the parallelism with the place structure of {{vla|pilno}} makes the additional syllable worthwhile.

{{ind|general-imported|conversion|effect on BAI}}  {{ind|general-imported|BAI selma'o|effect of conversion on}} Some BAI cmavo make sense with as well as without a SE cmavo; for example, {{vla|ka'a}}, the BAI corresponding to the gismu 
{{vla|klama}}, has five usable forms corresponding to the five places of {{vla|klama}} respectively:



;{{vla|ka'a}}
:with-goer

;{{vla|seka'a}}
:with-destination

;{{vla|teka'a}}
:with-origin

;{{vla|veka'a}}
:with-route

;{{vla|xeka'a}}
:with-means-of-transport

Any of these tags may be used to provide modal places for bridi, as in the following examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-r0QA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-r0QA}}
{{ind|example|Avon|example}}
{{ind|example|traveling salesperson|example}} (
{{judri|c9e6d2}}
:'''la .eivn. cu vecnu loi flira cinta ka'a mi'''
:<code>Avon sells a-mass-of face paint with-goer me.</code>
:''I am a traveling cosmetics salesperson for Avon.''
{{lex|example-random-id-r0QA}} may seem a bit strained, but it illustrates the way in which an existing selbri, {{vla|vecnu}} in this case, may have a place added to it which might otherwise seem utterly unrelated.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmJM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmJM}}
{{judri|c9e6d3}}
:'''mi cadzu seka'a la bratfyd.'''
:<code>I walk with-destination Bradford.</code>
:''I am walking to Bradford.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMjz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMjz}}
{{judri|c9e6d4}}
:'''bloti teka'a la nu,IORK.'''
:<code>[Observative:] is-a-boat with-origin New York</code>
:''A boat from New York!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmLX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmLX}}
{{judri|c9e6d5}}
:'''do bajra veka'a lo djine'''
:<code>You run with-route a circle.</code>
:''You are running in circles.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMMX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMMX}}
{{judri|c9e6d6}}
:'''mi citka xeka'a le vinji'''
:<code>I eat with-means-of-transport the airplane.</code>
:''I eat in the airplane.''

{{ind|general-imported|English prepositions|contrasted with modal tags in preciseness}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal tags|contrasted with English prepositions in preciseness}}  {{ind|general-imported|BAI cmavo|rationale for selection}} There are sixty-odd cmavo of selma'o BAI, based on selected gismu that seemed useful in a variety of settings. The list is somewhat biased toward English, because many of the cmavo were selected on the basis of corresponding English prepositions and preposition compounds such as “with”, “without”, and “by means of”. The BAI cmavo, however, are far more precise than English prepositions, because their meanings are fixed by the place structures of the corresponding gismu.

{{ind|general-imported|BAI selma'o|form of cmavo in}} All BAI cmavo have the form CV'V or CVV. Most of them are CV'V, where the C is the first consonant of the corresponding gismu and the two Vs are the two vowels of the gismu. The table in {{ls|section-irregular-BAI}} shows the exceptions.

{{ind|general-imported|vague relationship|modal tag for}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal tag|for vague relationship}} There is one additional BAI cmavo that is not derived from a gismu: {{vla|do'e}}. This cmavo is used when an extra place is needed, but it seems useful to be vague about the semantic implications of the extra place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2vMd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2vMd}}
{{judri|c9e6d7}}
:'''lo nanmu be do'e le berti cu klama le tcadu'''
:<code>Some man [related to] the north came to-the city.</code>
:''A man of the north came to the city.''

<!-- FIXME: what to do with these &quot;s? -->{{ind|general-imported|modal place|on description selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;of&quot;|in English|compared with do'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|do'e|compared with English &quot;of&quot;}} Here 
:{{jbo|le berti}} is provided as a modal place of the selbri {{vla|nanmu}}, but its exact significance is vague, and is paralleled in the colloquial translation by the vague English preposition “of”. {{lex|example-random-id-2vMd}} also illustrates a modal place bound into a selbri with {{vla|be}}. This construction is useful when the selbri of a description requires a modal place; this and other uses of {{vla|be}} are more fully explained in {{ls|section-be-sumti}}.

{{ssp|section-causals}}
==Modal sentence connection: the causals==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ri'a'''	BAI	''rinka modal: physical cause''
'''ki'u'''	BAI	''krinu modal: justification''
'''mu'i'''	BAI	''mukti modal: motivation''
'''ni'i'''	BAI	''nibli modal: logical entailment''
</tab>

This section has two purposes. On the one hand, it explains the grammatical construct called “modal sentence connection”. On the other, it exemplifies some of the more useful BAI cmavo: the causals. (There are other BAI cmavo which have causal implications: 
{{vla|ja'e}} means “with result”, and so {{vla|seja'e}} means “with cause of unspecified nature”; likewise, {{vla|gau}} means “with agent” and {{vla|tezu'e}} means “with purpose”. These other modal cmavo will not be further discussed here, as my purpose is to explain modal sentence connection rather than Lojbanic views of causation.)

{{ind|general-imported|causals|gismu}} There are four causal gismu in Lojban, distinguishing different versions of the relationships lumped in English as “causal”:

;{{vla|rinka}}
:''event x1 physically causes event x2''

;{{vla|krinu}}
:''event x1 is the justification for event x2''

;{{vla|mukti}}
:''event x1 is the (human) motive for event x2''

;{{vla|nibli}}
:''event x1 logically entails event x2''

{{ind|general-imported|modal causals|implication differences}}  {{ind|general-imported|causals|modal}}  {{ind|general-imported|modals|for causal gismu}} Each of these gismu has a related modal: {{vla|ri'a}}, {{vla|ki'u}}, 
{{vla|mu'i}}, and 
{{vla|ni'i}} respectively. Using these gismu and these modals, we can create various causal sentences with different implications:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmMz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmMz}}
{{judri|c9e7d1}}
:'''le spati cu banro ri'a le nu do djacu dunda fi le spati'''
:<code>The plant grows with-physical-cause the event-of you water give to the plant.</code>
:''The plant grows because you water it.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmN2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmN2}}
{{judri|c9e7d2}}
:'''la djan. cpacu le pamoi se jinga ki'u le nu la djan. jinga'''
:<code>John gets the first prize with-justification the event-of John wins.</code>
:''John got the first prize because he won.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMN7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMN7}}
{{judri|c9e7d3}}
:'''mi lebna le cukta mu'i le nu mi viska le cukta'''
:<code>I took the book with-motivation the event-of I saw the book.</code>
:''I took the book because I saw it.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMNc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMNc}}
{{ind|ekxample-imported|Socrates|example}}
{{judri|c9e7d4}}
:'''la sokrates. morsi binxo ni'i le nu la sokrates. remna'''
:<code>Socrates dead-became with-logical-justification Socrates is-human.</code>
:''Socrates died because Socrates is human.''

{{ind|general-imported|&quot;because&quot;|English word|four varieties of}} In {{lex|example-random-id-qmMz}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qMNc}}, the same English word “because” is used to translate all four modals, but the types of cause being expressed are quite different. Let us now focus on {{lex|example-random-id-qmMz}}, and explore some variations on it.

{{ind|general-imported|causals|claiming the relation contrasted with claiming cause and/or effect and/or relation}}  {{ind|general-imported|abstraction bridi|effect on claim of bridi}} As written, {{lex|example-random-id-qmMz}} claims that the plant grows, but only refers to the event of watering it in an abstraction bridi (abstractions are explained in 
{{lch|chapter-abstractions}}) without actually making a claim. If I express {{lex|example-random-id-qmMz}}, I have said that the plant in fact grows, but I have not said that you actually water it, merely that there is a causal relationship between watering and growing. This is semantically asymmetrical. Suppose I wanted to claim that the plant was being watered, and only mention its growth as ancillary information? Then we could reverse the main bridi and the abstraction bridi, saying:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ibro}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ibro}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}} 
{{judri|c9e7d5}}
:'''do djacu dunda fi le spati seri'a le nu ri banro'''
:<code>You water-give to the plant with-physical-effect it grows.</code>
:''You water the plant; therefore, it grows.''

with the {{vla|ri'a}} changed to {{vla|seri'a}}. In addition, there are also symmetrical forms:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1YHv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1YHv}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}} 
{{judri|c9e7d6}}
:'''le nu do djacu dunda fi le spati cu rinka le nu le spati cu banro'''
:<code>The event-of (you water-give to the plant) causes the event-of (the plant grows).</code>
:''Your watering the plant causes its growth. If you water the plant, then it grows.''

does not claim either event, but asserts only the causal relationship between them. So in {{lex|example-random-id-1YHv}}, I am not saying that the plant grows nor that you have in fact watered it. The second colloquial translation shows a form of “if-then” in English quite distinct from the logical connective “if-then” explained in {{lch|chapter-connectives}}.

Suppose we wish to claim both events as well as their causal relationship? We can use one of two methods:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMnX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMnX}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}} 
{{judri|c9e7d7}}
:'''le spati cu banro .iri'abo do djacu dunda fi le spati'''
:<code>The plant grows. Because you water-give to the plant.</code>
:''The plant grows because you water it.''

{{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMPn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMPn}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}} 
{{judri|c9e7d8}}
:'''do djacu dunda fi le spati .iseri'abo le spati cu banro'''
:<code>You water-give to the plant. Therefore it grows.</code>
:''You water the plant; therefore, it grows.''

The compound cmavo 
:{{jbo|.iri'abo}} and 

:{{jbo|.iseri'abo}} serve to connect two bridi, as the initial {{vla|i}} indicates. The final {{vla|bo}} is necessary to prevent the modal from “taking over” the following sumti. If the {{vla|bo}} were omitted from {{lex|example-random-id-qMnX}} we would have:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Wo6K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Wo6K}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}} 
{{judri|c9e7d9}}
:'''le spati cu banro .i ri'a do djacu dunda fi le spati'''
:<code>The plant grows. Because of you, [something] water-gives to the plant.</code>
:''The plant grows. Because of you, water is given to the plant.''

Because 
:{{jbo|ri'a do}} is a modal sumti in {{lex|example-random-id-Wo6K}}, there is no longer an explicit sumti in the x1 place of 
:{{jbo|djacu dunda}}, and the translation must be changed.

{{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|relation to modal of second sentence in}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|relation to modal of first sentence in}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|effect on modal}} The effect of sentences like {{lex|example-random-id-qMnX}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qMPn}} is that the modal, {{vla|ri'a}} in this example, no longer modifies an explicit sumti. Instead, the sumti is implicit, the event given by a full bridi. Furthermore, there is a second implication: that the first bridi fills the x2 place of the gismu {{vla|rinka}}; it specifies an event which is the effect. I am therefore claiming three things: that the plant grows, that you have watered it, and that there is a cause-and-effect relationship between the two.

{{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|with other than causals}} In principle, any modal tag can appear in a sentence connective of the type exemplified by {{lex|example-random-id-qMnX}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qMPn}}. However, it makes little sense to use any modals which do not expect events or other abstractions to fill the places of the corresponding gismu. The sentence connective 
:{{jbo|.ibaubo}} is perfectly grammatical, but it is hard to imagine any two sentences which could be connected by an “in-language” modal. This is because a sentence describes an event, and an event can be a cause or an effect, but not a language.

{{ssp|section-modal-connectives}}
==Other modal connections==
Like many Lojban grammatical constructions, sentence modal connection has both forethought and afterthought forms. (See {{lch|chapter-connectives}} for a more detailed discussion of Lojban connectives.) {{ls|section-causals}} exemplifies only afterthought modal connection, illustrated here by:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2D4c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2D4c}}
{{ind|example|grasp water|example}}
{{judri|c9e8d1}}
:'''mi jgari lei djacu .iri'abo mi jgari le kabri'''
:<code>I grasp the-mass-of water with-physical-cause I grasp the cup.</code>
:<code>Causing the mass of water to be grasped by me, I grasped the cup.</code>
:''I grasp the water because I grasp the cup.''

{{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought connection|definition}} An afterthought connection is one that is signaled only by a cmavo (or a compound cmavo, in this case) between the two constructs being connected. Forethought connection uses a signal both before the first construct and between the two: the use of “both” and “and” in the first half of this sentence represents a forethought connection (though not a modal one).

{{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought modal sentence connection}} To make forethought modal sentence connections in Lojban, place the modal plus {{vla|gi}} before the first bridi, and {{vla|gi}} between the two. No {{vla|i}} is used within the construct. The forethought equivalent of {{lex|example-random-id-2D4c}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-d2b9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-d2b9}}
{{judri|c9e8d2}}
:'''ri'agi mi jgari le kabri gi mi jgari lei djacu'''
:<code>With-physical-cause I grasp the cup, I grasp the-mass-of water.</code>
:''Because I grasp the cup, I grasp the water.''

{{ind|general-imported|forethought modal sentence connection|relation to modal of second bridi in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought modal sentence connection|relation to modal of first bridi in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought modal sentence connection for causals|order of cause and effect}} Note that the cause, the x1 of {{vla|rinka}} is now placed first. To keep the two bridi in the original order of {{lex|example-random-id-2D4c}}, we could say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rQ77}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rQ77}}
{{judri|c9e8d3}}
:'''seri'agi mi jgari lei djacu gi mi jgari le kabri'''
:<code>With-physical-effect I grasp the-mass-of water, I grasp the cup.</code>

In English, the sentence “Therefore I grasp the water, I grasp the cup” is ungrammatical, because “therefore” is not grammatically equivalent to “because”. In Lojban, 
:{{jbo|seri'agi}} can be used just like 
:{{jbo|ri'agi}}.

{{ind|general-imported|modal sentence connection|condensing}} When the two bridi joined by a modal connection have one or more elements (selbri or sumti or both) in common, there are various condensed forms that can be used in place of full modal sentence connection with both bridi completely stated.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti modal connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal sumti connection}} When the bridi are the same except for a single sumti, as in Examples 8.1 through 8.3, then a sumti modal connection may be employed:

{{dsp|example-random-id-o7FG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-o7FG}}
{{judri|c9e8d4}}
:'''mi jgari ri'agi le kabri gi lei djacu'''
:<code>I grasp because the cup, the-mass-of water.</code>{{lex|example-random-id-o7FG}} means exactly the same as {{lex|example-random-id-2D4c}} through {{lex|example-random-id-rQ77}}, but there is no idiomatic English translation that will distinguish it from them.

{{ind|general-imported|termset modal connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modals|termset connection}} If the two connected bridi are different in more than one sumti, then a termset may be employed. Termsets are explained more fully in {{ls|section-termsets}}, but are essentially a mechanism for creating connections between multiple sumti simultaneously.

{{dsp|example-random-id-LetE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LetE}}
{{judri|c9e8d5}}
:'''mi dunda le cukta la djan. .imu'ibo la djan. dunda lei jdini mi'''
:<code>I gave the book to John. Motivated-by John gave the-mass-of money to-me.</code>
:''I gave the book to John, because John gave money to me.''

means the same as:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|nu'u}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nu'i}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-tFSC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tFSC}}
{{judri|c9e8d6}}
:'''nu'i mu'igi la djan. lei jdini mi gi mi le cukta la djan. nu'u dunda'''
:<code>[start] because John, the-mass-of money, me; I, the book, John [end] gives.</code>

Here there are three sumti in each half of the termset, because the two bridi share only their selbri.

{{ind|general-imported|bridi-tail modal connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal bridi-tail connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal connection of selbri|using bridi-tail modal connection}} There is no modal connection between selbri as such: bridi which differ only in the selbri can be modally connected using bridi-tail modal connection. The bridi-tail construct is more fully explained in 
{{ls|section-compound-bridi}}, but essentially it consists of a selbri with optional sumti following it. {{lex|example-random-id-qMN7}} is suitable for bridi-tail connection, and could be shortened to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Do9b}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Do9b}}
{{judri|c9e8d7}}
:'''mi mu'igi viska le cukta gi lebna le cukta'''
:<code>I, because saw the book, took the book.</code>

Again, no straightforward English translation exists. It is even possible to shorten {{lex|example-random-id-Do9b}} further to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YXps}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YXps}}
{{judri|c9e8d8}}
:'''mi mu'igi viska gi lebna vau le cukta'''
:<code>I because saw, therefore took, the book.</code>

where 
:{{jbo|le cukta}} is set off by the non-elidable {{vla|vau}} and is made to belong to both bridi-tails &ndash; See {{ls|section-compound-bridi}} for more explanations.

{{ind|general-imported|shared bridi-tail sumti|avoiding}}  {{ind|general-imported|vau for shared bridi-tail sumti|avoiding}} Since this is a chapter on rearranging sumti, it is worth pointing out that {{lex|example-random-id-YXps}} can be further rearranged to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Pxca}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Pxca}}
{{judri|c9e8d9}}
:'''mi le cukta mu'igi viska gi lebna'''
:<code>I, the book, because saw, therefore took.</code>

which doesn't require the extra {{vla|vau}}; all sumti before a conjunction of bridi-tails are shared.

{{ind|general-imported|operand modal connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal operand connection}} Finally, mathematical operands can be modally connected.

{{dsp|example-random-id-J2T5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-J2T5}}
{{judri|c9e8d10}}
:'''li ny. du li vo .ini'ibo li ny. du li re su'i re'''
:<code>the number n = the-number 4. Entailed-by the-number n = the-number 2 + 2.</code>
:''n = 4 because n = 2 + 2.''

can be reduced to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Mfe4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Mfe4}}
{{judri|c9e8d11}}
:'''li ny. du li ni'igi vei re su'i re [ve'o] gi vo'''
:<code>the-number n = the-number because ( 2 + 2 ) therefore 4.</code>
:''n is 2 + 2, and is thus 4.''

The cmavo {{vla|vei}} and {{vla|ve'o}} represent mathematical parentheses, and are required so that 
:{{jbo|ni'igi}} affects more than just the immediately following operand, namely the first {{vla|re}}. (The right parenthesis, {{vla|ve'o}}, is an elidable terminator.) As usual, no English translation does {{lex|example-random-id-Mfe4}} justice.

{{ind|general-imported|modal connectives|fi'o prohibited in}}  {{ind|general-imported|fi'o|restriction on use}} Note: Due to restrictions on the Lojban parsing algorithm, it is not possible to form modal connectives using the 

:{{jbo|fi'o-}} plus-selbri form of modal. Only the predefined modals of selma'o BAI can be compounded as shown in {{ls|section-causals}} and {{ls|section-modal-connectives}}.

{{ssp|section-modal-selbri}}
==Modal selbri==
Consider the example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bT4c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bT4c}}
{{ind|example|under compulsion|example}}
{{judri|c9e9d1}}
:'''mi tavla bau la lojban. bai tu'a la frank.'''
:<code>I speak in-language Lojban with-compeller some-act-by Frank.</code>
:''I speak in Lojban, under compulsion by Frank.''

{{ind|general-imported|modal sumti|unspecified}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal sumti|leaving vague}} {{lex|example-random-id-bT4c}} has two modal sumti, using the modals 
{{vla|bau}} and {{vla|bai}}. Suppose we wanted to specify the language explicitly but be vague about who's doing the compelling. We can simplify {{lex|example-random-id-bT4c}} to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-dbSy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dbSy}}
{{ind|example|under compulsion|example}}
{{judri|c9e9d2}}
:'''mi tavla bau la lojban. bai [ku].'''
:<code>I speak in-language Lojban under-compulsion.</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-dbSy}}, the elidable terminator {{vla|ku}} has taken the place of the sumti which would normally follow {{vla|bai}}. Alternatively, we could specify the one who compels but keep the language vague:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Qc8w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Qc8w}}
{{ind|example|under compulsion|example}}
{{judri|c9e9d3}}
:'''mi tavla bau [ku] bai tu'a la frank.'''
:<code>I speak in-some-language under-compulsion-by some-act-by Frank.</code>

We are also free to move the modal-plus- {{vla|ku}} around the bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2utY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2utY}}
{{ind|example|under compulsion|example}}
{{judri|c9e9d4}}
:'''bau [ku] bai ku mi tavla'''
:<code>In-some-language under-compulsion I speak.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|modal followed by selbri|effect on eliding cu}} An alternative to using {{vla|ku}} is to place the modal cmavo right before the selbri, following the 
{{vla|cu}} which often appears there. When a modal is present, the {{vla|cu}} is almost never necessary.

{{dsp|example-random-id-613h}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-613h}}
{{judri|c9e9d5}}
:'''mi bai tavla bau la lojban.'''
:<code>I compelledly speak in-language Lojban.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|modal followed by selbri|contrasted with tanru modification in grammar}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal followed by selbri|compared with tanru modification in meaning}} In this use, the modal is like a tanru modifier semantically, although grammatically it is quite distinct. {{lex|example-random-id-613h}} is very similar in meaning to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pVUT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pVUT}}
{{judri|c9e9d6}}
:'''mi se bapli tavla bau la lojban.'''
:<code>I compelledly-speak in-language Lojban.</code>

The {{vla|se}} conversion is needed because 
:{{jbo|bapli tavla}} would be a “compeller type of speaker” rather than a “compelled (by someone) type of speaker”, which is what a 
:{{jbo|bai tavla}} is.

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o modal followed by selbri|effect on eliding fe'u}} If the modal preceding a selbri is constructed using {{vla|fi'o}}, then {{vla|fe'u}} is required to prevent the main selbri and the modal selbri from colliding:

{{dsp|example-random-id-SfwV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-SfwV}}
{{ind|example|see with eye|example}}
{{judri|c9e9d7}}
:'''mi fi'o kanla fe'u viska do'''
:<code>I with-eye see you.</code>
:''I see you with my eye(s).''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|bai ke}}  

{{ind|general-imported|modals|expanding scope over inner modal connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modals|expanding scope over non-logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|modals|expanding scope over logical connection with ke ... ke'e}} There are two other uses of modals. A modal can be attached to a pair of bridi-tails that have already been connected by a logical, non-logical, or modal connection (See {{lch|chapter-connectives}} for more on logical and non-logical connections):

{{dsp|example-random-id-vCzL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-vCzL}}
{{judri|c9e9d8}}
:'''mi bai ke ge klama le zarci gi cadzu le bisli [ke'e]'''
:<code>I under-compulsion (both go to-the market and walk on-the ice).</code>
:''Under compulsion, I both go to the market and walk on the ice.''

Here the {{vla|bai}} is spread over both 
:{{jbo|klama le zarci}} and 
:{{jbo|cadzu le bisli}}, and the 
:{{jbo|ge ... gi}} represents the logical connection “both-and” between the two.

{{ind|general-imported|modals|expanding scope over multiple sentences with tu'e…tu'u}} Similarly, a modal can be attached to multiple sentences that have been combined with {{vla|tu'e}} and {{vla|tu'u}}, which are explained in more detail in {{ls|section-i}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-boYr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-boYr}}
{{judri|c9e9d9}}
:'''bai tu'e mi klama le zarci .i mi cadzu le bisli [tu'u]'''
:<code>Under-compulsion [start] I go to-the market. I walk on-the ice [end].</code>

means the same thing as {{lex|example-random-id-vCzL}}.

Note: Either BAI modals or 
:{{jbo|fi'o-}} plus-selbri modals may correctly be used in any of the constructions discussed in this section.

{{ssp|section-modal-relative-phrases}}
==Modal relative phrases; Comparison==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''pe'''	GOI	''restrictive relative phrase''
'''ne'''	GOI	''incidental relative phrase''
'''mau'''	BAI	''zmadu modal''
'''me'a'''	BAI	''mleca modal''
</tab>

Relative phrases and clauses are explained in much more detail in {{lch|chapter-relative-clauses}}. However, there is a construction which combines a modal with a relative phrase which is relevant to this chapter. Consider the following examples of relative clauses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmPP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmPP}}
{{ind|example|Artur Rubenstein|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d1}}
:'''la .apasionatas. poi se cusku la .artr. rubnstain. cu se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata which is-expressed-by Arthur Rubinstein is-liked-by me.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmPr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmPr}}
{{ind|example|Beethoven|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d2}}
:'''la .apasionatas. noi se finti la betovn. cu se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata, which is-created-by Beethoven, is-liked-by me.</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-qmPP}}, 
:{{jbo|la .apasionatas.}} refers to a particular performance of the sonata, namely the one performed by Rubinstein. Therefore, the relative clause 
:{{jbo|poi se cusku}} uses the cmavo {{vla|poi}} (of selma'o NOI) to restrict the meaning of 
:{{jbo|la .apasionatas}} to the performance in question.

In {{lex|example-random-id-qmPr}}, however, 
:{{jbo|la .apasionatas.}} refers to the sonata as a whole, and the information that it was composed by Beethoven is merely incidental. The cmavo 
{{vla|noi}} (also of selma'o NOI) expresses the incidental nature of this relationship.

The cmavo {{vla|pe}} and {{vla|ne}} (of selma'o GOI) are roughly equivalent to {{vla|poi}} and {{vla|noi}} respectively, but are followed by sumti rather than full bridi. We can abbreviate {{lex|example-random-id-qmPP}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qmPr}} to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMq1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMq1}}
{{ind|example|Appassionata|example}}
{{ind|example|Artur Rubenstein|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d3}}
:'''la .apasionatas. pe la .artr. rubnstain. se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata of Arthur Rubinstein is-liked-by me.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMQ1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMQ1}}
{{ind|example|Beethoven|example}}
{{ind|example|Appassionata|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d4}}
:'''la .apasionatas. ne la betovn. se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata, which is of Beethoven, is-liked-by me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|relative phrases|contrasted with relative clauses in preciseness}} Here the precise selbri of the relative clauses is lost: all we can tell is that the Appassionata is connected in some way with Rubinstein (in {{lex|example-random-id-qMq1}}) and Beethoven (in {{lex|example-random-id-qMQ1}}), and that the relationships are respectively restrictive and incidental.

It happens that both {{vla|cusku}} and {{vla|finti}} have BAI cmavo, namely {{vla|cu'u}} and 
{{vla|fi'e}}. We can recast {{lex|example-random-id-qMq1}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qMQ1}} as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMqF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMqF}}
{{ind|example|Appassionata|example}}
{{ind|example|Artur Rubenstein|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d5}}
:'''la .apasionatas pe cu'u la .artr. rubnstain. cu se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata expressed-by Arthur Rubinstein is-liked-by me.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmqy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmqy}}
{{ind|example|Beethoven|example}}
{{ind|example|Appassionata|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d6}}
:'''la .apasionatas ne fi'e la betovn. cu se nelci mi'''
:<code>The Appassionata, invented-by Beethoven, is-liked-by me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|modals|improving relative phrase preciseness with }}  {{ind|general-imported|relative phrases|improving preciseness with modals}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative phrases with modals|compared to relative clauses in preciseness}} {{lex|example-random-id-qMqF}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qmqy}} have the full semantic content of {{lex|example-random-id-qmPP}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qmPr}} respectively.

<!-- FIXME: what to do with these &quot;s? -->{{ind|general-imported|&quot;less&quot;|English word|expressing with relative phrases}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;more&quot;|English word|expressing with relative phrases}} Modal relative phrases are often used with the BAI cmavo {{vla|mau}} and 
{{vla|me'a}}, which are based on the comparative gismu 
{{vla|zmadu}} (more than) and {{vla|mleca}} (less than) respectively. The place structures are:



;'''{{vla|zmadu}}:'''
:''x1 is more than x2 in property/quantity x3 by amount x4''

;'''{{vla|mleca}}:'''
:''x1 is less than x2 in property/quantity x3 by amount x4''

Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Jr4V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Jr4V}}
{{ind|example|likes more than|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d7}}
:'''la frank. nelci la betis. ne semau la meiris.'''
:<code>Frank likes Betty, which-is more-than Mary.</code>
:''Frank likes Betty more than (he likes) Mary.''
{{lex|example-random-id-Jr4V}} requires that Frank likes Betty, but adds the information that his liking for Betty exceeds his liking for Mary. The modal appears in the form {{vla|semau}} because the x2 place of {{vla|zmadu}} is the basis for comparison: in this case, Frank's liking for Mary.

{{dsp|example-random-id-ecf1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ecf1}}
{{ind|example|likes more than|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d8}}
:'''la frank. nelci la meiris. ne seme'a la betis.'''
:<code>Frank likes Mary, which-is less-than Betty.</code>
:''Frank likes Mary less than (he likes) Betty.''

{{ind|general-imported|me'a|avoiding in favor of semau}}  {{ind|general-imported|mau|avoiding in favor of seme'a}} Here we are told that Frank likes Mary less than he likes Betty; the information about the comparison is the same. It would be possible to rephrase {{lex|example-random-id-Jr4V}} using {{vla|me'a}} rather than 
{{vla|semau}}, and {{lex|example-random-id-ecf1}} using {{vla|mau}} rather than 
{{vla|seme'a}}, but such usage would be unnecessarily confusing. Like many BAI cmavo, {{vla|mau}} and 
{{vla|me'a}} are more useful when converted with 
{{vla|se}}.

<!-- FIXME: what to do with these &quot;s? -->{{ind|general-imported|&quot;less&quot;|English word|importance of relative phrase to}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;more&quot;|English word|importance of relative phrase to}} If the {{vla|ne}} were omitted in {{lex|example-random-id-Jr4V}} and {{lex|example-random-id-ecf1}}, the modal sumti ( 

:{{jbo|la meiris.}} and 
:{{jbo|la betis.}} respectively) would become attached to the bridi as a whole, producing a very different translation. {{lex|example-random-id-ecf1}} would become:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5QHA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5QHA}}
{{ind|example|likes more than|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d9}}
:'''la frank. nelci la meiris. seme'a la betis.'''
:<code>Frank likes Mary is-less-than Betty.</code>
:''Frank's liking Mary is less than Betty.''

which compares a liking with a person, and is therefore nonsense.

{{ind|general-imported|bridi-based comparison|contrasted with comparison with relative phrase|in claims about parts}}  {{ind|general-imported|comparison with relative phrase|contrasted with bridi-based comparison|in claims about parts}}  {{ind|general-imported|comparison|claims related to based on form}} Pure comparison, which states only the comparative information but says nothing about whether Frank actually likes either Mary or Betty (he may like neither, but dislike Betty less), would be expressed differently, as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AAQp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AAQp}}
{{ind|example|likes more than|example}}
{{judri|c9e10d10}}
:'''le ni la frank. nelci la betis. cu zmadu le ni la frank. nelci la meiris.'''
:<code>The quantity-of Frank's liking Betty is-more-than the quantity-of Frank's liking Mary.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|modals often attached with relative phrases|list}} The mechanisms explained in this section are appropriate to many modals other than {{vla|semau}} and {{vla|seme'a}}. Some other modals that are often associated with relative phrases are: {{vla|seba'i}} (“instead of”), {{vla|ci'u}} (“on scale”), {{vla|de'i}} ( “dated”), {{vla|du'i}} ( “as much as”).

Some BAI tags can be used equally well in relative phrases or attached to bridi; others seem useful only attached to bridi. But it is also possible that the usefulness of particular BAI modals is an English-speaker bias, and that speakers of other languages may find other BAIs useful in divergent ways.

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o modals|usage in relative phrases}} Note: The uses of modals discussed in this section are applicable both to BAI modals and to {{jbo|fi'o}}-plus-selbri modals.

{{ssp|section-mixed-connection}}
==Mixed modal connection==
It is possible to mix logical connection (explained in {{lch|chapter-connectives}}) with modal connection, in a way that simultaneously asserts the logical connection and the modal relationship. Consider the sentences:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4qz4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4qz4}}
{{judri|c9e11d1}}
:'''mi nelci do .ije mi nelci la djein.'''
:<code>I like you. And I like Jane.</code>

which is a logical connection, and

{{dsp|example-random-id-6EE5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6EE5}}
{{judri|c9e11d2}}
:'''mi nelci do .iki'ubo mi nelci la djein.'''
:<code>I like you. Justified-by I like Jane.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|of sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal connection|simultaneous with logical}}  {{ind|general-imported|connection|simultaneously modal and logical}} The meanings of {{lex|example-random-id-4qz4}} and {{lex|example-random-id-6EE5}} can be simultaneously expressed by combining the two compound cmavo, thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-W3Le}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-W3Le}}
{{judri|c9e11d3}}
:'''mi nelci do .ijeki'ubo mi nelci la djein.'''
:<code>I like you. And justified-by I like Jane.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|definition}} Here the two sentences 
:{{jbo|mi nelci do}} and 
:{{jbo|mi nelci la djein.}} are simultaneously asserted, their logical connection is asserted, and their causal relationship is asserted. The logical connective {{vla|je}} comes before the modal {{vla|ki'u}} in all such mixed connections.

Since 
:{{jbo|mi nelci do}} and 
:{{jbo|mi nelci la djein.}} differ only in the final sumti, we can transform {{lex|example-random-id-W3Le}} into a mixed sumti connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gE1z}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gE1z}}
{{judri|c9e11d4}}
:'''mi nelci do .eki'ubo la djein.'''
:''I like you and/because Jane.''

{{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|as proscribed in forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|afterthought}}  {{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|of sumti}} Note that this connection is an afterthought one. Mixed connectives are always afterthought; forethought connectives must be either logical or modal.

{{ind|general-imported|mixed modal connection|of bridi-tails}} There are numerous other afterthought logical and non-logical connectives that can have modal information planted within them. For example, a bridi-tail connected version of {{lex|example-random-id-gE1z}} would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7LmA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7LmA}}
{{judri|c9e11d5}}
:'''mi nelci do gi'eki'ubo nelci la djein.'''
:''I like you and/because like Jane.''

The following three complex examples all mean the same thing.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMRB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMRB}}
{{judri|c9e11d6}}
:'''mi bevri le dakli .ijeseri'abo tu'e mi bevri le gerku .ijadu'ibo mi bevri le mlatu [tu'u]'''
:<code>I carry the sack. And [effect] (I carry the dog. And/or [equal] I carry the cat.)</code>
:''I carry the sack. As a result I carry the dog or I carry the cat, equally.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qmRL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qmRL}}
{{judri|c9e11d7}}
:'''mi bevri le dakli gi'eseri'ake bevri le gerku gi'adu'ibo bevri le mlatu [ke'e]'''
:<code>I carry the sack and [effect] (carry the dog and/or [equal] carry the cat).</code>
:''I carry the sack and as a result carry the dog or carry the cat equally.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMSb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMSb}}
{{ind|example|carry sack|example}}
{{judri|c9e11d8}}
:'''mi bevri le dakli .eseri'ake le gerku .adu'ibo le mlatu [ke'e]'''
:<code>I carry the sack and [effect] (the cat and/or [equal] the dog).</code>
:''I carry the sack, and as a result the cat or the dog equally.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-qMRB}}, the {{vla|tu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|tu'u}} brackets are the equivalent of the {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} brackets in {{lex|example-random-id-qmRL}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qMSb}}, because {{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} cannot extend across more than one sentence. It would also be possible to change the 
:{{jbo|.ijeseri'abo}} to 
:{{jbo|.ije seri'a}}, which would show that the {{vla|tu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|tu'u}} portion was an effect, but would not pin down the 
:{{jbo|mi bevri le dakli}} portion as the cause. It is legal for a modal (or a tense; See {{lch|chapter-tenses}}) to modify the whole of a {{vla|tu'e}}&hellip;{{vla|tu'u}} construct.

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o|mixed modal connection with}} Note: The uses of modals discussed in this section are applicable both to BAI modals and to 
:{{jbo|fi'o-}} plus-selbri modals.

{{ssp|section-modal-jai}}
==Modal conversion: JAI==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''jai'''	JAI	''modal conversion''
'''fai'''	FA	''modal place structure tag''
</tab>

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|BAI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|SE selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion|swapping with modal place}} So far, conversion of numbered bridi places with SE and the addition of modal places with BAI have been two entirely separate operations. However, it is possible to convert a selbri in such a way that, rather than exchanging two numbered places, a modal place is made into a numbered place. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-KMMX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KMMX}}
{{judri|c9e12d1}}
:'''mi cusku bau la lojban.'''
:<code>I express [something] in-language Lojban.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|place structure|effect of modal conversion on}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion|modal}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal conversion|place structure of}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal conversion|grammar of}} has an explicit x1 place occupied by {{vla|mi}} and an explicit {{vla|bau}} place occupied by 
:{{jbo|la lojban.}} To exchange these two, we use a modal conversion operator consisting of 
{{vla|jai}} (of selma'o JAI) followed by the modal cmavo. Thus, the modal conversion of {{lex|example-random-id-KMMX}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KjyW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KjyW}}
{{judri|c9e12d2}}
:'''la lojban. jai bau cusku fai mi'''
:<code>Lojban is-the-language-of-expression used-by me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|fai|as allowing access to original first place in modal conversion}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal conversion|access to original first place with fai}} In {{lex|example-random-id-KjyW}}, the modal place 
:{{jbo|la lojban.}} has become the x1 place of the new selbri 
:{{jbo|jai bau cusku}}. What has happened to the old x1 place? There is no numbered place for it to move to, so it moves to a special “unnumbered place” marked by the tag {{vla|fai}} of selma'o FA.

{{ind|general-imported|fai|effect on numbering of place structure places}} Note: For the purposes of place numbering, {{vla|fai}} behaves like {{vla|fi'a}}; it does not affect the numbering of the other places around it.

{{ind|general-imported|modal conversions|in descriptions}} Like SE conversions, JAI conversions are especially convenient in descriptions. We may refer to “the language of an expression” as 
:{{jbo|le jai bau cusku}}, for example.

{{ind|general-imported|modal conversion|with no modal specified}}  {{ind|general-imported|jai without modal|meaning}} In addition, it is grammatical to use {{vla|jai}} without a following modal. This usage is not related to modals, but is explained here for completeness. The effect of {{vla|jai}} by itself is to send the x1 place, which should be an abstraction, into the {{vla|fai}} position, and to raise one of the sumti from the abstract sub-bridi into the x1 place of the main bridi. This feature is discussed in more detail in {{ls|section-sumti-raising}}. The following two examples mean the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMsd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMsd}}
{{judri|c9e12d3}}
:'''le nu mi lebna le cukta cu se krinu le nu mi viska le cukta'''
:<code>The event-of (I take the book) is-justified-by the event-of (I see the book).</code>
:''My taking the book is justified by my seeing it.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMse}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMse}}
{{judri|c9e12d4}}
:'''mi jai se krinu le nu mi viska le cukta kei [fai le nu mi lebna le cukta]'''
:<code>I am-justified by the event-of (I see the book) [namely, the event-of (I take the book)]</code>
:''I am justified in taking the book by seeing the book.''

{{ind|general-imported|modal conversion without modal|as vague}} {{lex|example-random-id-qMse}}, with the bracketed part omitted, allows us to say that “I am justified” whereas in fact it is my action that is justified. This construction is vague, but useful in representing natural-language methods of expression.

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o|and modal conversion}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal conversion with fi'o}} Note: The uses of modals discussed in this section are applicable both to BAI modals and to 
:{{jbo|fi'o-}} plus-selbri modals.

{{ssp|section-modal-negation}}
==Modal negation==
{{ind|general-imported|modals|negation of}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation of modals}} Negation is explained in detail in {{lch|chapter-negation}}. There are two forms of negation in Lojban: contradictory and scalar negation. Contradictory negation expresses what is false, whereas scalar negation says that some alternative to what has been stated is true. A simple example is the difference between “John didn't go to Paris” (contradictory negation) and “John went to (somewhere) other than Paris” (scalar negation).

{{ind|general-imported|modals|contradictory negation of}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation of modals|contradictory}} Contradictory negation involving BAI cmavo is performed by appending 
:{{jbo|-nai}} (of selma'o NAI) to the BAI. A common use of modals with 
:{{jbo|-nai}} is to deny a causal relationship:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ej84}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ej84}}
{{judri|c9e13d1}}
:'''mi nelci do mu'inai le nu do nelci mi'''
:''I like you, but not because you like me.''

{{ind|general-imported|contradictory negation of modals|explanation of meaning}} {{lex|example-random-id-ej84}} denies that the relationship between my liking you (which is asserted) and your liking me (which is not asserted) is one of motivation. Nothing is said about whether you like me or not, merely that that hypothetical liking is not the motivation for my liking you.

{{ind|general-imported|modals|scalar negation of}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation of modals|scalar}} Scalar negation is achieved by prefixing {{vla|na'e}} (of selma'o NAhE), or any of the other cmavo of NAhE, to the BAI cmavo.

{{dsp|example-random-id-9WC5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9WC5}}
{{ind|example|plant grows|example}}
{{judri|c9e13d2}}
:'''le spati cu banro na'emu'i le nu do djacu dunda fi le spati'''
:<code>The plant grows other-than-motivated-by the event-of you water-give to the plant.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|scalar negation of modals|explanation of meaning}} {{lex|example-random-id-9WC5}} says that the relationship between the plant's growth and your watering it is not one of motivation: the plant is not motivated to grow, as plants are not something which can have motivation as a rule. Implicitly, some other relationship between watering and growth exists, but {{lex|example-random-id-9WC5}} doesn't say what it is (presumably {{vla|ri'a}}).

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o modals|negation of by negating selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation of fi'o modals|by negating selbri}} Note: Modals made with {{vla|fi'o}} plus a selbri cannot be negated directly. The selbri can itself be negated either with contradictory or with scalar negation, however.

{{ssp|section-sticky-modals}}
==Sticky modals==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ki'''	KI	''stickiness flag''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|modals|making sticky}}  {{ind|general-imported|modals|making long-scope}}  {{ind|general-imported|sticky modals|definition}} Like tenses, modals can be made persistent from the bridi in which they appear to all following bridi. The effect of this “stickiness” is to make the modal, along with its following sumti, act as if it appeared in every successive bridi. Stickiness is put into effect by following the modal (but not any following sumti) with the cmavo {{vla|ki}} of selma'o KI. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-1UGf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1UGf}}
{{judri|c9e14d1}}
:'''mi tavla bau la lojban. bai ki tu'a la frank. .ibabo mi tavla bau la gliban.'''
:<code>I speak in-language Lojban compelled-by some-property-of Frank. Afterward, I speak in-language English.</code>

means the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-txFr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-txFr}}
{{judri|c9e14d2}}
:'''mi tavla bau la lojban. bai tu'a la frank. .ibabo mi tavla bau la gliban. bai tu'a la frank.'''
:<code>I speak in-language Lojban compelled-by some-property-of Frank. Afterward, I speak in-language English compelled-by some-property-of Frank.</code>

In {{lex|example-random-id-1UGf}}, {{vla|bai}} is made sticky, and so Frank's compelling is made applicable to every following bridi. {{vla|bau}} is not sticky, and so the language may vary from bridi to bridi, and if not specified in a particular bridi, no assumption can safely be made about its value.

{{ind|general-imported|sticky modals|canceling}} To cancel stickiness, use the form 
:{{jbo|BAI ki ku}}, which stops any modal value for the specified BAI from being passed to the next bridi. To cancel stickiness for all modals simultaneously, and also for any sticky tenses that exist ( {{vla|ki}} is used for both modals and tenses), use {{vla|ki}} by itself, either before the selbri or (in the form 
:{{jbo|ki ku}}) anywhere in the bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sYdo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sYdo}}
{{judri|c9e14d3}}
:'''mi ki tavla'''
:''I speak (no implication about language or compulsion).''

{{ind|general-imported|fi'o|proscribed for sticky modals}}  {{ind|general-imported|sticky modals|fi'o proscribed from}} Note: Modals made with {{vla|fi'o}}-plus-selbri cannot be made sticky. This is an unfortunate, but unavoidable, restriction.

{{ssp|section-connected-modals}}
==Logical and non-logical connection of modals==

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of modals}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|of modals}} Logical and non-logical connectives are explained in detail in {{lch|chapter-connectives}}. For the purposes of this chapter, it suffices to point out that a logical (or non-logical) connection between two bridi which differ only in a modal can be reduced to a single bridi with a connective between the modals. As a result, {{lex|example-random-id-qMsx}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qMte}} mean the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMsx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMsx}}
{{judri|c9e15d1}}
:'''la frank. bajra seka'a le zdani .ije la frank. bajra teka'a le zdani'''
:<code>Frank runs with-destination the house. And Frank runs with-origin the house.</code>
:''Frank runs to the house, and Frank runs from the house.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qMte}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qMte}}
{{judri|c9e15d2}}
:'''la frank. bajra seka'a je teka'a le zdani'''
:<code>Frank runs with-destination and with-origin the house.</code>
:''Frank runs to and from the house.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|je}} Neither example implies whether a single act, or two acts, of running is referred to. To compel the sentence to refer to a single act of running, you can use the form:

{{dsp|example-random-id-b0LW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-b0LW}}
{{judri|c9e15d3}}
:'''la frank. bajra seka'a le zdani ce'e teka'a le zdani'''
:<code>Frank runs with-destination the house [joined-to] with-origin the-house.</code>

The cmavo {{vla|ce'e}} creates a termset containing two terms (termsets are explained in {{lch|chapter-connectives}} and {{lch|chapter-quantifiers}}). When a termset contains more than one modal tag derived from a single BAI, the convention is that the two tags are derived from a common event.

{{ssp|section-irregular-BAI}}
==CV'V cmavo of selma'o BAI with irregular forms==
{{ind|general-imported|modal cmavo|regular form for derivation}} There are 65 cmavo of selma'o BAI, of which all but one ( {{vla|do'e}}, discussed in 
{{ls|section-BAI}}), are derived directly from selected gismu. Of these 64 cmavo, 36 are entirely regular and have the form CV'V, where C is the first consonant of the corresponding gismu, and the Vs are the two vowels of the gismu. The remaining BAI cmavo, which are irregular in one way or another, are listed in the table below. The table is divided into sub-tables according to the nature of the exception; some cmavo appear in more than one sub-table, and are so noted.
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''cmavo'''	gismu	''comments''

'''gau'''		''gasnu''

'''mau'''	zmadu	''uses 2nd consonant of gismu''
'''koi'''		''korbi''

{{ssp|section-all-BAI}}
==Complete table of BAI cmavo with rough English equivalents==
{{ind|general-imported|modal cmavo table|format of}}  {{ind|general-imported|modal cmavo|table with English equivalents}} The following table shows all the cmavo belonging to selma'o BAI, and has five columns. The first column is the cmavo itself; the second column is the gismu linked to it. The third column gives an English phrase which indicates the meaning of the cmavo; and the fourth column indicates its meaning when preceded by {{vla|se}}.

For those cmavo with meaningful {{vla|te}}, {{vla|ve}}, and even {{vla|xe}} conversions (depending on the number of places of the underlying gismu), the meanings of these are shown on one or two extra rows following the primary row for that cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|modal cmavo|basis in gismu place structure}} It should be emphasized that the place structures of the gismu control the meanings of the BAI cmavo. The English phrases shown here are only suggestive, and are often too broad or too narrow to correctly specify what the acceptable range of uses for the modal tag are.
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ba'i'''	basti	replaced by	''instead of''
'''bai'''	bapli	compelled by	''compelling''
'''bau'''	bangu	in language	''in language of''
'''be'i'''	benji	sent by	''transmitting''

The lujvo {{vla|tamsmi}} on which {{vla|tai}} is based is derived from the tanru {{jbo|tarmi simsa}} and has the place structure:

:{{vla|tamsmi}} = ''x1 has form x2, similar in form to x3 in property/quality x4''

This lujvo is employed because {{vla|tarmi}} does not have a place structure useful for the modal's purpose.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{csp|chapter-tenses}}
=Imaginary Journeys: The Lojban Space/Time Tense System=
{{image|chapter-tenses-picture|The picture for chapter 10|CLL-chapter-tenses.gif}}
{{ssp|section-tenses-introduction}}
==Introductory==
{{ind|general-imported|tense|explanation of presentation method}} This chapter attempts to document and explain the space/time tense system of Lojban. It does not attempt to answer all questions of the form “How do I say such-and-such (an English tense) in Lojban?” Instead, it explores the Lojban tense system from the inside, attempting to educate the reader into a Lojbanic viewpoint. Once the overall system is understood and the resources that it makes available are familiar, the reader should have some hope of using appropriate tense constructs and being correctly understood.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|Lojban contrasted with native languages}} The system of Lojban tenses presented here may seem really complex because of all the pieces and all the options; indeed, this chapter is the longest one in this book. But tense is in fact complex in every language. In your native language, the subtleties of tense are intuitive. In foreign languages, you are seldom taught the entire system until you have reached an advanced level. Lojban tenses are extremely systematic and productive, allowing you to express subtleties based on what they mean rather than on how they act similarly to English tenses. This chapter concentrates on presenting an intuitive approach to the meaning of Lojban tense words and how they may be creatively and productively combined.

{{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|Lojban contrasted with English in necessity}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|as mandatory in English}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|real relationship to time in English}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|historical definition}} What is “tense”? Historically, “tense” is the attribute of verbs in English and related languages that expresses the time of the action. In English, three tenses are traditionally recognized, conventionally called the past, the present, and the future. There are also a variety of compound tenses used in English. However, there is no simple relationship between the form of an English tense and the time actually expressed:

<!-- FIXME: should these be in an <example>? if so, will any random id work? -->
:''I go to London tomorrow.''
:''I will go to London tomorrow.''
:''I am going to London tomorrow.''

all mean the same thing, even though the first sentence uses the present tense; the second, the future tense; and the third, a compound tense usually called “present progressive”. Likewise, a newspaper headline says “JONES DIES”, although it is obvious that the time referred to must be in the past. Tense is a mandatory category of English: every sentence must be marked for tense, even if in a way contrary to logic, because every main verb has a tense marker built into to it. By contrast, Lojban brivla have no implicit tense marker attached to them.

{{ind|general-imported|elided tense|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|space location|as part of tense system (see also tense|spatial tense)}}  {{ind|general-imported|time|as part of tense system (see also tense|temporal tense)}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense system|and space location}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense system|and space location}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|selbri types applicable to}} In Lojban, the concept of tense extends to every selbri, not merely the verb-like ones. In addition, tense structures provide information about location in space as well as in time. All tense information is optional in Lojban: a sentence like:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cKSK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cKSK}}
{{judri|c10e1d1}}
{{ind|example|go to market|example}} 
:'''mi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I go-to the market.</code>
can be understood as:
:''I went to the market.''
:''I am going to the market.''
:''I have gone to the market.''
:''I will go to the market.''
:''I continually go to the market.''
as well as many other possibilities: context resolves which is correct.

{{ind|general-imported|cu|effect of tense specification}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense specification|effect on elidability of terminators}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense specification|effect on &quot;cu&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|position of in sentence}} The placement of a tense construct within a Lojban bridi is easy: right before the selbri. It goes immediately after the {{vla|cu}}, and can in fact always replace the {{vla|cu}} (although in very complex sentences the rules for eliding terminators may be changed as a result). In the following examples, {{vla|pu}} is the tense marker for “past time”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nFgv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nFgv}}
{{judri|c10e1d2}}
<!-- FIXME: not really a glossing situation -->
:'''mi cu pu klama le zarci'''
:'''mi pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I in-the-past go-to the market.</code>
:''I went to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|ku|with tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|with ku}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|position in sentence alternative}} It is also possible to put the tense somewhere else in the bridi by adding {{vla|ku}} after it. This {{vla|ku}} is an elidable terminator, but it's almost never possible to actually elide it except at the end of the bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5V3Y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5V3Y}}
{{judri|c10e1d3}}
:'''puku mi klama le zarci'''
:<code>In-the-past I go-to the market.</code>
:''Earlier, I went to the market.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-DpEI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DpEI}}
{{judri|c10e1d4}}
:'''mi klama puku le zarci'''
:<code>I go-to in-the-past the market.</code>
:''I went earlier to the market.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-0f11}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0f11}}
{{judri|c10e1d5}}
:'''mi klama le zarci pu [ku]'''
:<code>I go-to the market in-the-past.</code>
:''I went to the market earlier.''

{{ind|general-imported|tense|emphasizing by position in sentence}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|effect of different position in sentence}} {{lex|example-random-id-nFgv}} through {{lex|example-random-id-0f11}} are different only in emphasis. Abnormal order, such as {{lex|example-random-id-5V3Y}} through {{lex|example-random-id-0f11}} exhibit, adds emphasis to the words that have been moved; in this case, the tense cmavo {{vla|pu}}. Words at either end of the sentence tend to be more noticeable.

{{ssp|section-spatial-tenses}}
==Spatial tenses: FAhA and VA==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''vi'''	VA	''short distance''
'''va'''	VA	''medium distance''
'''vu'''	VA	''long distance''

'''zu'a'''	FAhA	''left''
'''ri'u'''	FAhA	''right''
'''ga'u'''	FAhA	''up''
'''ni'a'''	FAhA	''down''
'''ca'u'''	FAhA	''front''
'''ne'i'''	FAhA	''within''
'''be'a'''	FAhA	''north of''
</tab>

(The complete list of FAhA cmavo can be found in {{ls|section-tense-selmaho-summary}}.)

Why is this section about spatial tenses rather than the more familiar time tenses of 
{{ls|section-tenses-introduction}}, asks the reader? Because the model to be used in explaining both will be easier to grasp for space than for time. The explanation of time tenses will resume in 
{{ls|section-temporal-tenses}}.

{{ind|general-imported|temporal tense elision|compared with spatial tense elision in meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|compared with spatial tense in elidability}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|compared with temporal tense in elidability}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|as optional in English}} English doesn't have mandatory spatial tenses. Although there are plenty of ways in English of showing where an event happens, there is absolutely no need to do so. Considering this fact may give the reader a feel for what the optional Lojban time tenses are like. From the Lojban point of view, space and time are interchangeable, although they are not treated identically.

{{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|distance|specification with VA}}  {{ind|general-imported|VA selma'o|and distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|as an imaginary journey}}  {{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|and spatial tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|definition}} Lojban specifies the spatial tense of a bridi (the place at which it occurs) by using words from selma'o FAhA and VA to describe an imaginary journey from the speaker to the place referred to. FAhA cmavo specify the direction taken in the journey, whereas VA cmavo specify the distance gone. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hNAJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hNAJ}}
{{judri|c10e2d1}}
:'''le nanmu va batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [medium distance] bites the dog.</code>
:''Over there the man is biting the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|reference frame}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|referent of}}  {{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|ending point}}  {{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|starting point}}  {{ind|general-imported|man biting dog}} What is at a medium distance? The event referred to by the bridi: the man biting the dog. What is this event at a medium distance from? The speaker's location. We can understand the {{vla|va}} as saying: “If you want to get from the speaker's location to the location of the bridi, journey for a medium distance (in some direction unspecified).” This “imaginary journey” can be used to understand not only {{lex|example-random-id-hNAJ}}, but also every other spatial tense construct.

{{ind|general-imported|direction|specification with FAhA}}  {{ind|general-imported|FAhA selma'o|and direction}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|direction}} Suppose you specify a direction with a FAhA cmavo, rather than a distance with a VA cmavo:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5Qxr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5Qxr}}
{{judri|c10e2d2}}
:'''le nanmu zu'a batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [left] bites the dog.</code>

Here the imaginary journey is again from the speaker's location to the location of the bridi, but it is now performed by going to the left (in the speaker's reference frame) for an unspecified distance. So a reasonable translation is:

To my left, the man bites the dog.

The “my” does not have an explicit equivalent in the Lojban, because the speaker's location is understood as the starting point.

{{ind|general-imported|VA selma'o|relation of words to ti|ta, tu}}  {{ind|general-imported|zu'a|derivation of word}} (Etymologically, by the way, {{vla|zu'a}} is derived from {{vla|zunle}}, the gismu for “left”, whereas {{vla|vi}}, {{vla|va}}, and {{vla|vu}} are intended to be reminiscent of {{vla|ti}}, {{vla|ta}}, and {{vla|tu}}, the demonstrative pronouns “this-here”, “that-there”, and “that-yonder”.)

{{ind|general-imported|distance|order of relative to direction in spatial tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|direction|order of relative to distance in spatial tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tenses|order of direction and distance specifications}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|order of distance specification in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|order of direction specification in}} What about specifying both a direction and a distance? The rule here is that the direction must come before the distance:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LEIm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LEIm}}
{{judri|c10e2d3}}
:'''le nanmu zu'avi batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [left] [short distance] bites the dog.</code>
:''Slightly to my left, the man bites the dog.''

As explained in {{ls|section-tenses-introduction}}, it would be perfectly correct to use {{vla|ku}} to move this tense to the beginning or the end of the sentence to emphasize it:

{{dsp|example-random-id-uCGa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-uCGa}}
{{judri|c10e2d4}}
:'''zu'aviku le nanmu cu batci le gerku'''
:<code>[Left] [short distance] the man bites the dog.</code>
:''Slightly to my left, the man bites the dog.''

{{ssp|section-compound-spatial-tenses}}
==Compound spatial tenses==
{{ind|general-imported|compound tense|definition}} Humph, says the reader: this talk of “imaginary journeys” is all very well, but what's the point of it? &ndash; {{vla|zu'a}} means “on the left” and {{vla|vi}} means “nearby”, and there's no more to be said. The imaginary-journey model becomes more useful when so-called compound tenses are involved. A compound tense is exactly like a simple tense, but has several FAhAs run together:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rWtP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rWtP}}
{{judri|c10e3d1}}
{{ind|example|manhole|example}} 
:'''le nanmu ga'u zu'a batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [up] [left] bites the dog.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|stages of in compound tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound spatial tense|explanation of}} The proper interpretation of {{lex|example-random-id-rWtP}} is that the imaginary journey has two stages: first move from the speaker's location upward, and then to the left. A translation might read:

Left of a place above me, the man bites the dog.

(Perhaps the speaker is at the bottom of a manhole, and the dog-biting is going on at the edge of the street.)

{{ind|general-imported|compound tense ordering|Lojban contrasted with English}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound tense|Lojban contrasted with English in order of specification}} In the English translation, the keywords “left” and “above” occur in reverse order to the Lojban order. This effect is typical of what happens when we “unfold” Lojban compound tenses into their English equivalents, and shows why it is not very useful to try to memorize a list of Lojban tense constructs and their colloquial English equivalents.

The opposite order also makes sense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-d1gU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-d1gU}}
{{judri|c10e3d2}}
:'''le nanmu zu'a ga'u batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [left] [up] bites the dog.</code>
:''Above a place to the left of me, the man bites the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|compound spatial tense|effect of different ordering}} In ordinary space, the result of going up and then to the left is the same as that of going left and then up, but such a simple relationship does not apply in all environments or to all directions: going south, then east, then north may return one to the starting point, if that point is the North Pole.

{{ind|general-imported|compound spatial tense|with direction and distance}} Each direction can have a distance following:

{{dsp|example-random-id-G9at}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-G9at}}
{{judri|c10e3d3}}
:'''le nanmu zu'avi ga'uvu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [left] [short distance] [up] [long distance] bites the dog.</code>
:''Far above a place slightly to the left of me, the man bites the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|compound spatial tense|beginning with distance only}} A distance can also come at the beginning of the tense construct, without any specified direction. ( {{lex|example-random-id-hNAJ}}, with VA alone, is really a special case of this rule when no directions at all follow.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-9Tpz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9Tpz}}
{{judri|c10e3d4}}
:'''le nanmu vi zu'a batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [short distance] [left] bites the dog.</code>
:''Left of a place near me, the man bites the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|compound spatial tense|as direction with-or-without distance}} Any number of directions may be used in a compound tense, with or without specified distances for each:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mqTU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mqTU}}
{{judri|c10e3d5}}
:'''le nanmu ca'uvi ni'ava ri'uvu ne'i batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [front] [short] [down] [medium] [right] [long] [within] bites the dog.</code>
:''Within a place a long distance to the right of a place which is a medium distance downward from a place a short distance in front of me, the man bites the dog.''

Whew! It's a good thing tense constructs are optional: having to say all that could certainly be painful. Note, however, how much shorter the Lojban version of {{lex|example-random-id-mqTU}} is than the English version.

{{ssp|section-temporal-tenses}}
==Temporal tenses: PU and ZI==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''pu'''	PU	''past''
'''ca'''	PU	''present''
'''ba'''	PU	''future''

'''zi'''	ZI	''short time distance''
'''za'''	ZI	''medium time distance''
'''zu'''	ZI	''long time distance''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|order relative to spatial}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|order relative to temporal}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|rationale for relative order of temporal and spatial in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|order of temporal and spatial in}}  {{ind|general-imported|ZI selma'o|compared with VA}}  {{ind|general-imported|PU selma'o|compared with FAhA}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tenses|compared with spatial tenses}} Now that the reader understands spatial tenses, there are only two main facts to understand about temporal tenses: they work exactly like the spatial tenses, with selma'o PU and ZI standing in for FAhA and VA; and when both spatial and temporal tense cmavo are given in a single tense construct, the temporal tense is expressed first. (If space could be expressed before or after time at will, then certain constructions would be ambiguous.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-ameb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ameb}}
{{judri|c10e4d1}}
:'''le nanmu pu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [past] bites the dog.</code>
:''The man bit the dog.''

means that to reach the dog-biting, you must take an imaginary journey through time, moving towards the past an unspecified distance. (Of course, this journey is even more imaginary than the ones talked about in the previous sections, since time-travel is not an available option.)

{{ind|general-imported|space|contrasted with time in number of directions}}  {{ind|general-imported|time|contrasted with space in number of directions}} Lojban recognizes three temporal directions: {{vla|pu}} for the past, {{vla|ca}} for the present, and {{vla|ba}} for the future. (Etymologically, these derive from the corresponding gismu {{vla|purci}}, {{vla|cabna}}, and {{vla|balvi}}. See {{ls|section-tenses-vs-modals}} for an explanation of the exact relationship between the cmavo and the gismu.) There are many more spatial directions, since there are FAhA cmavo for both absolute and relative directions as well as “direction-like relationships” like “surrounding”, “within”, “touching”, etc. (See {{ls|section-tense-selmaho-summary}} for a complete list.) But there are really only two directions in time: forward and backward, toward the future and toward the past. Why, then, are there three cmavo of selma'o PU?

{{ind|general-imported|tense|as subjective perception}}  {{ind|general-imported|bu'u|compared with ca}}  {{ind|general-imported|ca|compared with bu'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|ca|rational for}} The reason is that tense is subjective: human beings perceive space and time in a way that does not necessarily agree with objective measurements. We have a sense of “now” which includes part of the objective past and part of the objective future, and so we naturally segment the time line into three parts. The Lojban design recognizes this human reality by providing a separate time-direction cmavo for the “zero direction”, Similarly, there is a FAhA cmavo for the zero space direction: {{vla|bu'u}}, which means something like “coinciding”.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|as observer-based}}  {{ind|general-imported|relativity theory|relation to Lojban tense system}} (Technical note for readers conversant with relativity theory: The Lojban time tenses reflect time as seen by the speaker, who is assumed to be a “point-like observer” in the relativistic sense: they do not say anything about physical relationships of relativistic interval, still less about implicit causality. The nature of tense is not only subjective but also observer-based.)

Here are some examples of temporal tenses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qDsX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qDsX}}
{{judri|c10e4d2}}
:'''le nanmu puzi batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [past] [short distance] bites the dog.</code>
:''A short time ago, the man bit the dog.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qDt1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qDt1}}
{{judri|c10e4d3}}
:'''le nanmu pu pu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [past] [past] bites the dog.</code>
:<code>Earlier than an earlier time than now, the man bit the dog.</code>
:''The man had bitten the dog.''
:''The man had been biting the dog.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qDtg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qDtg}}
{{judri|c10e4d4}}
:'''le nanmu ba puzi batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [future] [past] [short] bites the dog.</code>
:<code>Shortly earlier than some time later than now, the man will bite the dog.</code>
:<code>Soon before then, the man will have bitten the dog.</code>
:''The man will have just bitten the dog.''
:''The man will just have been biting the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|compound temporal tense|beginning with distance only}} What about the analogue of an initial VA without a direction? Lojban does allow an initial ZI with or without following PUs:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qDu0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qDu0}}
{{judri|c10e4d5}}
{{ind|example|nearby in time|example}} 
:'''le nanmu zi pu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [short] [past] bites the dog.</code>
:''Before a short time from or before now, the man bit or will bite the dog.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qDw0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qDw0}}
{{judri|c10e4d6}}
:'''le nanmu zu batci le gerku'''
