:<code>The man [long] bites the dog.</code>
:''A long time from or before now, the man will bite or bit the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|unspecified direction|temporal contrasted with in spatial}} {{lex|example-random-id-qDu0}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qDw0}} are perfectly legitimate, but may not be very much used: {{vla|zi}} by itself signals an event that happens at a time close to the present, but without saying whether it is in the past or the future. A rough translation might be “about now, but not exactly now”.

Because we can move in any direction in space, we are comfortable with the idea of events happening in an unspecified space direction ( “nearby” or “far away”), but we live only from past to future, and the idea of an event which happens “nearby in time” is a peculiar one. Lojban provides lots of such possibilities that don't seem all that useful to English-speakers, even though you can put them together productively; this fact may be a limitation of English.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|with both temporal and spatial}} Finally, here are examples which combine temporal and spatial tense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-vtUw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-vtUw}}
{{judri|c10e4d7}}
{{ind|example|long ago and far away|example}} 
:'''le nanmu puzu vu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The man [past] [long time] [long space] bites the dog.</code>
:''Long ago and far away, the man bit the dog.''

Alternatively,

{{dsp|example-random-id-Jsw5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Jsw5}}
{{judri|c10e4d8}}
:'''le nanmu batci le gerku puzuvuku'''
:<code>The man bites the dog [past] [long time] [long space].</code>
:''The man bit the dog long ago and far away.''

{{ssp|section-interval-sizes}}
==Interval sizes: VEhA and ZEhA==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ve'i'''	VEhA	''short space interval''
'''ve'a'''	VEhA	''medium space interval''
'''ve'u'''	VEhA	''long space interval''

'''ze'i'''	ZEhA	''short time interval''
'''ze'a'''	ZEhA	''medium time interval''
'''ze'u'''	ZEhA	''long time interval''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|tense|interval contrasted with point}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|point contrasted with interval}} So far, we have considered only events that are usually thought of as happening at a particular point in space and time: a man biting a dog at a specified place and time. But Lojbanic events may be much more “spread out” than that: 
:{{jbo|mi vasxu}} (I breathe) is something which is true during the whole of my life from birth to death, and over the entire part of the earth where I spend my life. The cmavo of VEhA (for space) and ZEhA (for time) can be added to any of the tense constructs we have already studied to specify the size of the space or length of the time over which the bridi is claimed to be true.

{{dsp|example-random-id-Pgzz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Pgzz}}
{{judri|c10e5d1}}
{{ind|example|child on ice|example}} 
:'''le verba ve'i cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [small space interval] walks-on the ice.</code>
:<code>In a small space, the child walks on the ice.</code>
:''The child walks about a small area of the ice.''

means that her walking was done in a small area. Like the distances, the interval sizes are classified only roughly as “small, medium, large”, and are relative to the context: a small part of a room might be a large part of a table in that room.

Here is an example using a time interval:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ap7g}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ap7g}}
{{judri|c10e5d2}}
:'''le verba ze'a cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [medium time interval] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''For a medium time, the child walks/walked/will walk on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|interval|relative order with direction and distance in tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|order of direction|distance and interval in}} Note that with no time direction word, {{lex|example-random-id-ap7g}} does not say when the walking happened: that would be determined by context. It is possible to specify both directions or distances and an interval, in which case the interval always comes afterward:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gHPI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gHPI}}
{{judri|c10e5d3}}
:'''le verba pu ze'a cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [past] [medium time interval] walks-on the ice.</code>
:<code>For a medium time, the child walked on the ice.</code>
:''The child walked on the ice for a while.''

{{ind|general-imported|interval direction|specifying}}  {{ind|general-imported|ca|meaning when following interval specification}}  {{ind|general-imported|direction|following interval in tense construct}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|followed by direction in tense construct}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|specifying relation of interval to point specified by direction and distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|specifying relation to point specified by direction and distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|relation of point specified by direction and distance to interval}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|relation of interval to point specified by direction and distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|relation to point specified by direction and distance}} In {{lex|example-random-id-gHPI}}, the relationship of the interval to the specified point in time or space is indeterminate. Does the interval start at the point, end at the point, or is it centered on the point? By adding an additional direction cmavo after the interval, this question can be conclusively answered:

{{dsp|example-random-id-q4Aw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-q4Aw}}
{{judri|c10e5d4}}
:'''mi ca ze'ica cusku dei'''
:<code>I [present] [short time interval - present] express this-utterance.</code>
:''I am now saying this sentence.''

{{ind|general-imported|interval size|as context-dependent}} means that for an interval starting a short time in the past and extending to a short time in the future, I am expressing the utterance which is {{lex|example-random-id-q4Aw}}. Of course, “short” is relative, as always in tenses. Even a long sentence takes up only a short part of a whole day; in a geological context, the era of 
<emphasis>Homo sapiens</emphasis> would only be a {{vla|ze'i}} interval.

By contrast,

{{dsp|example-random-id-imdX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-imdX}}
{{judri|c10e5d5}}
:'''mi ca ze'ipu cusku dei'''
:<code>I [present] [short time interval - past] express this-utterance.</code>
:''I have just been saying this sentence.''

{{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|with interval direction}}  {{ind|general-imported|pu|meaning when following interval specification}} means that for a short time interval extending from the past to the present I have been expressing {{lex|example-random-id-imdX}}. Here the imaginary journey starts at the present, lays down one end point of the interval, moves into the past, and lays down the other endpoint. Another example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AqvW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AqvW}}
{{judri|c10e5d6}}
:'''mi pu ze'aba citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [past] [medium time interval - future] eat my meal.</code>
:<code>For a medium time afterward, I ate my meal.</code>
:''I ate my meal for a while.''

With {{vla|ca}} instead of {{vla|ba}}, {{lex|example-random-id-AqvW}} becomes {{lex|example-random-id-a5dp}},

{{dsp|example-random-id-a5dp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-a5dp}}
{{judri|c10e5d7}}
:'''mi pu ze'aca citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [past] [medium time interval - present] eat my meal.</code>
:<code>For a medium time before and afterward, I ate my meal.</code>
:''I ate my meal for a while.''

because the interval would then be centered on the past moment rather than oriented toward the future of that moment. The colloquial English translations are the same &ndash; English is not well-suited to representing this distinction.

Here are some examples of the use of space intervals with and without specified directions:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Mrzt}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Mrzt}}
{{judri|c10e5d8}}
{{ind|example|fish on right|example}} 
:'''ta ri'u ve'i finpe'''
:<code>That-there [right] [short space interval] is-a-fish.</code>
:''That thing on my right is a fish.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-Mrzt}}, there is no equivalent in the colloquial English translation of the “small interval” which the fish occupies. Neither the Lojban nor the English expresses the orientation of the fish. Compare {{lex|example-random-id-AVU3}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AVU3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AVU3}}
{{judri|c10e5d9}}
:'''ta ri'u ve'ica'u finpe'''
:<code>That-there [right] [short space interval - front] is-a-fish.</code>
:''That thing on my right extending forwards is a fish.''

Here the space interval occupied by the fish extends from a point on my right to another point in front of the first point.

{{ssp|section-vagueness}}
==Vague intervals and non-specific tenses==
{{ind|general-imported|interval size|vague}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval size|unspecified}} What is the significance of failing to specify an interval size of the type discussed in 
{{ls|section-interval-sizes}}? The Lojban rule is that if no interval size is given, the size of the space or time interval is left vague by the speaker. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-naft}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-naft}}
{{judri|c10e6d1}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market.</code>

really means:

:''At a moment in the past, and possibly other moments as well, the event “I went to the market” was in progress.''
{{ind|general-imported|tense direction|implications on scope of event}}  {{ind|general-imported|past event|possible extension into present}} The vague or unspecified interval contains an instant in the speaker's past. However, there is no indication whether or not the whole interval is in the speaker's past! It is entirely possible that the interval during which the going-to-the-market is happening stretches into the speaker's present or even future.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|Lojban contrasted with English in implications of completeness}} {{lex|example-random-id-naft}} points up a fundamental difference between Lojban tenses and English tenses. An English past-tense sentence like “I went to the market” generally signifies that the going-to-the-market is entirely in the past; that is, that the event is complete at the time of speaking. Lojban {{vla|pu}} has no such implication.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|aorist}}  {{ind|general-imported|aorist|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|Classical Greek aorist tense|compared with Lojban tense}} This property of a past tense is sometimes called “aorist”, in reference to a similar concept in the tense system of Classical Greek. All of the Lojban tenses have the same property, however:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xQ0w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xQ0w}}
{{judri|c10e6d3}}
:'''le tricu ba crino'''
:<code>The tree [future] is-green.</code>
:''The tree will be green.''

{{ind|general-imported|future event|possible extension into present}} does not imply (as the colloquial English translation does) that the tree is not green now. The vague interval throughout which the tree is, in fact, green may have already started.

This general principle does not mean that Lojban has no way of indicating that a tree will be green but is not yet green. Indeed, there are several ways of expressing that concept: See {{ls|section-event-contours}} (event contours) and 
{{ls|section-connected-tenses}} (logical connection between tenses).

{{ssp|section-dimensionality}}
==Dimensionality: VIhA==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''vi'i'''	VIhA	''on a line''
'''vi'a'''	VIhA	''in an area''
'''vi'u'''	VIhA	''through a volume''
'''vi'e'''	VIhA	''throughout a space/time interval''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|three-dimensional}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|two-dimensional}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|one-dimensional}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|planar}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|linear}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|contrasted with temporal in dimensionality}} The cmavo of ZEhA are sufficient to express time intervals. One fundamental difference between space and time, however, is that space is multi-dimensional. Sometimes we want to say not only that something moves over a small interval, but also perhaps that it moves in a line. Lojban allows for this. I can specify that a motion “in a small space” is more specifically “in a short line”, “in a small area”, or “through a small volume”.

What about the child walking on the ice in {{lex|example-random-id-Pgzz}} through {{lex|example-random-id-gHPI}}? Given the nature of ice, probably the area interpretation is most sensible. I can make this assumption explicit with the appropriate member of selma'o VIhA:

{{dsp|example-random-id-vKp6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-vKp6}}
{{judri|c10e7d1}}
:'''le verba ve'a vi'a cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [medium space interval] [2-dimensional] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''In a medium-sized area, the child walks on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|size|order with dimensionality in spatial tense intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|dimensionality|order with size in spatial tense intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense intervals|order of size and dimensionality in}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense intervals|order of VEhA and VIhA in}} Space intervals can contain either VEhA or VIhA or both, but if both, VEhA must come first, as {{lex|example-random-id-vKp6}} shows.

{{ind|general-imported|dimensionality|of walking}}  {{ind|general-imported|dimensionality of interval|as subjective}} The reader may wish to raise a philosophical point here. (Readers who don't wish to, should skip this paragraph.) The ice may be two-dimensional, or more accurately its surface may be, but since the child is three-dimensional, her walking must also be. The subjective nature of Lojban tense comes to the rescue here: the action is essentially planar, and the third dimension of height is simply irrelevant to walking. Even walking on a mountain could be called 
{{vla|vi'a}}, because relatively speaking the mountain is associated with an essentially two-dimensional surface. Motion which is not confined to such a surface (e.g., flying, or walking through a three-dimensional network of tunnels, or climbing among mountains rather than on a single mountain) would be properly described with 
{{vla|vi'u}}. So the cognitive, rather than the physical, dimensionality controls the choice of VIhA cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|4-dimensional interaction with temporal tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|interaction with 4-dimensional spatial tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|futureward|as a spatial tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|pastward|as a spatial tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|space-time dimension for intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tense|four-dimensional}}  {{ind|general-imported|Einsteinian|space-time intervals with 4 dimensions}} VIhA has a member {{vla|vi'e}} which indicates a 4-dimensional interval, one that involves both space and time. This allows the spatial tenses to invade, to some degree, the temporal tenses; it is possible to make statements about space-time considered as an Einsteinian whole. (There are presently no cmavo of FAhA assigned to “pastward” and “futureward” considered as space rather than time directions &ndash; they could be added, though, if Lojbanists find space-time expression useful.) If a temporal tense cmavo is used in the same tense construct with a 
{{vla|vi'e}} interval, the resulting tense may be self-contradictory.

{{ssp|section-movement}}
==Movement in space: MOhI==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''mo'i'''	MOhI	''movement flag''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|movement specification|interaction with direction in tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|direction|interaction with movement specification in tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|expressing movement in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|static contrasted with moving}} All the information carried by the tense constructs so far presented has been presumed to be static: the bridi is occurring somewhere or other in space and time, more or less remote from the speaker. Suppose the truth of the bridi itself depends on the result of a movement, or represents an action being done while the speaker is moving? This too can be represented by the tense system, using the cmavo 
{{vla|mo'i}} (of selma'o MOhI) plus a spatial direction and optional distance; the direction now refers to a direction of motion rather than a static direction from the speaker.

{{ind|general-imported|on right|contrasted with toward right}}  {{ind|general-imported|toward right|contrasted with on right}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-d8yP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-d8yP}}
{{ind|example|toward my right|example}}
{{judri|c10e8d1}}
:'''le verba mo'i ri'u cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [movement] [right] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The child walks toward my right on the ice.''

This is quite different from:

{{dsp|example-random-id-abBF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-abBF}}
{{judri|c10e8d2}}
:'''le verba ri'u cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [right] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''To the right of me, the child walks on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|reference frame|specifying for direction tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|direction|reference frame for}}  {{ind|general-imported|reference frame for directions in tenses}} In either case, however, the reference frame for defining “right” and “left” is the speaker's, not the child's. This can be changed thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mfgA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mfgA}}
{{judri|c10e8d3}}
{{ind|example|toward her right|example}} 
:'''le verba mo'i ri'u cadzu le bisli ma'i vo'a'''
:<code>The child [movement] [right] walks on the ice in-reference-frame the-x1-place.</code>
:''The child walks toward her right on the ice.''
{{lex|example-random-id-mfgA}} is analogous to {{lex|example-random-id-d8yP}}. The cmavo {{vla|ma'i}} belongs to selma'o BAI (explained in 
{{ls|section-BAI}}), and allows specifying a reference frame.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|order of movement specification in}}  {{ind|general-imported|movement|order in tense constructs}} Both a regular and a {{vla|mo'i}}-flagged spatial tense can be combined, with the {{vla|mo'i}} construct coming last:

{{dsp|example-random-id-fusc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fusc}}
{{judri|c10e8d4}}
:'''le verba zu'avu mo'i ri'uvi cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [left] [long] [movement] [right] [short] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''Far to the left of me, the child walks a short distance toward my right on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|movement|with multiple directions}}  {{ind|general-imported|directions|multiple with movement}}  {{ind|general-imported|complex movements|expressing}} It is not grammatical to use multiple directions like 
:{{jbo|zu'a ca'u}} after {{vla|mo'i}}, but complex movements can be expressed in a separate bridi.

Here is an example of a movement tense on a bridi not inherently involving movement:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Avnq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Avnq}}
{{judri|c10e8d5}}
{{ind|example|eat in airplane|example}} 
:'''mi mo'i ca'uvu citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [movement] [front] [long] eat my meal.</code>
:''While moving a long way forward, I eat my meal.''

(Perhaps I am eating in an airplane.)

{{ind|general-imported|time travel}}  {{ind|general-imported|movement|time}} There is no parallel facility in Lojban at present for expressing movement in time &ndash; time travel &ndash; but one could be added easily if it ever becomes useful.

{{ssp|section-interval-properties}}
==Interval properties: TAhE and {{vla|roi}}==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''di'i'''	TAhE	''regularly''
'''na'o'''	TAhE	''typically''
'''ru'i'''	TAhE	''continuously''
'''ta'e'''	TAhE	''habitually''

'''di'inai'''	TAhE	''irregularly''
'''na'onai'''	TAhE	''atypically''
'''ru'inai'''	TAhE	''intermittently''
'''ta'enai'''	TAhE	''contrary to habit''

'''roi'''	ROI	''“n” times''
'''roinai'''	ROI	''other than “n” times''

'''ze'e'''	ZEhA	''whole time interval''
'''ve'e'''	VEhA	''whole space interval''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|spread of actions over}}  {{ind|general-imported|discrete|of tense intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|continuous|of tense intervals}} Consider Lojban bridi which express events taking place in time. Whether a very short interval (a point) or a long interval of time is involved, the event may not be spread consistently throughout that interval. Lojban can use the cmavo of selma'o TAhE to express the idea of continuous or non-continuous actions.

{{dsp|example-random-id-GCXM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GCXM}}
{{judri|c10e9d1}}
{{ind|example|attend school|example}} 
:'''mi puzu ze'u velckule'''
:<code>I [past] [long distance] [long interval] am-a-school-attendee (pupil).</code>
:''Long ago I attended school for a long time.''

probably does not mean that I attended school continuously throughout the whole of that long-ago interval. Actually, I attended school every day, except for school holidays. More explicitly,

{{dsp|example-random-id-JM1W}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JM1W}}
{{judri|c10e9d2}}
{{ind|example|regularly|example}}  
:'''mi puzu ze'u di'i velckule'''
:<code>I [past] [long distance] [long interval] [regularly] am-a-pupil.</code>
:''Long ago I regularly attended school for a long time.''

{{ind|general-imported|interval spread|mutually contrasted}} The four TAhE cmavo are differentiated as follows: {{vla|ru'i}} covers the entirety of the interval, 
{{vla|di'i}} covers the parts of the interval which are systematically spaced subintervals; 
{{vla|na'o}} covers part of the interval, but exactly which part is determined by context; 
{{vla|ta'e}} covers part of the interval, selected with reference to the behavior of the actor (who often, but not always, appears in the x1 place of the bridi).

{{ind|general-imported|interval spread|with unspecified interval}} Using TAhE does not require being so specific. Either the time direction or the time interval or both may be omitted (in which case they are vague). For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eb2h}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eb2h}}
{{judri|c10e9d3}}
:'''mi ba ta'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [future] [habitually] go-to the market.</code>
:<code>I will habitually go to the market.</code>
:''I will make a habit of going to the market.''

specifies the future, but the duration of the interval is indefinite. Similarly,

{{dsp|example-random-id-RQTF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RQTF}}
{{judri|c10e9d4}}
:'''mi na'o klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [typically] go-to the market.</code>
:''I typically go/went/will go to the market.''

illustrates an interval property in isolation. There are no distance or direction cmavo, so the point of time is vague; likewise, there is no interval cmavo, so the length of the interval during which these goings-to-the-market take place is also vague. As always, context will determine these vague values.

{{ind|general-imported|interval spread|expressing English &quot;intermittently&quot;}} “Intermittently” is the polar opposite notion to “continuously”, and is expressed not with its own cmavo, but by adding the negation suffix 
:{{jbo|-nai}} (which belongs to selma'o NAI) to {{vla|ru'i}}. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mvdN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mvdN}}
{{judri|c10e9d5}}
{{ind|example|intermittently|example}}  
:'''le verba ru'inai cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [continuously-not] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The child intermittently walks on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|interval spread|negation with nai}} As shown in the cmavo table above, all the cmavo of TAhE may be negated with 
:{{jbo|-nai}}; {{vla|ru'inai}} and {{vla|di'inai}} are probably the most useful.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|quantified}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantified temporal tense|definition}} An intermittent event can also be specified by counting the number of times during the interval that it takes place. The cmavo {{vla|roi}} (which belongs to selma'o ROI) can be appended to a number to make a quantified tense. Quantified tenses are common in English, but not so commonly named: they are exemplified by the adverbs “never”, “once”, “twice”, “thrice”, ... “always”, and by the related phrases “many times”, “a few times”, “too many times”, and so on. All of these are handled in Lojban by a number plus {{jbo|-roi}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdW2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdW2}}
{{judri|c10e9d6}}
{{ind|example|once|example}}  
:'''mi paroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [one time] go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market once.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdwP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdwP}}
{{judri|c10e9d7}}
:'''mi du'eroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [too-many times] go-to the market.</code>
:''I go to the market too often.''

{{ind|general-imported|temporal tense|quantified with direction}} With the quantified tense alone, we don't know whether the past, the present, or the future is intended, but of course the quantified tense need not stand alone:

{{dsp|example-random-id-TYve}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TYve}}
{{judri|c10e9d8}}
:'''mi pu reroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past] [two times] go-to the market.</code>
:''I went to the market twice.''

{{ind|general-imported|quantified temporal tense with direction|Lojban contrasted with English in implications}} The English is slightly over-specific here: it entails that both goings-to-the-market were in the past, which may or may not be true in the Lojban sentence, since the implied interval is vague. Therefore, the interval may start in the past but extend into the present or even the future.

{{ind|general-imported|quantified temporal tense|negating with nai}} Adding 
:{{jbo|-nai}} to {{vla|roi}} is also permitted, and has the meaning “other than (the number specified)”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rXXf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rXXf}}
{{judri|c10e9d9}}
{{ind|example|rat eats cheese|example}} 
:'''le ratcu reroinai citka le cirla'''
:<code>The rat [twice-not] eats the cheese.</code>
:''The rat eats the cheese other than twice.''

This may mean that the rat eats the cheese fewer times, or more times, or not at all.

{{ind|general-imported|whole time interval|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantified temporal tenses|&quot;once&quot; contrasted with &quot;only once&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantified temporal tenses|caveat on implication of}} It is necessary to be careful with sentences like {{lex|example-random-id-qdW2}} and {{lex|example-random-id-TYve}}, where a quantified tense appears without an interval. What {{lex|example-random-id-TYve}} really says is that during an interval of unspecified size, at least part of which was set in the past, the event of my going to the market happened twice. The example says nothing about what happened outside that vague time interval. This is often less than we mean. If we want to nail down that I went to the market once and only once, we can use the cmavo 
{{vla|ze'e}} which represents the “whole time interval”: conceptually, an interval which stretches from time's beginning to its end:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8WJS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8WJS}}
{{judri|c10e9d10}}
{{ind|example|only once|example}}  
:'''mi ze'e paroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [whole interval] [once] go-to the market.</code>

Since specifying no ZEhA leaves the interval vague, {{lex|example-random-id-TYve}} might in appropriate context mean the same as {{lex|example-random-id-8WJS}} after all &ndash; but {{lex|example-random-id-8WJS}} allows us to be specific when specificity is necessary.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|PU selma'o}}  
{{ind|general-imported|ze'eca|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ze'eba|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ze'epu|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ze'e|effect on following PU direction}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal direction|exception in meaning when following ze'e}} A PU cmavo following {{vla|ze'e}} has a slightly different meaning from one that follows another ZEhA cmavo. The compound cmavo 

:{{jbo|ze'epu}} signifies the interval stretching from the infinite past to the reference point (wherever the imaginary journey has taken you); 

:{{jbo|ze'eba}} is the interval stretching from the reference point to the infinite future. The remaining form, 

:{{jbo|ze'eca}}, makes specific the “whole of time” interpretation just given. These compound forms make it possible to assert that something has never happened without asserting that it never will.

{{dsp|example-random-id-gA7X}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gA7X}}
{{judri|c10e9d11}}
{{ind|example|have never|example}}  
:'''mi ze'epu noroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [whole interval] [past] [never] go-to the market.</code>
:''I have never gone to the market.''

says nothing about whether I might go in future.

{{ind|general-imported|quantified space}} The space equivalent of {{vla|ze'e}} is 
{{vla|ve'e}}, and it can be used in the same way with a quantified space tense: see 
{{ls|section-fehe}} for an explanation of space interval modifiers.

{{ssp|section-event-contours}}
==Event contours: ZAhO and {{vla|re'u}}==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''pu'o'''	ZAhO	''inchoative''
'''ca'o'''	ZAhO	''continuitive''
'''ba'o'''	ZAhO	''perfective''
'''co'a'''	ZAhO	''initiative''
'''co'u'''	ZAhO	''cessitive''
'''mo'u'''	ZAhO	''completitive''
'''za'o'''	ZAhO	''superfective''
'''co'i'''	ZAhO	''achievative''
'''de'a'''	ZAhO	''pausative''
'''di'a'''	ZAhO	''resumptive''

'''re'u'''	ROI	''ordinal tense''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|aspect|natural languages compared with respect to}}  {{ind|general-imported|aspect|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|resumptive event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|pausative event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|achievative event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|superfective event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|completitive event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|cessitive event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|initiative event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|perfective event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|continuitive event contour}}  {{ind|general-imported|inchoative event contour}} The cmavo of selma'o ZAhO express the Lojban version of what is traditionally called “aspect”. This is not a notion well expressed by English tenses, but many languages (including Chinese and Russian among Lojban's six source languages) consider it more important than the specification of mere position in time.

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|order with respect to TAhE and ROI}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|events|considered as a process}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|definition}} The “event contours” of selma'o ZAhO, with their bizarre keywords, represent the natural portions of an event considered as a process, an occurrence with an internal structure including a beginning, a middle, and an end. Since the keywords are scarcely self-explanatory, each ZAhO will be explained in detail here. Note that from the viewpoint of Lojban syntax, ZAhOs are interval modifiers like TAhEs or ROI compounds; if both are found in a single tense, the TAhE/ROI comes first and the ZAhO afterward. The imaginary journey described by other tense cmavo moves us to the portion of the event-as-process which the ZAhO specifies.

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|as characteristic portions of events}}  {{ind|general-imported|speaker-relative viewpoint|contrasted with event-relative viewpoint}}  {{ind|general-imported|event-relative viewpoint|contrasted with speaker-relative viewpoint}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|viewpoint of PU contrasted with viewpoint of ZAhO}}  {{ind|general-imported|PU tenses|contrasted with ZAhO tenses in viewpoint}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|as timeless in perspective}} It is important to understand that ZAhO cmavo, unlike the other tense cmavo, specify characteristic portions of the event, and are seen from an essentially timeless perspective. The “beginning” of an event is the same whether the event is in the speaker's present, past, or future. It is especially important not to confuse the speaker-relative viewpoint of the PU tenses with the event-relative viewpoint of the ZAhO tenses.

{{ind|general-imported|ca'o|derivation of word}}  {{ind|general-imported|ba'o|derivation of word}}  {{ind|general-imported|pu'o|derivation of word}} The cmavo {{vla|pu'o}}, {{vla|ca'o}}, and {{vla|ba'o}} (etymologically derived from the PU cmavo) refer to an event that has not yet begun, that is in progress, or that has ended, respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdwz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdwz}}
{{judri|c10e10d1}}
{{ind|example|on verge|example}}
:'''mi pu'o damba'''
:<code>I [inchoative] fight.</code>
:''I'm on the verge of fighting.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdX7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdX7}}
{{judri|c10e10d2}}
{{ind|example|continues|example}}
:'''la stiv. ca'o bacru'''
:<code>Steve [continuitive] utters.</code>
:''Steve continues to talk.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdxB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdxB}}
{{ind|example|finished|example}}
{{judri|c10e10d3}}
:'''le verba ba'o cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The child [perfective] walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The child is finished walking on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|tense direction|contrasted with event contours in implication of extent}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|contrasted with tense direction in implication of extent}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|implications on scope of event}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|perfective}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|continuitive}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|inchoative}} As discussed in {{ls|section-vagueness}}, the simple PU cmavo make no assumptions about whether the scope of a past, present, or future event extends into one of the other tenses as well. {{lex|example-random-id-qdwz}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qdxB}} illustrate that these ZAhO cmavo do make such assumptions possible: the event in 10.1 has not yet begun, definitively; likewise, the event in 10.3 is definitely over.

{{ind|general-imported|ba'o|as futureward of event}}  {{ind|general-imported|pu'o|as pastward of event}}  {{ind|general-imported|ba'o|explanation of derivation}}  {{ind|general-imported|pu'o|explanation of derivation}} Note that in {{lex|example-random-id-qdwz}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qdxB}}, {{vla|pu'o}} and {{vla|ba'o}} may appear to be reversed: {{vla|pu'o}}, although etymologically connected with {{vla|pu}}, is referring to a future event; whereas 
{{vla|ba'o}}, connected with {{vla|ba}}, is referring to a past event. This is the natural result of the event-centered view of ZAhO cmavo. The inchoative, or 
{{vla|pu'o}}, part of an event, is in the “pastward” portion of that event, when seen from the perspective of the event itself. It is only by inference that we suppose that {{lex|example-random-id-qdwz}} refers to the speaker's future: in fact, no PU tense is given, so the inchoative part of the event need not be coincident with the speaker's present: {{vla|pu'o}} is not necessarily, though in fact often is, the same as 
:{{jbo|ca pu'o}}.

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|cessative}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|initiative}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|division of the event into}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|points associated with}} The cmavo in {{lex|example-random-id-qdwz}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qdxB}} refer to spans of time. There are also two points of time that can be usefully associated with an event: the beginning, marked by {{vla|co'a}}, and the end, marked by {{vla|co'u}}. Specifically, {{vla|co'a}} marks the boundary between the {{vla|pu'o}} and {{vla|ca'o}} parts of an event, and {{vla|co'u}} marks the boundary between the {{vla|ca'o}} and {{vla|ba'o}} parts:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdxH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdxH}}
{{judri|c10e10d4}}
:'''mi ba co'a citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [future] [initiative] eat my meal.</code>
:''I will begin to eat my meal.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdY5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdY5}}
{{judri|c10e10d5}}
:'''mi pu co'u citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [past] [cessitive] eat my meal.</code>
:''I ceased eating my meal.''

Compare {{lex|example-random-id-qdxH}} with:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ChHI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ChHI}}
{{judri|c10e10d6}}
:'''mi ba di'i co'a bajra'''
:<code>I [future] [regularly] [initiative] run.</code>
:''I will regularly begin to run.''

which illustrates the combination of a TAhE with a ZAhO.

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|completitive}}  {{ind|general-imported|stop|contrasted with finish}}  {{ind|general-imported|finish|contrasted with stop}}  {{ind|general-imported|actual stop|contrasted with natural end}}  {{ind|general-imported|natural end|contrasted with actual stop}} A process can have two end points, one reflecting the “natural end” (when the process is complete) and the other reflecting the “actual stopping point” (whether complete or not). {{lex|example-random-id-qdY5}} may be contrasted with:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3s6c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3s6c}}
{{judri|c10e10d7}}
:'''mi pu mo'u citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [past] [completitive] eat my meal.</code>
:''I finished eating my meal.''

In {{lex|example-random-id-3s6c}}, the meal has reached its natural end; in {{lex|example-random-id-qdY5}}, the meal has merely ceased, without necessarily reaching its natural end.

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|resumptive}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|pausative}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|resumption}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|interruption}}  {{ind|general-imported|begin|contrasted with resume}}  {{ind|general-imported|resume|contrasted with begin}}  {{ind|general-imported|pause|contrasted with stop}}  {{ind|general-imported|stop|contrasted with pause}} A process such as eating a meal does not necessarily proceed uninterrupted. If it is interrupted, there are two more relevant point events: the point just before the interruption, marked by {{vla|de'a}}, and the point just after the interruption, marked by 
{{vla|di'a}}. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qdyD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qdyD}}
{{judri|c10e10d8}}
:'''mi pu de'a citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [past] [pausative] eat my meal.</code>
:''I stopped eating my meal (with the intention of resuming).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE08}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE08}}
{{judri|c10e10d9}}
:'''mi ba di'a citka le mi sanmi'''
:<code>I [future] [resumptive] eat my meal.</code>
:''I will resume eating my meal.''

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|superfective}}  {{ind|general-imported|natural end|continuing beyond}} In addition, it is possible for a process to continue beyond its natural end. The span of time between the natural and the actual end points is represented by 
{{vla|za'o}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jSQ4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jSQ4}}
{{judri|c10e10d10}}
{{ind|example|too long|example}}
{{ind|example|kept on too long|example}}
:'''le ctuca pu za'o ciksi le cmaci seldanfu le tadgri'''
:<code>The teacher [past] [superfective] explained the mathematics problem to the student-group.</code>
:''The teacher kept on explaining the mathematics problem to the class too long.''

That is, the teacher went on explaining after the class already understood the problem.

{{ind|general-imported|point|event considered as}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|achievative}} An entire event can be treated as a single moment using the cmavo {{vla|co'i}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-odH5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-odH5}}
{{judri|c10e10d11}}
:'''la djan. pu co'i catra la djim'''
:<code>John [past] [achievative] kills Jim.</code>
:''John was at the point in time where he killed Jim.''

{{ind|general-imported|cycles}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordinal tense}} Finally, since an activity is cyclical, an individual cycle can be referred to using a number followed by {{vla|re'u}}, which is the other cmavo of selma'o ROI:

{{dsp|example-random-id-msrS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-msrS}}
{{judri|c10e10d12}}
:'''mi pare'u klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [first time] go-to the store.</code>
:''I go to the store for the first time (within a vague interval).''

Note the difference between:

{{dsp|example-random-id-j3DQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-j3DQ}}
{{judri|c10e10d13}}
:'''mi pare'u paroi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [first time] [one time] go-to the store.</code>
:''For the first time, I go to the store once.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-IBns}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-IBns}}
{{judri|c10e10d14}}
:'''mi paroi pare'u klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [one time] [first time] go-to the store.</code>
:''There is one occasion on which I go to the store for the first time.''

{{ssp|section-fehe}}
==Space interval modifiers: FEhE==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''fe'e'''	FEhE	''space interval modifier flag''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|tense|order of spatial interval modifiers in }}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial interval modifiers|order in tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial intervals|expressing degree of continuity over}}  {{ind|general-imported|space intervals|compared with time intervals in continuity}} Like time intervals, space intervals can also be continuous, discontinuous, or repetitive. Rather than having a whole separate set of selma'o for space interval properties, we instead prefix the flag 
{{vla|fe'e}} to the cmavo used for time interval properties. A space interval property would be placed just after the space interval size and/or dimensionality cmavo:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qe09}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qe09}}
{{judri|c10e11d1}}
{{ind|example|sow grain|example}}
:'''ko vi'i fe'e di'i sombo le gurni'''
:<code>You-imperative [1-dimensional] [space:] [regularly] sow the grain.</code>
:''Sow the grain in a line and evenly!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qe1z}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qe1z}}
{{judri|c10e11d2}}
{{ind|example|salad ingredients|example}}
:'''mi fe'e ciroi tervecnu lo selsalta'''
:<code>I [space:] [three places] buy those-which-are salad-ingredients.</code>
:''I buy salad ingredients in three locations.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE1z}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE1z}}
{{judri|c10e11d3}}
{{ind|example|always and everywhere|example}}
:'''ze'e roroi ve'e fe'e roroi ku li re su'i re du li vo'''
:<code>[whole time] [all times] [whole space] [space:] [all places] The-number 2 + 2 = the-number 4.</code>
:''Always and everywhere, two plus two is four.''

As shown in {{lex|example-random-id-qE1z}}, when a tense comes first in a bridi, rather than in its normal position before the selbri (in this case {{vla|du}}), it is emphasized.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|ZAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial contours|expressing}} The {{vla|fe'e}} marker can also be used for the same purpose before members of ZAhO. (The cmavo {{vla|be'a}} belongs to selma'o FAhA; it is the space direction meaning “north of”.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-L4un}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-L4un}}
{{judri|c10e11d4}}
{{ind|example|rock face|example}}
{{ind|example|south face|example}}
:'''tu ve'abe'a fe'e co'a rokci'''
:<code>That-yonder [medium space interval - north] [space] [initiative] is-a-rock.</code>
:<code>That is the beginning of a rock extending to my north.</code>
:''That is the south face of a rock.''

{{ind|general-imported|event contours|temporal contrasted with spatial}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial contours|contrasted with temporal event contours}}  {{ind|general-imported|beginning point|spatial}} Here the notion of a “beginning point” represented by the cmavo {{vla|co'a}} is transferred from “beginning in time” to “beginning in space” under the influence of the {{vla|fe'e}} flag. Space is not inherently oriented, unlike time, which flows from past to future: therefore, some indication of orientation is necessary, and the {{jbo|ve'abe'a}} provides an orientation in which the south face is the “beginning” and the north face is the “end”, since the rock extends from south (near me) to north (away from me).

{{ind|general-imported|FAhA selma'o|use in specifying space/time mapping direction}}  {{ind|general-imported|space/time metaphor|expressing direction mapping for}}  {{ind|general-imported|space|as time-based metaphor}}  {{ind|general-imported|time|as space-based metaphor}} Many natural languages represent time by a space-based metaphor: in English, what is past is said to be “behind us”. In other languages, the metaphor is reversed. Here, Lojban is representing space (or space interval modifiers) by a time-based metaphor: the choice of a FAhA cmavo following a VEhA cmavo indicates which direction is mapped onto the future. (The choice of future rather than past is arbitrary, but convenient for English-speakers.)

{{ind|general-imported|fe'e|effect of TAhE/ROI with ZAhO on}}  {{ind|general-imported|ZAhO selma'o|effect on fe'e flag for TAhE and ROI}}  {{ind|general-imported|ROI selma'o|effect of ZAhO on fe'e flag}}  {{ind|general-imported|TAhE selma'o|effect of ZAhO on fe'e flag}} If both a TAhE (or ROI) and a ZAhO are present as space interval modifiers, the {{vla|fe'e}} flag must be prefixed to each.

{{ssp|section-tcita}}
==Tenses as sumti tcita==
{{ind|general-imported|argument tags|based on tenses (see also sumti tcita)}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|based on tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|temporal information|adding to a sentence with tense sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial information|adding to a sentence with tense sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|use as sumti tcita}} So far, we have seen tenses only just before the selbri, or (equivalently in meaning) floating about the bridi with {{vla|ku}}. There is another major use for tenses in Lojban: as sumti tcita, or argument tags. A tense may be used to add spatial or temporal information to a bridi as, in effect, an additional place:

{{dsp|example-random-id-v761}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-v761}}
{{judri|c10e12d1}}
:'''mi klama le zarci ca le nu do klama le zdani'''
:<code>I go-to the market [present] the event-of you go-to the house.</code>
:''I go to the market when you go to the house.''

{{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|based on tense direction}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense direction|as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|ca|meaning as a sumti tcita}} Here {{vla|ca}} does not appear before the selbri, nor with {{vla|ku}}; instead, it governs the following sumti, the 
:{{jbo|le nu}} construct. What {{lex|example-random-id-v761}} asserts is that the action of the main bridi is happening at the same time as the event mentioned by that sumti. So {{vla|ca}}, which means “now” when used with a selbri, means “simultaneously-with” when used with a sumti. Consider another example:

{{ind|general-imported|pu|meaning as a sumti tcita}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-4aPT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4aPT}}
{{judri|c10e12d2}}
:'''mi klama le zarci pu le nu do pu klama le zdani'''
:<code>I go-to the market [past] the event-of you [past] go-to the house.</code>

The second {{vla|pu}} is simply the past tense marker for the event of your going to the house, and says that this event is in the speaker's past. How are we to understand the first {{vla|pu}}, the sumti tcita?

{{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|starting at a different point}}  {{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|starting point}} All of our imaginary journeys so far have started at the speaker's location in space and time. Now we are specifying an imaginary journey that starts at a different location, namely at the event of your going to the house. {{lex|example-random-id-4aPT}} then says that my going to the market is in the past, relative not to the speaker's present moment, but instead relative to the moment when you went to the house. {{lex|example-random-id-4aPT}} can therefore be translated:

:''I had gone to the market before you went to the house.''
{{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|based on tense distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense distance|as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial tenses|as sumti tcita}} (Other translations are possible, depending on the ever-present context.) Spatial direction and distance sumti tcita are exactly analogous:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qe2C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qe2C}}
{{judri|c10e12d3}}
{{ind|example|rat eats cheese|example}}
{{ind|example|near the park|example}}
:'''le ratcu cu citka le cirla vi le panka'''
:<code>The rat eats the cheese [short distance] the park.</code>
:''The rat eats the cheese near the park.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE2t}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE2t}}
{{judri|c10e12d4}}
{{ind|example|rat eats cheese|example}}
{{ind|example|near the faraway park|example}}
:'''le ratcu cu citka le cirla vi le vu panka'''
:<code>The rat eats the cheese [short distance] the [long distance] park</code>
:''The rat eats the cheese near the faraway park.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qe3g}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qe3g}}
{{judri|c10e12d5}}
{{ind|example|rat eats cheese|example}}
{{ind|example|far away from the nearby park|example}}
:'''le ratcu cu citka le cirla vu le vi panka'''
:<code>The rat eats the cheese [long distance] the [short distance] park</code>
:''The rat eats the cheese far away from the nearby park.''

{{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on event contours|relation of main bridi to sumti process in}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|event contours contrasted with direction/distance as basis for}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense direction/distance as sumti tcita|contrasted with event contours}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours as sumti tcita|contrasted with direction and distance}}  {{ind|general-imported|ZAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|based on spatial contours}}  {{ind|general-imported|spatial contours|as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita|based on event contours}}  {{ind|general-imported|event contours|as sumti tcita}} The event contours of selma'o ZAhO (and their space equivalents, prefixed with 
{{vla|fe'e}}) are also useful as sumti tcita. The interpretation of ZAhO tcita differs from that of FAhA, VA, PU, and ZI tcita, however. The event described in the sumti is viewed as a process, and the action of the main bridi occurs at the phase of the process which the ZAhO specifies, or at least some part of that phase. The action of the main bridi itself is seen as a point event, so that there is no issue about which phase of the main bridi is intended. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Y2Kb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Y2Kb}}
{{judri|c10e12d6}}
{{ind|example|in the aftermath|example}}
{{ind|example|die after living|example}}
:'''mi morsi ba'o le nu mi jmive'''
:<code>I am-dead [perfective] the event-of I live.</code>
:''I die in the aftermath of my living.''

Here the (point-)event of my being dead is the portion of my living-process which occurs after the process is complete. Contrast {{lex|example-random-id-Y2Kb}} with:

{{dsp|example-random-id-18dT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-18dT}}
{{judri|c10e12d7}}
:'''mi morsi ba le nu mi jmive'''
:<code>I am-dead [future] the event-of I live.</code>

As explained in {{ls|section-vagueness}}, {{lex|example-random-id-18dT}} does not exclude the possibility that I died before I ceased to live!

Likewise, we might say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jJzr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jJzr}}
{{judri|c10e12d8}}
:'''mi klama le zarci pu'o le nu mi citka'''
:<code>I go-to the store [inchoative] the event-of I eat</code>

which indicates that before my eating begins, I go to the store, whereas

{{dsp|example-random-id-0VJp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0VJp}}
{{judri|c10e12d9}}
:'''mi klama le zarci ba'o le nu mi citka'''
:<code>I go-to the store [perfective] the event-of I eat</code>

would indicate that I go to the store after I am finished eating.

Here is an example which mixes temporal ZAhO (as a tense) and spatial ZAhO (as a sumti tcita):

{{dsp|example-random-id-PABV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PABV}}
{{judri|c10e12d10}}
{{ind|example|too long|example}}
{{ind|example|boat sailed|example}}
:'''le bloti pu za'o xelklama fe'e ba'o le lalxu'''
:<code>The boat [past] [superfective] is-a-transport-mechanism [space] [perfective] the lake.</code>
:''The boat sailed for too long and beyond the lake.''

Probably it sailed up onto the dock. One point of clarification: although {{vla|xelklama}} appears to mean simply “is-a-mode-of-transport”, it does not &ndash; the bridi of {{lex|example-random-id-PABV}} has four omitted arguments, and thus has the (physical) journey which goes on too long as part of its meaning.

{{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on quantified tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantified tenses|as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on interval properties}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval properties|meaning as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on interval continuousness}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval continuousness|meaning as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on dimension}}  {{ind|general-imported|dimension|meaning as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti tcita based on interval size}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval size|meaning as sumti tcita}} The remaining tense cmavo, which have to do with interval size, dimension, and continuousness (or lack thereof) are interpreted to let the sumti specify the particular interval over which the main bridi operates:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bLaQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bLaQ}}
{{judri|c10e12d11}}
{{ind|example|twice today|example}}
:'''mi klama le zarci reroi le ca djedi'''
:<code>I go-to the market [twice] the [present] day.</code>
:''I go/went/will go to the market twice today.''

{{ind|general-imported|tense inside sumti|contrasted with tense as sumti tcita}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense as sumti tcita|contrasted with tense inside sumti}} Be careful not to confuse a tense used as a sumti tcita with a tense used within a seltcita sumti:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sTxE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sTxE}}
{{judri|c10e12d12}}
{{ind|example|snow falls|example}}
:'''loi snime cu carvi ze'u le ca dunra'''
:<code>Some-of-the-mass-of snow rains [long time interval] the [present] winter.</code>
:''Snow falls during this winter.''

claims that the interval specified by “this winter” is long, as events of snowfall go, whereas

{{dsp|example-random-id-MXvK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MXvK}}
{{judri|c10e12d13}}
:'''loi snime cu carvi ca le ze'u dunra'''
:<code>Some-of-the-mass-of snow rains [present] the [long time] winter.</code>
:''Snow falls in the long winter.''

claims that during some part of the winter, which is long as winters go, snow falls.

{{ssp|section-sticky-tenses}}
==Sticky and multiple tenses: KI==

The following cmavo is discussed in this section:
<tab class=wikitable>
cmavo	selma'o	subclass	meaning
'''ki'''	KI	''sticky tense set/reset''
</tab>

{{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey origin|with sticky tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|sticky tenses|effect on future tense meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|sticky tenses|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|scope of}} So far we have only considered tenses in isolated bridi. Lojban provides several ways for a tense to continue in effect over more than a single bridi. This property is known as “stickiness”: the tense gets “stuck” and remains in effect until explicitly “unstuck”. In the metaphor of the imaginary journey, the place and time set by a sticky tense may be thought of as a campsite or way-station: it provides a permanent origin with respect to which other tenses are understood. Later imaginary journeys start from that point rather than from the speaker.

To make a tense sticky, suffix {{vla|ki}} to it:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rIuI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rIuI}}
{{judri|c10e13d1}}
:'''mi puki klama le zarci .i le nanmu cu batci le gerku'''
:<code>I [past] [sticky] go-to the market. The man bites the dog.</code>
:''I went to the market. The man bit the dog.''

Here the use of 
:{{jbo|puki}} rather than just {{vla|pu}} ensures that the tense will affect the next sentence as well. Otherwise, since the second sentence is tenseless, there would be no way of determining its tense; the event of the second sentence might happen before, after, or simultaneously with that of the first sentence.

(The last statement does not apply when the two sentences form part of a narrative. See {{ls|section-story-time}} for an explanation of “story time”, which employs a different set of conventions.)

What if the second sentence has a tense anyway?

{{ind|general-imported|tense|effect of sticky tense on}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-L9GA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-L9GA}}
{{judri|c10e13d2}}
:'''mi puki klama le zarci .i le nanmu pu batci le gerku'''
:<code>I [past] [sticky] go-to the market. The man [past] bites the dog.</code>

Here the second {{vla|pu}} does not replace the sticky tense, but adds to it, in the sense that the starting point of its imaginary journey is taken to be the previously set sticky time. So the translation of {{lex|example-random-id-L9GA}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-oJQz}}
{{judri|c10e13d3}}
{{ind|example|had earlier|example}}
I went to the market. The man had earlier bitten the dog.

{{ind|general-imported|compound tense|compared with tense in scope of sticky tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense in scope of sticky tense|compared with compound tense}} and it is equivalent in meaning (when considered in isolation from any other sentences) to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-N5xa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-N5xa}}
{{judri|c10e13d4}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci .i le nanmu pupu batci le gerku'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market. The man [past] [past] bites the dog.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|compound tense|compared with multiple tenses in sentence}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|multiple in sentence compared with compound tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|multiple in sentence}} The point has not been discussed so far, but it is perfectly grammatical to have more than one tense construct in a sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-t7YR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-t7YR}}
{{judri|c10e13d5}}
:'''puku mi ba klama le zarci'''
:<code>[past] I [future] go-to the market.</code>
:''Earlier, I was going to go to the market.''

Here there are two tenses in the same bridi, the first floating free and specified by 
:{{jbo|puku}}, the second in the usual place and specified by {{vla|ba}}. They are considered cumulative in the same way as the two tenses in separate sentences of {{lex|example-random-id-N5xa}}. {{lex|example-random-id-t7YR}} is therefore equivalent in meaning, except for emphasis, to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mRPV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mRPV}}
{{judri|c10e13d6}}
:'''mi puba klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past] [future] go-to the market.</code>
:''I was going to go to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|multiple tenses|effect of order in sentence}} Compare {{lex|example-random-id-qE4G}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qE4m}}, which have a different meaning from {{lex|example-random-id-t7YR}} and {{lex|example-random-id-mRPV}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE4G}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE4G}}
{{judri|c10e13d7}}
:'''mi ba klama le zarci puku'''
:<code>I [future] go-to the market [past].</code>
:''I will have gone to the market earlier.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE4m}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE4m}}
{{judri|c10e13d8}}
:'''mi bapu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [future] [past] go-to the market.</code>
:''I will have gone to the market.''

So when multiple tense constructs in a single bridi are involved, order counts &ndash; the tenses cannot be shifted around as freely as if there were only one tense to worry about.

{{ind|general-imported|sticky tenses|from part of a multiple tense}} But why bother to allow multiple tense constructs at all? They specify separate portions of the imaginary journey, and can be useful in order to make part of a tense sticky. Consider {{lex|example-random-id-gg9C}}, which adds a second bridi and a {{vla|ki}} to {{lex|example-random-id-t7YR}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gg9C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gg9C}}
{{judri|c10e13d9}}
:'''pukiku mi ba klama le zarci .i le nanmu cu batci le gerku'''
:<code>[past] [sticky] I [future] go-to the market. The man bites the dog.</code>

What is the implied tense of the second sentence? Not {{vla|puba}}, but only {{vla|pu}}, since only {{vla|pu}} was made sticky with {{vla|ki}}. So the translation is:

:''I was going to go to the market. The man bit the dog.''
{{ind|general-imported|sumti with tense|effect of main bridi tense on}}  {{ind|general-imported|embedded bridi tenses|effect of main bridi tense on}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense on main bridi|effect on embedded sumti with tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense on main bridi|effect on embedded bridi tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|on embedded bridi}} Lojban has several ways of embedding a bridi within another bridi: descriptions, abstractors, relative clauses. (Technically, descriptions contain selbri rather than bridi.) Any of the selbri of these subordinate bridi may have tenses attached. These tenses are interpreted relative to the tense of the main bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yxFP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yxFP}}
{{judri|c10e13d10}}
{{ind|example|former market|example}}
:'''mi pu klama le ba'o zarci'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the [perfective] market</code>
:''I went to the former market.''

The significance of the {{vla|ba'o}} in {{lex|example-random-id-yxFP}} is that the speaker's destination is described as being “in the aftermath of being a market”; that is, it is a market no longer. In particular, the time at which it was no longer a market is in the speaker's past, because the 
{{vla|ba'o}} is interpreted relative to the {{vla|pu}} tense of the main bridi.

Here is an example involving an abstraction bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NfS1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NfS1}}
{{judri|c10e13d11}}
:'''mi ca jinvi le du'u mi ba morsi'''
:<code>I now opine the fact-that I will-be dead.</code>
:''I now believe that I will be dead.''

Here the event of being dead is said to be in the future with respect to the opinion, which is in the present.

{{ind|general-imported|ki|with no tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|sticky tenses|canceling}} {{vla|ki}} may also be used as a tense by itself. This cancels all stickiness and returns the bridi and all following bridi to the speaker's location in both space and time.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|handling multiple episodes}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|subscripting}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|for sticky tense}} In complex descriptions, multiple tenses may be saved and then used by adding a subscript to 
{{vla|ki}}. A time made sticky with 
:{{jbo|kixipa}} (ki-sub-1) can be returned to by specifying 
:{{jbo|kixipa}} as a tense by itself. In the case of written expression, the writer's here-and-now is often different from the reader's, and a pair of subscripted {{vla|ki}} tenses could be used to distinguish the two.

{{ssp|section-story-time}}
==Story time==
{{ind|general-imported|stories|flow of time in}}  {{ind|general-imported|story time|rationale for}}  {{ind|general-imported|story time|definition}} Making strict use of the conventions explained in {{ls|section-sticky-tenses}} would be intolerably awkward when a story is being told. The time at which a story is told by the narrator is usually unimportant to the story. What matters is the flow of time within the story itself. The term “story” in this section refers to any series of statements related in more-or-less time-sequential order, not just a fictional one.

{{ind|general-imported|story time|tenseless sentences in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenseless sentences in story time}}  {{ind|general-imported|story time|as a convention for inferring tense}} Lojban speakers use a different set of conventions, commonly called “story time”, for inferring tense within a story. It is presumed that the event described by each sentence takes place some time more or less after the previous ones. Therefore, tenseless sentences are implicitly tensed as “what happens next”. In particular, any sticky time setting is advanced by each sentence.

The following mini-story illustrates the important features of story time. A sentence-by-sentence explication follows:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qE94}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qE94}}
{{judri|c10e14d1}}
{{ind|example|cave|example}}
:'''puzuki ku ne'iki le kevna le ninmu goi ko'a zutse le rokci'''
:<code>[past] [long] [sticky] [,] [inside] [sticky] the cave, the woman defined-as she-1 sat-on the rock</code>
:''Long ago, in a cave, a woman sat on a rock.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qEa4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qEa4}}
{{judri|c10e14d2}}
:'''.i ko'a citka loi kanba rectu'''
:<code>She-1 [tenseless] eat some-of-the-mass-of goat flesh.</code>
:''She was eating goat's meat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qEa7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qEa7}}
{{judri|c10e14d3}}
{{ind|example|flashbacks in story time|example}}
:'''.i ko'a pu jukpa ri le mudyfagri'''
:<code>She [past] cook the-last-mentioned by-method the wood-fire.</code>
:''She had cooked the meat over a wood fire.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qEao}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qEao}}
{{judri|c10e14d4}}
:'''.i lei rectu cu zanglare'''
:<code>The-mass-of flesh is-(favorable)-warm.</code>
:''The meat was pleasantly warm.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qebJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qebJ}}
{{judri|c10e14d5}}
:'''.i le labno goi ko'e bazaki nenri klama le kevna'''
:<code>The wolf defined-as it-2 [future] [medium] [sticky] within-came to-the cave.</code>
:''A while later, a wolf came into the cave.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qebT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qebT}}
{{judri|c10e14d6}}
:'''.i ko'e lebna lei rectu ko'a'''
:<code>It-2 [tenseless] takes the-mass-of flesh from-her-1.</code>
:''It took the meat from her.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qeBW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qeBW}}
{{judri|c10e14d7}}
:'''.i ko'e bartu klama'''
:<code>It-2 out ran</code>
:''It ran out.''

{{ind|general-imported|story tense|Lojban convention contrasted with English convention}} {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}} sets both the time (long ago) and the place (in a cave) using 
{{vla|ki}}, just like the sentence sequences in {{ls|section-sticky-tenses}}. No further space cmavo are used in the rest of the story, so the place is assumed to remain unchanged. The English translation of {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}} is marked for past tense also, as the conventions of English storytelling require: consequently, all other English translation sentences are also in the past tense. (We don't notice how strange this is; even stories about the future are written in past tense!) This conventional use of past tense is not used in Lojban narratives.{{lex|example-random-id-qEa4}} is tenseless. Outside story time, it would be assumed that its event happens simultaneously with that of {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}}, since a sticky tense is in effect; the rules of story time, however, imply that the event occurs afterwards, and that the story time has advanced (changing the sticky time set in {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}}).{{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}} has an explicit tense. This is taken relative to the latest setting of the sticky time; therefore, the event of {{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}} happens before that of {{lex|example-random-id-qEa4}}. It cannot be determined if {{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}} happens before or after {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}}.{{lex|example-random-id-qEao}} is again tenseless. Story time was not changed by the flashback in {{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}}, so {{lex|example-random-id-qEao}} happens after {{lex|example-random-id-qEa4}}.{{lex|example-random-id-qebJ}} specifies the future (relative to {{lex|example-random-id-qEao}}) and makes it sticky. So all further events happen after {{lex|example-random-id-qebJ}}.{{lex|example-random-id-qebT}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qeBW}} are again tenseless, and so happen after {{lex|example-random-id-qebJ}}. (Story time is changed.)

So the overall order is {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}} - {{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}} - {{lex|example-random-id-qEa4}} - {{lex|example-random-id-qEao}} - (medium interval) - {{lex|example-random-id-qebJ}} - {{lex|example-random-id-qebT}} - {{lex|example-random-id-qeBW}}. It is also possible that {{lex|example-random-id-qEa7}} happens before {{lex|example-random-id-qE94}}.

<!-- So the overall order is 14.1 - 14.3 - 14.2 - 14.4 - (medium interval) - 14.5 - 14.6 - 14.7. It is also possible that 14.3 happens before 14.1.</para> -->
{{ind|general-imported|story time|with no initial sticky time}} If no sticky time (or space) is set initially, the story is set at an unspecified time (or space): the effect is like that of choosing an arbitrary reference point and making it sticky. This style is common in stories that are jokes. The same convention may be used if the context specifies the sticky time sufficiently.

{{ssp|section-sub-bridi-tenses}}
==Tenses in subordinate bridi==
{{ind|general-imported|subordinate clauses|tense usage rules in English}} English has a set of rules, formally known as “sequence of tense rules”, for determining what tense should be used in a subordinate clause, depending on the tense used in the main sentence. Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qECX}}
{{judri|c10e15d1}}
John says that George is going to the market.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qeds}}
{{judri|c10e15d2}}
John says that George went to the market.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qEE5}}
{{judri|c10e15d3}}
John said that George went to the market.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qeFQ}}
{{judri|c10e15d4}}
John said that George had gone to the market.

In {{lex|example-random-id-qECX}} and {{lex|example-random-id-qeds}}, the tense of the main sentence is the present: “says”. If George goes when John speaks, we get the present tense “is going” ( “goes” would be unidiomatic); if George goes before John speaks, we get the past tense “went”. But if the tense of the main sentence is the past, with “said”, then the tense required in the subordinate clause is different. If George goes when John speaks, we get the past tense “went”; if George goes before John speaks, we get the past-perfect tense “had gone”.

The rule of English, therefore, is that both the tense of the main sentence and the tense of the subordinate clause are understood relative to the speaker of the main sentence (not John, but the person who speaks {{lex|example-random-id-qECX}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qeFQ}}).

{{ind|general-imported|subordinate clause tense|effect of main bridi tense on}}  {{ind|general-imported|subordinate clause tense|Lojban compared with Esperanto}}  {{ind|general-imported|subordinate clause tense|Lojban compared with Russian}}  {{ind|general-imported|subordinate clause tense|Lojban contrasted with English}}  {{ind|general-imported|sequence of tense rules|Lojban contrasted with English}} Lojban, like Russian and Esperanto, uses a different convention. A tense in a subordinate bridi is understood to be relative to the tense already set in the main bridi. Thus {{lex|example-random-id-qECX}} through {{lex|example-random-id-qeFQ}} can be expressed in Lojban respectively thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qega}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qega}}
{{judri|c10e15d5}}
{{ind|example|John says that George goes to market|example}}
:'''la djan. ca cusku le se du'u la djordj. ca klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [present] says the statement-that George [present] goes-to the market.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qeGL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qeGL}}
{{judri|c10e15d6}}
:'''la djan. ca cusku le se du'u la djordj. pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [present] says the statement-that George [past] goes-to the market.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qEGL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qEGL}}
{{judri|c10e15d7}}
:'''la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la djordj. ca klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [past] says the statement-that George [present] goes-to the market.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qegV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qegV}}
{{judri|c10e15d8}}
:'''la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la djordj. pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [past] says the statement-that George [past] goes-to the market.</code>

Probably the most counterintuitive of the Lojban examples is {{lex|example-random-id-qEGL}}. The {{vla|ca}} looks quite odd, as if George were going to the market right now, rather than back when John spoke. But this {{vla|ca}} is really a {{vla|ca}} with respect to a reference point specified by the outer {{vla|pu}}. This behavior is the same as the additive behavior of multiple tenses in the same bridi, as explained in 
{{ls|section-sticky-tenses}}.

{{ind|general-imported|nau|syntax}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|overriding to speaker's current}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|speaker's current}} There is a special cmavo {{vla|nau}} (of selma'o CUhE) which can be used to override these rules and get to the speaker's current reference point. (Yes, it sounds like English “now”.) It is not grammatical to combine {{vla|nau}} with any other cmavo in a tense, except by way of a logical or non-logical connection (see 
{{ls|section-connected-tenses}}). Here is a convoluted sentence with several nested bridi which uses {{vla|nau}} at the lowest level:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Yjop}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Yjop}}
{{judri|c10e15d9}}
:'''la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la .alis pu cusku le se du'u la djordj. pu cusku le se du'u la maris. nau klama le zarci'''
:<code>John [past] says the statement-that Alice [past] says the statement-that George [past] says the statement that Mary [now] goes-to the market.</code>
:''John said that Alice had said that George had earlier said that Mary is now going to the market.''

{{ind|general-imported|sticky tenses|effect of nau on}}  {{ind|general-imported|nau|effect on sticky tenses}} The use of {{vla|nau}} does not affect sticky tenses.

{{ssp|section-tense-connection}}
==Tense relations between sentences==
{{ind|general-imported|tense with sumti tcita|asymmetry of}} The sumti tcita method, explained in {{ls|section-tcita}}, of asserting a tense relationship between two events suffers from asymmetry. Specifically,

{{dsp|example-random-id-vreo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-vreo}}
{{judri|c10e16d1}}
:'''le verba cu cadzu le bisli zu'a le nu le nanmu cu batci le gerku'''
:<code>The child walks-on the ice [left] the event-of the man bites the dog.</code>
:''The child walks on the ice to the left of where the man bites the dog.''

{{ind|general-imported|sentences|connecting with tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|connecting sentences in with}} which specifies an imaginary journey leftward from the man biting the dog to the child walking on the ice, claims only that the child walks on the ice. By the nature of 
:{{jbo|le nu}}, the man's biting the dog is merely referred to without being claimed. If it seems desirable to claim both, each event can be expressed as a main sentence bridi, with a special form of {{vla|i}} connecting them:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9Q0x}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9Q0x}}
{{judri|c10e16d2}}
:'''le nanmu cu batci le gerku .izu'abo le verba cu cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The man bites the dog. [Left] the child walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The man bites the dog. To the left, the child walks on the ice.''

:{{jbo|.izu'abo}} is a compound cmavo: the {{vla|i}} separates the sentences and the {{vla|zu'a}} is the tense. The {{vla|bo}} is required to prevent the {{vla|zu'a}} from gobbling up the following sumti, namely 
:{{jbo|le verba}}.

{{ind|general-imported|tense|sumti tcita form contrasted with connected sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense connection of sentences|contrasted with sumti tcita form}}  {{ind|general-imported|imaginary journey|origin of in tense-connected sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense connection of sentences|order of}} Note that the bridi in {{lex|example-random-id-9Q0x}} appear in the reverse order from their appearance in {{lex|example-random-id-vreo}}. With 
:{{jbo|.izu'abo}} (and all other afterthought tense connectives) the sentence specifying the origin of the journey comes first. This is a natural order for sentences, but requires some care when converting between this form and the sumti tcita form.{{lex|example-random-id-9Q0x}} means the same thing as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ne2C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ne2C}}
{{judri|c10e16d3}}
:'''le nanmu cu batci le gerku .i zu'a la'edi'u le verba cu cadzu le bisli'''
:<code>The man bites the dog. [Left] the-referent-of-the-last-sentence the child walks-on the ice.</code>
:''The man bites the dog. Left of what I just mentioned, the child walks on the ice.''

{{ind|general-imported|tense connected sentences|importance of bo in}} If the {{vla|bo}} is omitted in {{lex|example-random-id-9Q0x}}, the meaning changes:
